answer: The inheritance chain matters in `Config.from_object` in `src/flask/config.py`. When `from_object` gets a class (or an import string resolved by `werkzeug.utils.import_string`), it loops over `dir(obj)` and copies every uppercase name using `getattr(obj, key)`. `dir()` includes attributes inherited from base classes, and `getattr` follows the class MRO. So a child config class gets every uppercase setting from its parents, and any value it redefines overrides the parent's. Nothing is merged explicitly; it relies entirely on Python attribute lookup. Lowercase attributes are skipped. `@property` values only work if the class is instantiated first, as the docstring warns.

`CertParamType.convert` in `src/flask/cli.py` first imports `ssl` and raises `click.BadParameter` if Python lacks SSL support. It then tries `self.path_type`, a `click.Path` requiring an existing, non-directory, resolved file. If that raises `BadParameter`, it lowercases the value with `click.STRING`. If the value is "adhoc", it checks that `cryptography` is importable (otherwise `BadParameter`) and returns "adhoc". Otherwise it calls `import_string(value, silent=True)` and returns the object if it is an `ssl.SSLContext`. If none of these match, the bare `raise` re-raises the original path error. `_validate_key` later checks that `--key` is consistent with the result and pairs file certificates with their key.

The test (`test_dotted_name_not_allowed` in `tests/test_blueprints.py`) checks the guard in `Blueprint.__init__` in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, which raises `ValueError("'name' may not contain a dot '.' character.")`. Flask uses dots as the separator for nesting and endpoint namespacing. `Blueprint.register` builds names as "prefix.name", `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule` builds endpoints as "name_prefix.name.endpoint", and `Request.blueprint` / `_split_blueprint_path` in `helpers.py` split endpoints on dots. A dotted blueprint name would make nesting, `url_for`, and handler scoping ambiguous. `Blueprint.add_url_rule` likewise rejects dotted endpoints and view function names.

In `src/flask/json/tag.py`, `TagTuple.to_json` calls `self.serializer.tag(item)` for each element. `TaggedJSONSerializer.tag` walks `self.order`, calls each tag's `check`, and dispatches to `JSONTag.tag`, which calls `to_json` again. Containers re-enter the same loop: `PassList.to_json`, `PassDict.to_json`, `TagDict.to_json`, and `TagTuple.to_json` all call `serializer.tag` recursively. Nothing tracks objects already visited. A cycle, such as a tuple containing a list that contains the tuple, therefore recurses until `RecursionError`. This is triggered from `TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps`, used by `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session` in `sessions.py`.

It is the `TestUrlFor` class in `tests/test_helpers.py`. It contains tests such as `test_url_for_with_anchor`, `test_url_for_with_scheme`, `test_url_for_with_scheme_not_external`, and `test_url_for_with_alternating_schemes`, plus method-based routing tests. These exercise `Flask.url_for` in `src/flask/app.py`, including the `_anchor` quoting, the `_scheme` / `_external` check, and `_method` passed to `MapAdapter.build`. The `flask.url_for` wrapper in `src/flask/helpers.py` is also covered.

`SecureCookieSession.__getitem__`, `get`, and `setdefault` in `src/flask/sessions.py` set `accessed = True` on every read. Writes go through the `CallbackDict` `on_update` hook, which sets `modified`. In `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session`, `accessed` only adds a `Vary: Cookie` header. The expensive signing step (`get_signing_serializer(...).dumps(dict(session))` with `TaggedJSONSerializer`) runs only when `should_set_cookie` returns true, meaning the session was modified or is permanent with `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST`. So frequent reads cost only a cheap attribute assignment and do not cause re-signing. The real impact is the `Vary` header, which reduces downstream cache hits.

`Flask.handle_exception` in `src/flask/app.py`, called from `wsgi_app`, first captures `sys.exc_info()` and sends the `got_request_exception` signal. It reads `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS`; if that is None, propagation follows `self.testing or self.debug`. If propagating, it re-raises with a bare `raise` when the active exception is `e`, otherwise `raise e`. If not, it calls `log_exception`, wraps the error in `InternalServerError(original_exception=e)`, and looks up a handler with `_find_error_handler` from `sansio/app.py`. Any handler found is called through `ensure_sync`. The result goes to `finalize_request(..., from_error_handler=True)`, which logs and ignores failures during response processing.

`Scaffold` in `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py` holds the shared static configuration: `static_folder`, `static_url_path`, and `has_static_folder`. The sans-IO `App` and `Blueprint` build on it, and IO-specific behaviour lives in `Flask` (`src/flask/app.py`) and `Blueprint` (`src/flask/blueprints.py`). Both define identical `get_send_file_max_age` methods, which read `current_app.config["SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT"]`, and identical `send_static_file` methods, which call `helpers.send_from_directory` with that `max_age`. Caching therefore always follows app config. `Flask.__init__` registers the "static" route through a weakref lambda. `sansio` `Blueprint.register` adds the blueprint's static rule through `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule`. `_prepare_send_file_kwargs` fills in the remaining defaults.

The inheritance chain matters in Config.from_object in src/flask/config.py. If given a string, it first resolves the object with werkzeug's import_string. It then loops over dir(obj) and copies every uppercase name using getattr(obj, key). dir() returns attributes inherited from base classes, and getattr follows Python's method resolution order. So uppercase settings defined on a parent class are loaded too, and a child class's value for the same name overrides the parent's. Only uppercase attributes become Config keys. Instances are resolved the same way, so properties can supply computed values. No extra merging logic exists; class inheritance alone decides the result.

CertParamType.convert in src/flask/cli.py first checks that the ssl module is importable, raising BadParameter otherwise. It then tries self.path_type, a click.Path(exists=True, dir_okay=False, resolve_path=True), and returns the path if the file exists. On BadParameter it normalizes the value with click.STRING and lowercases it. If the value is "adhoc", it checks that cryptography is installed and returns "adhoc". Otherwise it calls import_string(value, silent=True) and returns the object if it is an ssl.SSLContext; if not, it re-raises. The companion _validate_key callback then checks that --key is used only with a file certificate and is not combined with adhoc or an SSLContext.

test_dotted_names_not_allowed in tests/test_blueprints.py checks that sansio Blueprint.__init__ in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py raises ValueError when "." is in the name. Dots are reserved as the nesting separator in endpoint names, for example "parent.child.view". These names are built by Blueprint.register and add_url_rule and parsed by helpers._split_blueprint_path, Request.blueprints and App._find_error_handler. A dotted blueprint name would make endpoint and blueprint lookups ambiguous, so the error is raised at construction time. A related check rejects empty names.

In src/flask/json/tag.py, TagTuple.to_json returns [self.serializer.tag(item) for item in value]. TaggedJSONSerializer.tag loops over self.order and calls check on each tag. For a match it calls JSONTag.tag, which returns {key: self.to_json(value)}, and that calls back into TagTuple.to_json, or into PassList.to_json or TagDict.to_json for nested lists and dicts. The full path is TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps → tag → JSONTag.tag → to_json → serializer.tag, and so on. There is no visited-set or depth guard. A tuple that contains a mutable list or dict holding the same tuple therefore recurses until Python raises RecursionError. Session saving through SecureCookieSessionInterface reaches this path via its signing serializer.

It is class TestUrlFor in tests/test_helpers.py. Its tests include test_url_for_with_anchor, test_url_for_with_scheme, test_url_for_with_scheme_not_external, test_url_for_with_alternating_schemes and test_url_with_method. They exercise flask.url_for in src/flask/helpers.py, which delegates to Flask.url_for in src/flask/app.py.

SecureCookieSession.__getitem__, get and setdefault in src/flask/sessions.py set self.accessed = True on every read. The assignment itself is cheap and does not serialize anything. Its effect shows up in SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session: an accessed session adds "Vary: Cookie", which reduces caching. Whether the cookie string is re-signed is decided by SessionInterface.should_set_cookie, which checks session.modified or permanent plus SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST. When that is true, get_signing_serializer (URLSafeTimedSerializer with TaggedJSONSerializer and _lazy_sha1) dumps the whole session again. So read-heavy traffic mainly costs cache headers, not extra serialization unless refresh is enabled.

Flask.handle_exception in src/flask/app.py first sends the got_request_exception signal. It then reads self.config["PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS"]; if that is None, it falls back to self.testing or self.debug. If propagation is on, it re-raises the original exception, using a bare raise when it is the active exception. Otherwise it calls self.log_exception and wraps the error in InternalServerError(original_exception=e). It looks up a 500 handler with self._find_error_handler(server_error, request.blueprints) from sansio/app.py and runs it through ensure_sync if one exists. Finally it returns self.finalize_request(server_error, from_error_handler=True). wsgi_app reaches this via full_dispatch_request and handle_user_exception.

Flask in src/flask/app.py and Blueprint in src/flask/blueprints.py both build on sansio Scaffold, which holds the static_folder and static_url_path properties and has_static_folder. Flask.__init__ registers a "/<path:filename>" static rule bound to send_static_file. Sansio Blueprint.register in sansio/blueprints.py adds the blueprint's own static rule, using endpoint "static", through BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule. Both classes implement get_send_file_max_age the same way. It reads current_app.config["SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT"], converts timedeltas to seconds, and returns None by default. Both send_static_file methods pass that value to helpers.send_from_directory, so caching stays consistent while blueprint static serving stays decoupled until registration.

In src/flask/config.py, Config.from_object resolves configuration through inheritance. If it is given a string, it first imports the object with werkzeug's import_string. It then loops over dir(obj), keeps only the uppercase names, and sets self[key] = getattr(obj, key). Because dir() includes attributes inherited through the class MRO, a child configuration class picks up all of its parent's uppercase settings. getattr returns the most-derived value, so a child's override replaces the parent's default. Only class attributes count; @property values need an instance. The values are written into the Config dict as they are found, so later from_object or from_mapping calls can overwrite them.

It copies every uppercase attribute into the config with `getattr`. So uppercase settings defined only on a parent class are inherited. Values redefined on the child class shadow the parent's through normal attribute lookup. Because `getattr` returns the most-derived value, the child's setting wins. `tests/test_config.py` (`test_config_from_class`) checks this by defining a `Base` class with a `TEST_KEY` and a subclass adding `SECRET_KEY`, then asserting both are loaded.

`CertParamType.convert` in `src/flask/cli.py` tries three things in order. First it delegates to a `click.Path(exists=True, dir_okay=False, resolve_path=True)` converter, so an existing file path is returned as-is. Otherwise it calls `werkzeug.utils.import_string(value, silent=True)`. If the result is an `ssl.SSLContext`, that object is returned. If none of these match, the original `BadParameter` is re-raised. `_validate_key` then checks the `--key` combination.

`test_dotted_name_not_allowed` in `tests/test_blueprints.py` asserts that `flask.Blueprint("app.ui", __name__)` raises `ValueError`. The check is in `Blueprint.__init__` in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, which raises if `"."` is in the name. Flask uses dots as the separator between blueprint names and endpoint names, for example `"parent.child.index"`. Several places split on that dot: `Blueprint.add_url_rule` (which also rejects dotted endpoints), nested blueprint registration (`Blueprint.register` building `name_prefix`), `request.blueprints`, and `url_for` resolving relative `.endpoint` names. A dotted blueprint name would make endpoint and blueprint lookup ambiguous, so the test enforces this rule early.

In `src/flask/json/tag.py`, `TagTuple.to_json` returns `[self.serializer.tag(item) for item in value]`. `TaggedJSONSerializer.tag` loops over `self.order` and calls each tag's `check`. The matching tag's `JSONTag.tag` then calls `to_json` again. Nested items therefore recurse through `TagTuple`, `PassList` and `TagDict` (`PassDict` similarly). A tuple can only become circular through a mutable container, such as a tuple holding a list that contains the tuple. That cycle alternates `TagTuple.to_json`, `serializer.tag`, `PassList.to_json` and back to `serializer.tag` indefinitely. Nothing tracks visited objects, so this ends in `RecursionError`.

It includes `test_url_for_with_anchor`, `test_url_for_with_scheme`, `test_url_for_with_scheme_not_external`, `test_url_for_with_alternating_schemes` and `test_url_with_method`. In `src/flask/sessions.py`, `SecureCookieSession.__getitem__`, `get` and `setdefault` set `self.accessed = True` on every read. Setting a boolean is cheap, and it does not by itself trigger cookie serialization. `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session` only uses `accessed` to add `Vary: Cookie`. It calls `get_signing_serializer(app).dumps(dict(session))` only when `should_set_cookie` is true. That means the session was `modified`, or it is permanent with `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST` enabled. So frequent reads cost little: the signing and `TaggedJSONSerializer` serialization cost depends on modifications and refresh settings, not on reads.

`Flask.handle_exception` in `src/flask/app.py` first sends the `got_request_exception` signal. It then reads `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` from `self.config`. If that is `None`, it falls back to `self.testing or self.debug`. When propagation is on, it re-raises the original exception, preserving the traceback if it is the current one. Otherwise it calls `log_exception`, wraps the error in `werkzeug.exceptions.InternalServerError(original_exception=e)`, and looks up a 500 handler via `_find_error_handler(server_error, request.blueprints)`. It runs that handler through `ensure_sync`, then returns `finalize_request(server_error, from_error_handler=True)`. `wsgi_app` calls it when `full_dispatch_request` raises.

Both `Flask` (`src/flask/app.py`) and `Blueprint` (`src/flask/blueprints.py`) inherit static-folder handling from `Scaffold` in `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py`. That provides `static_folder`, `static_url_path` and `has_static_folder`. The app registers its `/static/<path:filename>` rule in `Flask.__init__`. A blueprint registers its static rule in `Blueprint.register` (in `sansio/blueprints.py`) through `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule`, using deferred functions recorded with `record`. Both rules point to their own `send_static_file`. Each calls `send_from_directory` with `max_age=self.get_send_file_max_age(filename)`. That reads `current_app.config["SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT"]`, so caching behaves the same for both.

In testing/conftest.py, the mock_timing fixture builds a MockTiming dataclass. Its patch(monkeypatch) imports _pytest.timing and calls monkeypatch.setattr three times: timing.sleep becomes self.sleep, timing.time becomes self.time, and timing.perf_counter also becomes self.time. These attribute swaps on the _pytest.timing module are the interception points; production code calls timing.time() and similar at call time, so it sees the fakes. The calls are independent and run in order. MonkeyPatch records each original value in its _setattr list and restores them in reverse order in undo() at fixture teardown. The only shared side effect is the single _current_time field: sleep advances it, while time and perf_counter both read it, giving one deterministic clock.

Decorate test_1 with @pytest.mark.parametrize("arg,expected", [...]) and give each argument a default value. That keeps the function callable on its own, and test_1 still exists as a test, though node IDs become test_1[id]. Use ids= or pytest.param(..., id=...) for stable, readable IDs. You can attach marks per case, such as xfail or skip. Alternatives are a parametrized fixture (@pytest.fixture(params=...) read through request.param) or a pytest_generate_tests hook in conftest.py that calls metafunc.parametrize from external data. Python.py's Metafunc handles the expansion. Test selection by the bare name test_1 with -k still matches every case.

In src/_pytest/main.py, _bestrelpath_cache is a dataclass that subclasses dict[Path, str]. It stores a root path and overrides __missing__, which calls bestrelpath(self.path, path), stores the result and returns it. Session keeps one instance as _bestrelpathcache, which _node_location_to_relpath uses. Reporting asks for node locations very often, and bestrelpath (from _pytest.pathlib) does real path computation. Using dict's __missing__ hook gives lazy compute-on-first-access with plain C-speed dict lookups afterwards. It needs no extra wrapper logic and no explicit "if key in cache" branch, and it stays a normal mapping with a minimal footprint.

In src/_pytest/compat.py, NotSetType is an enum.Enum with a single member, token. The constant NOTSET: Final = NotSetType.token is exported. It is a typed sentinel meaning "argument not provided", kept distinct from None, which can be a legitimate user value. Because it is a one-member enum, type checkers can narrow "x is NOTSET" through Literal and Final semantics. Signatures can be annotated as T | NotSetType without leaking an object() placeholder. Internals such as Parser.addini defaults, Config.getini handling and fixture/param plumbing can tell "unset" apart from explicit values. Public APIs keep their documented defaults, while the internal representation stays private and type-safe.

The logic is in ReprFuncArgs.toterminal(tw) in src/_pytest/_code/code.py. It loops over self.args (name, value pairs) and builds ns = f"{name} = {value}". If len(ns) + len(linesofar) + 2 > tw.fullwidth, it flushes the current linesofar with tw.line() and starts a new line with ns. Otherwise it appends ", " + ns, or sets linesofar to ns if the line is empty. After the loop it emits any leftover linesofar and a trailing blank line. The terminal width comes from TerminalWriter.fullwidth in _pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py.

In src/_pytest/_py/path.py, Visitor.__init__ wraps the fil and rec arguments in FNMatcher only when they are strings. This happens once per LocalPath.visit() call, not per directory or entry, so memory cost is negligible because FNMatcher holds only a pattern string. The traversal cost actually comes from Visitor.gen, which calls the matchers for every entry. FNMatcher.__call__ checks path separators and may prefix the pattern with "*" + sep, then calls fnmatch.fnmatch. That cost is paid per entry, partly offset by fnmatch's internal compiled-pattern cache. Repeated cost only appears if callers invoke visit() many times, for example nested, which rebuilds Visitors.

import_path in src/_pytest/pathlib.py dispatches on ImportMode. With prepend or append, resolve_pkg_root_and_module_name and resolve_package_path walk up the __init__.py packages to get a dotted name and root. That root is inserted at the front or end of sys.path, then importlib.import_module runs and the result is read from sys.modules. That makes sys.modules, keyed by module name, the cache. A mismatch check compares mod.__file__ to the path with _is_same (samefile), raising ImportPathMismatchError unless PY_IGNORE_IMPORTMISMATCH is set. With importlib mode, the canonical name is tried first. Otherwise module_name_from_path derives a unique name relative to root; an existing sys.modules entry is reused, else _import_module_using_spec loads it and insert_missing_modules fills in parents.

In src/_pytest/fixtures.py, FixtureFunctionMarker.__call__ first rejects classes with ValueError. Next, if the function is already a FixtureFunctionDefinition, the wrapper that a prior @pytest.fixture returned, it raises ValueError saying "@pytest.fixture is being applied more than once to the same function". If the function has a pytestmark attribute, it only issues the MARKED_FIXTURE warning from _pytest/deprecated.py, because marks on fixtures have no effect. It then builds FixtureFunctionDefinition(function=..., fixture_function_marker=self) and fails if the name is "request". Semantically, the isinstance check catches true double fixture registration, a hard error. The pytestmark check catches mark decorators misapplied to fixtures, a deprecated but tolerated misuse.

`MockTiming.patch` in `src/_pytest/timing.py` imports `_pytest.timing` itself and makes three `monkeypatch.setattr` calls on that module. Those calls replace `timing.sleep` with `self.sleep`, `timing.time` with `self.time`, and `timing.perf_counter` with `self.time`. Each `MonkeyPatch.setattr` (in `src/_pytest/monkeypatch.py`) saves the original attribute in its `_setattr` list. `MonkeyPatch.undo` later restores them in reverse order. The three calls are independent, so their order has no observable effect. The only shared state is the dataclass's `_current_time` float: `sleep` advances it, and `time` and `perf_counter` both read it. This means `Instant`/`Duration` see one deterministic, consistent clock. Nothing in the real `time` module is touched.

Keep the name `test_1` and decorate it with `@pytest.mark.parametrize("arg,expected", [...])`. Put the original scenario first, optionally as `pytest.param(..., id="default")`, so the old case still runs. The decorator is `_ParametrizeMarkDecorator`, with `ParameterSet` and `ParameterSet._for_parametrize` in `src/_pytest/mark/structures.py`. In `src/_pytest/python.py`, `pytest_generate_tests` calls `Metafunc.parametrize`, which builds a `CallSpec2` per case. `IdMaker` generates ids, and `PyCollector._genfunctions` creates one `Function` per case. One compatibility caveat: node ids change from `test_1` to `test_1[...]`, which affects `-k` expressions, caches and CI selectors. You can also put data in fixtures with `params=` (`FixtureFunctionMarker`) to keep the test signature unchanged.

`_bestrelpath_cache` in `src/_pytest/main.py` subclasses `dict[Path, str]` and stores a base `path`. Its `__missing__` computes `bestrelpath(self.path, path)` from `src/_pytest/pathlib.py`, stores the result under that key and returns it. So a normal `cache[node_path]` lookup computes the value on first access and then serves it from the dict. `Session._node_location_to_relpath` uses it while building `Item.location` and report locations for every test. Many items share the same file, so caching avoids repeated, relatively costly path computations. Using the dict protocol needs no explicit "check-then-compute" code at call sites and keeps lookups at C-level dict speed.

In `src/_pytest/compat.py`, `NotSetType` is an `enum.Enum` with a single member `token`, exported as `NOTSET: Final = NotSetType.token`. It is a typed sentinel meaning "argument not provided", which is distinct from `None`, a legitimate value. Because it is a one-member enum, type checkers can narrow `X | NotSetType` with `is NOTSET` checks, which a plain `object()` cannot do. Internal defaults use it without exposing it as a meaningful public value: `Function.__init__(callobj=NOTSET)` in `python.py`, `FixtureManager.parsefactories(nodeid=NOTSET)` in `fixtures.py`, and `Pytester.popen`/`run(stdin=CLOSE_STDIN)` in `pytester.py`. Similar but separate sentinels are `Notset` in `config/__init__.py` and `monkeypatch.py`, and `NotSet` in `argparsing.py`.

The logic is in `ReprFuncArgs.toterminal(tw)` in `src/_pytest/_code/code.py`. It loops over `self.args` (name, value) pairs and formats each as `"name = value"`. If adding that string plus 2 separator characters to the accumulated line would exceed `tw.fullwidth`, it flushes the current line with `tw.line` and starts a new one. Otherwise it appends with `", "`. It writes any remainder at the end, then a blank line. The arguments come from `FormattedExcinfo.repr_args`, which renders values with `saferepr` when `funcargs=True`. `TerminalWriter.fullwidth` in `src/_pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py` comes from `get_terminal_width()` unless it has been overridden.

The premise is mostly mistaken. In `src/_pytest/_py/path.py`, `Visitor.__init__` creates an `FNMatcher` only once per `visit()` call, and only when `fil` or `rec` is a string. It is not created per directory or per entry. `FNMatcher` just stores the pattern string, so memory cost is negligible. The real per-entry costs are in `Visitor.gen`, the recursive generator. It calls `LocalPath.listdir`, calls `check(dir=1)` (a `stat`) on each entry, and calls `FNMatcher.__call__` for each one. That call redoes pattern normalization (`os.sep` handling, prefixing `*`) and calls `fnmatch.fnmatch`, which caches compiled regexes. Deep trees mostly add generator-recursion overhead and syscalls, not matcher allocations.

`import_path` in `src/_pytest/pathlib.py` depends on `ImportMode`. In `prepend`/`append` mode, `resolve_pkg_root_and_module_name` derives the package root and dotted name. It inserts the root into `sys.path`, calls `importlib.import_module`, and takes the module from `sys.modules`. It then compares `mod.__file__` with the path via `_is_same` and raises `ImportPathMismatchError` on mismatch, unless `PY_IGNORE_IMPORTMISMATCH` is set. In `importlib` mode, it first returns `sys.modules[module_name_from_path(...)]` if present. Otherwise it tries `_import_module_using_spec`, checked by `spec_matches_module_path`, and falls back to `insert_missing_modules`. Identity is keyed by module name, so one file reached under different names can produce duplicate module objects or a mismatch error.

In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, `FixtureFunctionMarker.__call__` first rejects classes with `ValueError`. It then checks `isinstance(function, FixtureFunctionDefinition)` and raises `ValueError` ("@pytest.fixture is being applied more than once to the same function"). Next, if `hasattr(function, "pytestmark")`, it issues the `MARKED_FIXTURE` deprecation warning (`PytestRemovedIn9Warning`, from `deprecated.py`) and continues. It then wraps the function in `FixtureFunctionDefinition` and fails if the name is `request`. The difference: a `FixtureFunctionDefinition` instance proves the object is already a fixture, so applying it twice is a hard error. `pytestmark` only means marks were applied below the decorator; this is legal but has no effect, so it only warns. `store_mark` in `mark/structures.py` handles marks applied above `@fixture`.

ConnectionError is defined in requests/exceptions.py as a subclass of RequestException, which itself extends IOError. It gives callers one type for "could not reach or talk to the server", separate from HTTPError (bad status) and InvalidURL/MissingSchema (bad input). HTTPAdapter.send in requests/adapters.py does the translation from urllib3. ProtocolError and OSError become ConnectionError. MaxRetryError becomes ConnectTimeout, RetryError, ProxyError, SSLError or plain ConnectionError, depending on its reason. ClosedPoolError also becomes ConnectionError. ConnectTimeout, ProxyError and SSLError all subclass ConnectionError. So one `except ConnectionError` catches every network-level failure. Meanwhile ReadTimeout (only a Timeout) and HTTPError stay distinguishable.

The checks live in requests/models.py. PreparedRequest.prepare_body first raises NotImplementedError if a streamed body is combined with files. When files are given, it calls RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data). That method raises ValueError("Files must be provided.") if files is empty. It raises ValueError("Data must not be a string.") when data is a str or bytes, which is what test_conflicting_post_params in tests/test_requests.py expects. Valid inputs are normalised with to_key_val_list from requests/utils.py and packed into urllib3 RequestField objects. encode_multipart_formdata then builds the body and content type. Data alone goes through _encode_params instead. The check does not prevent the ValueError; it deliberately rejects the ambiguous data-string-plus-files combination early.

RequestException.__init__ in requests/exceptions.py pops optional `response` and `request` keyword arguments and stores them as attributes. If a response is given and no request was passed, it fills in request from response.request, when that attribute exists. It then calls IOError.__init__ with the remaining arguments. So callers like Response.raise_for_status (HTTPError(..., response=self)) and resolve_redirects (TooManyRedirects(..., response=resp)) only need to pass the response. Older code that passes only messages, or only `request`, still works. Because every subclass inherits this logic, behaviour is uniform across the hierarchy. JSONDecodeError calls into the chain explicitly to cope with its multiple inheritance.

SessionRedirectMixin.should_strip_auth in requests/sessions.py returns True if the hostname changes. It then has a special case: going from http on port 80 (or none) to https on port 443 (or none) returns False. This keeps Authorization across the common HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade, which earlier requests releases allowed. Otherwise it treats any scheme or port change as a new protection space, in line with RFC 7235's scheme+host+port rule. The exception is default-port equivalence: it uses DEFAULT_PORTS (from requests/utils.py) so an explicit default port counts the same as no port. rebuild_auth calls it to delete the Authorization header, then reapplies netrc credentials when trust_env is set.

Inside its loop, resolve_redirects in requests/sessions.py does the following:
- It copies the request and appends the response to hist, setting resp.history.
- It reads resp.content so the connection returns to the pool. On ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError or RuntimeError it falls back to resp.raw.read(decode_content=False).
- It raises TooManyRedirects once max_redirects is reached, then calls resp.close().
- It rebuilds the URL, method, cookies, auth and proxies.
- For codes other than 307/308 it drops the body and Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding headers.
- It calls rewind_body (requests/utils.py) only when _body_position is not None and a length or encoding header remains.
Finally, it either yields the next request (yield_requests) or sends it with allow_redirects=False and the caller's stream setting.

TooManyRedirects is defined in requests/exceptions.py. It is raised only in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in requests/sessions.py, when len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects. max_redirects defaults to DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT (30) in requests/models.py. It is raised with the message "Exceeded N redirects." and response=resp. The usual chain is requests.get, then api.request, Session.request and Session.send. Inside send, when allow_redirects is true, it runs resolve_redirects(r, request, ...) and collects the results into history. Each step calls self.send again with allow_redirects=False. When allow_redirects is false, send uses next(resolve_redirects(..., yield_requests=True)) to fill Response.next. RequestException.__init__ then takes request from the response.

PreparedRequest.__init__ in requests/models.py sets _body_position to None, and copy() preserves it. In prepare_body, for streamed bodies with tell(), it stores the integer from body.tell(). If tell() raises OSError, it stores a unique object() sentinel instead. The three states carry different meanings:
- None means there is no stream position to track.
- An int is the exact offset to seek back to.
- The sentinel means rewinding was expected but is impossible.
resolve_redirects treats any non-None value as "needs rewind". rewind_body in requests/utils.py seeks only for ints and raises UnrewindableBodyError otherwise. A boolean could not hold the offset or tell apart "untracked" from "failed", which would risk silently resending a partially consumed body.

CaseInsensitiveDict in requests/structures.py is a MutableMapping that keeps _store, an OrderedDict mapping key.lower() to (original_key, value). Every __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__ calls str.lower(), which allocates a new string, then hashes it and indexes into a tuple. Mixin methods such as __contains__ and get go through __getitem__ and catch KeyError, adding Python-level calls and exception overhead. Common patterns like `if k in headers: headers[k]` repeat the lowering, hashing and lookup. __eq__, copy and lower_items rebuild whole structures. Across thousands of header operations, for example in PreparedRequest.prepare_headers, merge_setting and HTTPAdapter.build_response, these per-call costs add up because nothing caches the lowered keys.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, ConnectionError subclasses RequestException (itself an IOError). HTTPAdapter.send in src/requests/adapters.py raises it when urllib3 fails at the transport level: ProtocolError, OSError, ClosedPoolError, or a MaxRetryError whose reason is not a timeout, proxy, SSL or retry error. ProxyError, SSLError and ConnectTimeout subclass it. Callers can therefore catch "could not reach or talk to the server" on its own. This stays separate from HTTPError (raised by Response.raise_for_status), ReadTimeout, InvalidURL and similar errors. Catching RequestException still covers everything. The response and request keyword arguments are preserved through RequestException.__init__ for diagnostics.

The checks live in src/requests/models.py. PreparedRequest.prepare_body first rejects stream-like data combined with files by raising NotImplementedError. Otherwise, when files are present, it calls RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data). That method raises ValueError("Files must be provided.") if files is empty, and ValueError("Data must not be a string.") if data is a str or bytes. That second check is what the conflicting-params test triggers. Valid data is normalized with to_key_val_list from src/requests/utils.py and turned into RequestFields. urllib3's encode_multipart_formdata then encodes them and sets the multipart Content-Type. _encode_params handles data alone. Passing data as a dict or a list of 2-tuples avoids the error.

RequestException.__init__ in src/requests/exceptions.py pops optional response and request keyword arguments. It stores response, then sets request. If no request was given but the response has a .request attribute, it takes the request from response.request. The remaining arguments go to IOError.__init__, so old positional-message usage keeps working. Every subclass inherits this behaviour, including HTTPError raised from Response.raise_for_status and TooManyRedirects raised in Session.resolve_redirects. JSONDecodeError is the exception: it initializes both CompatJSONDecodeError and InvalidJSONError explicitly and defines __reduce__ so it can still be pickled. Raise sites can pass only response=..., and callers still get the request.

SessionRedirectMixin.should_strip_auth in src/requests/sessions.py returns True when the hostnames differ. It then has a special case: http on port 80 or no port redirecting to https on port 443 or no port returns False. The code comment says this is not in RFC 7235 but is kept for backward compatibility with older requests, which allowed same-host redirects. For other cases it applies RFC-style origin checks. A changed scheme or a changed non-default port strips credentials, while default ports (DEFAULT_PORTS or None) on the same scheme are treated as equal. rebuild_auth calls it to delete the Authorization header, then may re-apply netrc credentials via get_netrc_auth.

In src/requests/sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects loops while get_redirect_target returns a URL. On each pass it copies the request, appends the response to hist and sets resp.history. It reads resp.content so the socket can return to the pool, falling back to resp.raw.read(decode_content=False) on ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError or RuntimeError. It enforces max_redirects, then calls resp.close(). After rebuild_method it drops body headers for 301/302/303, and it refreshes cookies, proxies and auth. It calls utils.rewind_body only when _body_position is not None and a Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header remains. It then sends with the caller's stream flag and allow_redirects=False, or yields the request when yield_requests is set.

TooManyRedirects is raised only in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in src/requests/sessions.py. The condition is len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects, and the call is TooManyRedirects(f"Exceeded {self.max_redirects} redirects.", response=resp). The usual chain is api.request (or get, post, etc.) → Session.request → Session.send. Session.send runs HTTPAdapter.send and, with allow_redirects, consumes self.resolve_redirects(r, request, **kwargs) into history. Without allow_redirects, Session.send instead calls next(resolve_redirects(..., yield_requests=True)) to build Response.next. max_redirects defaults to DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT (30) from models.py and is set in Session.__init__. RequestException.__init__ then fills .request from response.request.

PreparedRequest.prepare_body in src/requests/models.py sets _body_position only for streamed bodies. It records body.tell(), or a fresh object() sentinel if tell() raises OSError. That gives three states. None means there is nothing to rewind, so resolve_redirects skips rewinding. An integer is the exact offset that utils.rewind_body seeks back to. The sentinel means rewinding is needed but impossible: rewind_body sees a non-integer and raises UnrewindableBodyError rather than silently resending a partly consumed body. A boolean could not store the seek offset and could not separate "no rewind needed" from "rewind needed but impossible". PreparedRequest.copy preserves the value.

CaseInsensitiveDict in src/requests/structures.py stores entries in an OrderedDict under key.lower(), with (original_key, value) tuples as values. Every __getitem__, __setitem__ and __delitem__ calls lower(), which allocates a new string whose hash must be recomputed, and __setitem__ also allocates a tuple. Methods inherited from MutableMapping (__contains__, get, setdefault, update) route through these Python-level methods, so "if k in headers: headers[k]" lowercases and looks up twice. Copying and __eq__ rebuild or re-lower every key. This happens in prepare_headers, merge_setting, check_header_validity and build_response. Across thousands of requests these constant per-operation costs add up to significant CPU and garbage-collection overhead.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, ConnectionError subclasses RequestException (an IOError), not Python's builtin ConnectionError. This gives one catchable class for transport failures, separate from HTTPError (raised by Response.raise_for_status), Timeout-only cases and URL/schema errors. Its subclasses ProxyError, SSLError and ConnectTimeout (which also inherits Timeout) refine it. In adapters.py, HTTPAdapter.send maps urllib3 errors onto it. ProtocolError/OSError and ClosedPoolError become ConnectionError. MaxRetryError becomes ConnectTimeout, RetryError, ProxyError, SSLError or plain ConnectionError, depending on e.reason. models.Response.iter_content also converts ReadTimeoutError into ConnectionError. The request/response context comes from RequestException.__init__. Callers can therefore catch "network unreachable" failures specifically, before falling back to RequestException.

The checks are in src/requests/models.py. PreparedRequest.prepare_body decides the path: json is used only when there is no data or files. Streamed bodies combined with files raise NotImplementedError. If files is set, it calls RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data). Otherwise it calls _encode_params. _encode_files raises ValueError("Files must be provided.") when files is empty. It raises ValueError("Data must not be a string.") when data is a str/bytes (basestring from compat.py), which is what the conflicting data-plus-files test triggers. When valid, it normalizes data and files with utils.to_key_val_list and guesses filenames with utils.guess_filename. It builds urllib3 RequestField objects and calls urllib3.filepost.encode_multipart_formdata. prepare_content_length then sets the Content-Length header. Passing data as a dict or list of tuples avoids the error.

RequestException.__init__ in src/requests/exceptions.py pops optional "response" and "request" keyword arguments and stores them as attributes. If a response was given but no request, and the response has a .request attribute, it sets self.request = response.request. It then calls IOError.__init__ with the remaining arguments. Raisers can therefore pass only response=…, as in Response.raise_for_status (HTTPError) and resolve_redirects (TooManyRedirects). Adapters pass request=…. Every subclass gets the same .request/.response interface without its own constructor. Old positional-message usage still works because the class remains an IOError. JSONDecodeError, which also inherits from InvalidJSONError, overrides __reduce__ so pickling keeps the JSON decoder's arguments despite this kwargs handling.

SessionRedirectMixin.should_strip_auth in src/requests/sessions.py always strips credentials when the hostname changes, which is the RFC 7235 protection against leaking credentials to another host. On the same host it allows one explicit exception: http on port 80 or default, redirecting to https on port 443 or default, keeps Authorization. The code comments say RFC 7235 does not specify this; it is kept so older behaviour of allowing same-host redirects does not break. Next, it does not strip if the scheme is unchanged and both ports are defaults (DEFAULT_PORTS from utils.py, or None). Otherwise it strips when the port or scheme changed. rebuild_auth applies the decision by deleting the Authorization header and possibly re-applying netrc credentials.

In SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects (sessions.py), each loop iteration copies the request, appends the response to hist, and sets resp.history = hist[1:]. It reads resp.content, falling back to resp.raw.read(decode_content=False) on ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError or RuntimeError, so the connection can be released. It checks max_redirects and then calls resp.close(). It rebuilds the URL, method, cookies, proxies and auth. For non-307/308 redirects it drops the body and the Content-Length, Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding headers. For a 307/308 with a recorded _body_position and length headers, it calls utils.rewind_body before resending with allow_redirects=False. In Session.send, a list comprehension drains the generator to build history. With allow_redirects=False it is used lazily (yield_requests=True) to set r._next. The stream flag is passed through to each send.

TooManyRedirects is defined in src/requests/exceptions.py and raised only in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in src/requests/sessions.py. The raise happens when len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects, with the message f"Exceeded {self.max_redirects} redirects." and response=resp. max_redirects defaults to DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT (30) from models.py. The call chain is: requests.api.request (or get/post…) → Session.request → Session.send. Session.send calls adapter.send, extracts cookies, then runs history = [resp for resp in gen] on self.resolve_redirects(r, request, **kwargs) when allow_redirects is true. Iteration reaches the limit check, and RequestException.__init__ fills .request from response.request. The HTTPAdapter itself never follows redirects, because it calls urlopen with redirect=False.

In PreparedRequest.prepare_body (models.py), _body_position has three states. None means there is no stream body position to restore. An int is the actual offset to seek back to, recorded via body.tell(). A fresh object() is a sentinel meaning tell() raised OSError, so a stream exists but cannot be rewound. resolve_redirects treats any non-None value with Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding as needing a rewind and calls utils.rewind_body. rewind_body seeks only if the value is an integer; the sentinel raises UnrewindableBodyError instead of resending an empty or partial body or hanging. A boolean could not hold the offset or tell "not applicable" from "failed". PreparedRequest.copy keeps the value.

CaseInsensitiveDict in src/requests/structures.py stores self._store[key.lower()] = (key, value). Every __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__ calls str.lower(), allocating a new string, and indexes into a tuple, all through Python-level method calls rather than C dict fast paths. The inherited Mapping.get and __contains__ go through __getitem__ and catch KeyError, so misses pay for an exception. __eq__ rebuilds dicts from lower_items(), copy rebuilds the whole store, and iteration uses generators. Requests repeats such lookups per request, for example: merge_setting, prepare_headers (rebuilds the dict and validates each header), "Content-Length" in headers checks, get_encoding_from_headers, and redirect header pops. Each operation is O(1) but has a large constant cost, which adds up at thousands of operations.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, ConnectionError subclasses RequestException. ProxyError and SSLError subclass it, and ConnectTimeout inherits from both ConnectionError and Timeout. This gives callers one catch target for transport-level failures, separate from HTTPError (bad status from raise_for_status), ReadTimeout, InvalidURL, TooManyRedirects and similar. In src/requests/adapters.py, HTTPAdapter.send maps urllib3 failures onto it. ProtocolError, OSError and ClosedPoolError become ConnectionError. MaxRetryError becomes ConnectTimeout, RetryError, ProxyError or SSLError when its reason matches, and ConnectionError otherwise. Response.iter_content in models.py also wraps ReadTimeoutError as ConnectionError. Because it ultimately derives from IOError and stores request/response, users can tell retryable "couldn't reach server" problems apart from protocol or application errors.

The logic is in src/requests/models.py. PreparedRequest.prepare_body decides the path. A streamed body combined with files raises NotImplementedError. Otherwise, if files is set, it calls RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data). _encode_files raises ValueError("Files must be provided.") when files is empty, and ValueError("Data must not be a string.") when data is str or bytes (basestring from compat.py). Otherwise it normalizes both inputs with to_key_val_list from utils.py, which itself raises ValueError for str, bytes, bool or int. It then encodes field values to UTF-8, builds urllib3 RequestField objects, and calls encode_multipart_formdata. Passing data as a dict or list of 2-tuples is what avoids the ValueError the test checks for.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, RequestException.__init__ pops the optional response and request keyword arguments before calling IOError.__init__. If a response is given but no request, and the response has a request attribute, it sets self.request = response.request. Callers can therefore pass only response, as Response.raise_for_status does with HTTPError and resolve_redirects does with TooManyRedirects. Callers can also pass request explicitly, as HTTPAdapter.send does. Removing the extra keyword arguments keeps IOError's signature intact. JSONDecodeError builds on this with cooperative initialization: it calls CompatJSONDecodeError.__init__ first, then InvalidJSONError.__init__ with self.args. Its __reduce__ uses the JSON class's version so pickling still works across the multiple-inheritance MRO.

In src/requests/sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.should_strip_auth always strips auth when the hostname changes. It then makes one exception: an old scheme of http with port 80 or None, moving to https with port 443 or None, returns False and keeps the Authorization header. This preserves the behaviour of older versions, which allowed same-host redirects, and moving to TLS doesn't expose credentials to a weaker channel. Next, if the scheme is unchanged and both ports are default (DEFAULT_PORTS from utils.py), it keeps auth. Otherwise any port or scheme change strips auth, matching RFC 7235's protection space keyed on scheme, host and port. rebuild_auth calls it and then re-applies netrc credentials.

In src/requests/sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects first appends resp to the local hist and sets resp.history = hist[1:]. It then reads resp.content to drain the socket. If that raises ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError or RuntimeError (content already consumed by streaming), it falls back to resp.raw.read(decode_content=False). It checks max_redirects, then calls resp.close() to return the connection to the pool. For redirects other than 307/308 it drops the body and the Content-Length, Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding headers. Otherwise it computes rewindable from _body_position and those length headers, and calls rewind_body from utils.py to seek the file back. The stream flag is passed on to self.send. yield_requests lets Session.send compute Response.next without sending anything.

TooManyRedirects is defined in src/requests/exceptions.py as a subclass of RequestException. It is raised only in src/requests/sessions.py, in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects, when len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects, using response=resp. max_redirects defaults to DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT (30) from models.py. The call chain is: api.request (or get, post and so on) → Session.request → Session.send. When allow_redirects is true, Session.send creates the generator self.resolve_redirects(r, request, **kwargs) and drains it with a list comprehension. Each loop iteration calls self.send(..., allow_redirects=False), and that response's redirect target drives the next iteration. Each pass grows the history until the limit check fires. RequestException.__init__ then fills in request from response.request.

PreparedRequest.prepare_body in models.py sets _body_position only for streamed bodies that have tell(). It records the integer offset when tell() succeeds, and a sentinel object() when tell() raises OSError. That gives three states. None means there is no file-like body to rewind (for example bytes or form data). An integer means rewinding is possible, and the offset is needed because a boolean can't hold the seek position, including partially read files. The sentinel means rewinding was needed but cannot be done. In resolve_redirects (sessions.py), "is not None" marks both the integer and sentinel cases as rewindable. rewind_body in utils.py then seeks to integers (integer_types) and raises UnrewindableBodyError for the sentinel, rather than hanging the connection.

In src/requests/structures.py, every CaseInsensitiveDict __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__ call runs key.lower(), which allocates a new string each time. Lookups go through Python-level methods over an OrderedDict that stores (key, value) tuples, and then index into the tuple. The MutableMapping mixins (get, __contains__, pop, setdefault, update) are built on __getitem__ plus try/except KeyError. So a common "in" check followed by indexing lowers and hashes twice, and misses pay for raising an exception. copy() and __eq__ rebuild whole new instances. The request path repeats this work many times: merge_setting in sessions.py, prepare_headers in models.py, PreparedRequest.copy on each redirect, and HTTPAdapter.build_response. Across thousands of requests, these interpreter-level costs add up compared with a plain C-level dict.

`MockTiming` lives in `src/_pytest/timing.py`. Its `patch(monkeypatch)` imports the `_pytest.timing` module itself and calls `monkeypatch.setattr` three times: `"sleep"` → `self.sleep`, `"time"` → `self.time`, `"perf_counter"` → `self.time`. The interception points are those module attributes. `Instant` reads `time()` and `perf_counter()` through `default_factory` lambdas at call time, and pytest code calls `timing.sleep` or `timing.time`, so all of them see the mocks. Each `MonkeyPatch.setattr` (in `monkeypatch.py`) saves the old value in `_setattr`, and `undo()` restores them in reverse order. The three calls are independent, so their order has no side effects. However, `time` and `perf_counter` both return the same `_current_time`, which only `sleep` advances.

`test_1` appears in `bench/xunit.py` (inside the generated classes `Test{i}`). To make it data-driven, decorate it with `@pytest.mark.parametrize("x", [...])` or pass `pytest.param(..., id=..., marks=...)` values. `ParameterSet._for_parametrize` and `Metafunc.parametrize` in `python.py` expand it into `CallSpec2` entries, and `IdMaker` builds node IDs like `test_1[...]`. Keep the old behaviour as one of the cases. Do not give the argument a default value: `_validate_if_using_arg_names` rejects parametrizing an argument that already has a default. If you need the old node ID unchanged, an indirect fixture with `params` is an alternative.

In `src/_pytest/main.py`, `_bestrelpath_cache` is a dataclass that subclasses `dict[Path, str]`, uses `__slots__ = ("path",)`, and stores the root path. Its `__missing__` calls `bestrelpath(self.path, path)`, stores the result and returns it. `Session._node_location_to_relpath` simply indexes `self._bestrelpath_cache[node_path]`. The source comments that bestrelpath is "a quite slow function", and it runs for every node location during reporting. The `__missing__` hook gives lazy computation on the first access and a plain C-level dict lookup afterwards. No explicit membership check or separate cache logic is needed.

The logic is in `ReprFuncArgs.toterminal` in `src/_pytest/_code/code.py`. It keeps a `linesofar` string and, for each `(name, value)`, builds `ns = f"{name} = {value}"`. If `len(ns) + len(linesofar) + 2 > tw.fullwidth`, it flushes `linesofar` with `tw.line` and starts a new line with `ns`. Otherwise it appends `", " + ns`, or starts with `ns` if the line is empty. After the loop it emits any remainder and then a blank line. The arguments come from `FormattedExcinfo.repr_args`, which uses `saferepr` (optionally truncated) when `funcargs` is set.

The premise is largely wrong. In `src/_pytest/_py/path.py`, `Visitor.__init__` wraps a string `fil` or `rec` in `FNMatcher` once per `LocalPath.visit()` call, not once per directory, so the memory cost is negligible: each `FNMatcher` only stores the pattern. The real costs are elsewhere:
- `FNMatcher.__call__` runs on every path, doing separator replacement, `basename` or full-path selection, and `fnmatch.fnmatch` (whose compiled regexes are cached).
- `Visitor.gen` recurses through nested generators with `yield from`.
- Each directory calls `listdir()` plus `check(dir=1)`/`stat` calls and optional sorting.
For large trees, I/O and per-entry matching dominate, not object construction.

`import_path` is in `src/_pytest/pathlib.py`.
- **prepend/append modes:** `resolve_pkg_root_and_module_name` derives the module name from the `__init__.py` package structure (`resolve_package_path`), not from `sys.path`. It inserts or appends `pkg_root` into `sys.path`, calls `importlib.import_module`, and reads `sys.modules`. Unless `PY_IGNORE_IMPORTMISMATCH` is set, it compares `mod.__file__` (normalised from `.pyc` and `__init__.py`) with `_is_same`/`samefile` and raises `ImportPathMismatchError` on a mismatch.
- **importlib mode:** it first returns any existing `sys.modules[module_name]`. Otherwise `_import_module_using_spec` finds a spec via `meta_path`, checks `spec_matches_module_path`, registers the module, and calls `insert_missing_modules`. If that fails it falls back to `module_name_from_path`.
`sys.modules` is the single cache.

`FixtureFunctionMarker.__call__` in `src/_pytest/fixtures.py` runs these checks in order:
1. It raises `ValueError` for classes.
2. If `isinstance(function, FixtureFunctionDefinition)`, it raises `ValueError("@pytest.fixture is being applied more than once to the same function ...")`.
3. If `hasattr(function, "pytestmark")`, it emits `warnings.warn(MARKED_FIXTURE)` (a `PytestRemovedIn9Warning`).
4. It wraps the function in `FixtureFunctionDefinition` and fails if the name is `"request"`.
The isinstance check catches a hard error: the object is already a fixture wrapper. The `pytestmark` check only detects marks applied beneath the decorator, which have no effect on fixtures, so it is a deprecation rather than an error. Marks applied above an existing fixture are caught separately by `store_mark` in `mark/structures.py`, via `getfixturemarker`.

In src/flask/sessions.py, SecureCookieSession subclasses werkzeug's CallbackDict. Its on_update callback sets self.modified and self.accessed to True on any mutation, and __getitem__, get and setdefault also set accessed. This does not coordinate concurrent requests. Each request deserializes its own copy from the cookie in SecureCookieSessionInterface.open_session. save_session then writes the cookie only when should_set_cookie allows it (modified, or permanent with SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST). It adds Vary: Cookie when the session was accessed. So the guarantee is per request: in-memory changes reach the outgoing cookie. Concurrent requests are last-write-wins on the client. Mutating nested values needs a manual session.modified = True.

ScriptInfo in src/flask/cli.py takes both create_app and app_import_path. ScriptInfo.load_app uses them in order. It calls the create_app callable if one was given. Otherwise it resolves app_import_path (from --app or FLASK_APP) via prepare_import and locate_app. Otherwise it searches wsgi.py or app.py. The callable form supports custom scripts built with FlaskGroup(create_app=...) for application factories without an importable path. The import path form serves the generic flask command.

SecureCookieSessionInterface.get_signing_serializer builds a new itsdangerous URLSafeTimedSerializer on every open_session and save_session call. It rebuilds the key list from SECRET_KEY plus SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS, using salt "cookie-session", hashlib.sha1 and HMAC key derivation. Calling it "a bottleneck" overstates things. Construction is cheap; the main cost is repeated allocation and key derivation inside sign and unsign per request. Under high concurrency this adds CPU work and GIL contention that a cached serializer could reduce. It is not usually a dominant cost.

In src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py, Blueprint.register sets self._got_registered_once = True. Blueprint._check_setup_finished, called by the @setupmethod decorator from sansio/scaffold.py, raises an AssertionError if a setup method such as route or before_request is called afterwards. Blueprint setup is deferred: record and record_once store callbacks in deferred_functions, which run only during registration. Later calls would silently never apply, so the flag makes that mistake fail loudly.

In tests/type_check/typing_route.py, a function decorated with @app.route (for example a json-list view) is annotated as returning list[t.Any]. The route decorator in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py is typed with T_route bound to RouteCallable from src/flask/typing.py. RouteCallable requires returning ResponseReturnValue, whose ResponseValue union includes list[t.Any]. mypy and pyright check these files, configured in pyproject.toml (files include tests/type_check) and run by the tox typing environment. Nothing runs these views; type checking alone validates them.

tests/type_check/typing_route.py defines StatusJSON as a TypedDict and a view annotated to return it. In src/flask/typing.py, ResponseValue includes Mapping[str, t.Any], so a TypedDict satisfies it while keeping key-level typing. The HTTP status is not part of the body type. It lives in the separate tuple forms of ResponseReturnValue, (ResponseValue, int) and the header variants. At runtime Flask.make_response in src/flask/app.py serializes the dict via self.json.response and applies the status separately.

TestStreaming in tests/test_helpers.py tests stream_with_context from src/flask/helpers.py. Its methods are test_streaming_with_context, test_streaming_with_context_as_decorator and test_streaming_with_context_and_custom_close. The pattern is a decorator/wrapper: stream_with_context wraps the generator and keeps the request context pushed while the response body is iterated, then pops it on close. The views only yield data and never manage context lifecycle; the wrapper and the test client handle it.

In src/flask/json/tag.py, TagList.to_json returns [self.serializer.tag(item) for item in value]. TaggedJSONSerializer.tag walks self.order and applies the first tag whose check() matches, such as TagDict, TagTuple, TagBytes, TagMarkup, TagUUID or TagDateTime. That is how mixed item types are dispatched. A nested list matches TagList again, so recursion goes through serializer.tag. TagList.to_python returns the value unchanged. On decode, TaggedJSONSerializer.loads uses _untag_scan, which recurses into lists and dicts and calls untag on single-key tagged dicts.

In flask/views.py, MethodView.__init_subclass__ does not pick a winner between parents. It merges them. If the subclass defines no "methods" in its own __dict__, it builds an empty set. It then loops over cls.__bases__ and unions in each base's non-empty methods attribute. Next it checks every name in http_method_funcs ("get", "post", and so on) with hasattr(cls, key) and adds key.upper(). If the resulting set is non-empty, it is assigned to cls.methods. Multiple inheritance therefore yields the union of all parents' methods plus any handler methods visible through the MRO. Only an explicit methods attribute on the subclass bypasses this merge.

In src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py, Blueprint.add_url_rule first checks that the endpoint and view_func.__name__ contain no dots. It then calls self.record(lambda s: s.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, view_func, provide_automatic_options=..., **options)). Blueprint.record appends the callable to self.deferred_functions, after _check_setup_finished warns if the blueprint was already registered. Nothing is registered at that point because no app or BlueprintSetupState exists yet. Later, Blueprint.register calls make_setup_state and invokes each deferred function with that state. BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule then applies url_prefix, subdomain, the dotted name_prefix endpoint and merged defaults before calling app.add_url_rule.

In src/flask/json/tag.py, TaggedJSONSerializer.loads parses the string with flask.json's loads and passes the result to _untag_scan. _untag_scan walks dicts and lists recursively, rebuilding children first. Each single-key dict is handed to untag. TaggedJSONSerializer.untag looks up that key in self.tags. For the " b" key this finds TagBytes and calls tag.to_python(value[key]). TagBytes.to_python returns b64decode(value). The bytes decoding therefore happens inside untag, invoked bottom-up by _untag_scan after JSON parsing.

My best reading is that this refers to after_this_request in src/flask/ctx.py. It appends the function to the active RequestContext's _after_request_functions list. That list lives only as long as the current request context, so registration fails outside a request and does not carry over to copied or nested contexts. Flask.process_response runs these callbacks before the blueprint and app after_request hooks, and each must return a response. If an unhandled exception skips normal response processing, conditionally registered callbacks never run. A callback registered while the list is being iterated is picked up during that same pass. Ordering and execution therefore depend on hidden per-request state, not on the decorator itself.

This is somewhat speculative. Blueprint.app_template_filter and add_app_template_filter in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py record a deferred closure that writes into app.jinja_env.filters. Repeating this across many distinct blueprints creates one closure per filter per blueprint. Each is executed in Blueprint.register. Touching app.jinja_env forces Flask.create_jinja_environment early, and every registration mutates the single shared environment's filters dict. Identically named filters silently overwrite one another, with the last one winning. Jinja's template cache may also need rebuilding if filters change after templates load. The cost is mainly redundant startup work and wasted memory rather than any per-request isolation benefit.

This is in App._find_error_handler in src/flask/sansio/app.py. It first calls _get_exc_class_and_code(type(e)). The outermost loop is over the code, trying the specific HTTP code first and then None. Inside that, it loops over names = (*blueprints, None), innermost blueprint first and the app last. For each, it reads self.error_handler_spec[name][c] and skips empty maps. It then walks exc_class.__mro__ and returns the first handler_map.get(cls) match. So the actual nesting is status code, then blueprint scopes, then the exception MRO. It returns None if nothing matches.

This is the small fake path-like helper class in tests/test_helpers.py, used to test send_file and send_from_directory with os.PathLike objects. Its __fspath__ method simply returns the stored path string, self.path. os.fspath(obj) therefore yields that plain str path, which Werkzeug's send_file then handles like an ordinary filename.

In tests/test_logging.py, test_existing_handler adds a logging.StreamHandler to logging.root and then checks that app.logger.handlers is empty. This verifies that create_logger in src/flask/logging.py calls has_level_handler(logger) before adding default_handler. has_level_handler walks up the logger hierarchy and finds the root's handler at an effective level. Because a handler already exists, Flask does not attach its own default_handler. This prevents duplicate log output when the user has already configured logging.

The test `test_open_resource_with_encoding` in tests/test_helpers.py is parametrized over encodings such as "utf-8" and "utf-16-le". It writes a text file into `tmp_path` and creates `Flask("test", root_path=tmp_path)`. It then calls `app.open_resource("test.txt", "r", encoding=encoding)`. In src/flask/app.py, `Flask.open_resource(resource, mode="rb", encoding=None)` rejects any mode outside "r", "rt" and "rb" with a ValueError. It builds the path with `os.path.join(self.root_path, resource)`. For "rb" it calls `open(path, mode)` and ignores the encoding. Otherwise it passes the value straight through as `open(path, mode, encoding=encoding)`, so the file decodes correctly.

`AsyncMethodView` in tests/test_async.py subclasses `MethodView` from src/flask/views.py. `MethodView` already does the dispatch work. `__init_subclass__` collects the HTTP method names, and `dispatch_request` looks up `getattr(self, request.method.lower())` with a fallback from HEAD to GET. It then calls the handler through `current_app.ensure_sync(meth)(**kwargs)`. `Flask.ensure_sync` turns coroutine functions into sync calls using `async_to_sync` from asgiref. `View.as_view` also wraps `dispatch_request` with `ensure_sync`. Async support therefore lives in one central place, so `MethodView` needs no separate async dispatch path. Inheriting reuses routing, `methods` discovery, decorators and `as_view` without duplicating them.

`test_locate_app_raises` in tests/test_cli.py is parametrized over `(iname, aname)` pairs. Examples are ("cliapp.app", "notanapp"), ("cliapp.factory", 'create_app2("foo")'), ("cliapp.factory", "create_app("), ("cliapp.factory", "no_app"), ("cliapp.importerrorapp", None) and ("cliapp.message.txt", None). Each case asserts `pytest.raises(NoAppException)`. `locate_app` in src/flask/cli.py turns every failure into `NoAppException`. An ImportError becomes "While importing..." when it was raised inside the module, or "Could not import" otherwise. `find_app_by_string` converts SyntaxError from `ast.parse`, AttributeError and TypeError. `find_best_app` raises when no app or factory is found. Because of this, every parameter combination fails with the same exception type.

`App.__init__` in src/flask/sansio/app.py first calls `Scaffold.__init__`, which sets `root_path` via `get_root_path(import_name)`. If no `instance_path` is given, it calls `auto_find_instance_path()`. That uses `find_package()` and returns either `package_path/instance` or `prefix/var/<name>-instance`. Next, `self.config = self.make_config(instance_relative_config)` runs. `make_config` starts from `root_path = self.root_path` and replaces it with `self.instance_path` when instance-relative mode is on. It then copies `default_config` and returns `self.config_class(root_path, defaults)`. `Config.__init__` in src/flask/config.py stores the value as `self.root_path`.

`App._find_error_handler` in src/flask/sansio/app.py first calls `_get_exc_class_and_code(type(e))`. It then loops over the HTTP code (then None), over the request's blueprint names plus None (the app), and over `exc_class.__mro__`. Inside these loops it calls `handler_map.get(cls)` against `error_handler_spec[name][c]`. The cost is therefore proportional to code variants times blueprint nesting times MRO depth. Every raised error repeats the whole walk, because resolved handlers are never cached. Each lookup is an O(1) dict access, so the overhead is small unless inheritance chains and blueprint stacks are deep. Empty handler maps are skipped early.

`TagBytes` in src/flask/json/tag.py is a `JSONTag` with key " b", and its `check` method is `isinstance(value, bytes)`. `to_json` returns `b64encode(value).decode("ascii")`, which is a JSON-safe ASCII string. `to_python` reverses this with `b64decode(value)`, returning the exact original bytes. `JSONTag.tag` wraps the result as `{" b": ...}`. `TaggedJSONSerializer.untag` recognises single-key dicts whose key is a registered tag and dispatches to `to_python`. `dumps` and `loads` apply `tag` and `untag` recursively. Base64 is lossless, so the round trip is bijective. The ordered `default_tags` list keeps tag selection deterministic.

`Flask.test_cli_runner(**kwargs)` in src/flask/app.py builds `test_cli_runner_class`, which defaults to `FlaskCliRunner`, passing `self` as the app. `FlaskCliRunner` in src/flask/testing.py subclasses `click.testing.CliRunner` and stores the app. Its `invoke(cli=None, args=None, **kwargs)` falls back to `self.app.cli`, the app's `AppGroup`. If no `obj` is given, it injects `ScriptInfo(create_app=lambda: self.app)`. `ScriptInfo.load_app` in src/flask/cli.py, the loading helper, then returns that exact app. `with_appcontext` and `FlaskGroup` use it to push an app context. Finally, `CliRunner.invoke` runs the command with isolated streams and environment.

`_AppCtxGlobals` in src/flask/ctx.py stores its data in `__dict__`. `__getattr__` and `__delattr__` catch KeyError and raise `AttributeError(name) from None`, so attribute syntax behaves like a normal object. The explicit helpers allow defaults. `get(name, default=None)` returns `__dict__.get`. `pop(name, default=_sentinel)` raises KeyError when the key is missing and no default is passed, otherwise it returns the default. `setdefault` inserts and returns the value. `__contains__`, `__iter__` and `__repr__` round out the dict-like interface. Strict attribute access therefore sits beside optional default-returning methods.

In `src/flask/json/provider.py`, `DefaultJSONProvider` has a class attribute `ensure_ascii = True`. `DefaultJSONProvider.dumps` passes it to the standard library with `kwargs.setdefault("ensure_ascii", self.ensure_ascii)` before calling `json.dumps`. When it is True, every non-ASCII character is escaped as a `\uXXXX` sequence, with surrogate pairs for astral characters, so the output is pure ASCII. When an app sets `app.json.ensure_ascii = False`, or uses a subclass that does, Unicode characters are written literally. `response()` and `flask.json.dumps`/`jsonify` inherit this behavior through `app.json`. The setting only affects the textual representation, not the decoded data.

In `src/flask/sessions.py`, `_lazy_sha1(string=b"")` simply returns `hashlib.sha1(string)` when called. `SecureCookieSessionInterface.digest_method = staticmethod(_lazy_sha1)` stores this function rather than `hashlib.sha1` itself. So the `hashlib.sha1` attribute is not looked up when the module is imported or the class is defined. On FIPS-restricted builds where SHA-1 is unavailable, importing Flask therefore does not fail. The lookup only happens when `get_signing_serializer` builds an itsdangerous `URLSafeTimedSerializer` with `signer_kwargs={"key_derivation": "hmac", "digest_method": self.digest_method}` and a signature is computed. This lets developers override `digest_method` first.

`TagMarkup` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` (key `" m"`) has `check` testing `callable(getattr(value, "__html__", None))` and `to_json` returning `str(value.__html__())`. The helpers it delegates to are not in Flask. `__html__` is defined on the object itself, typically `markupsafe.Markup.__html__` from the external markupsafe package, and `str` is the builtin. Reverse conversion in `to_python` calls `markupsafe.Markup(value)`. In the pipeline, `TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps` calls `TaggedJSONSerializer.tag`, which calls `JSONTag.tag` and then `TagMarkup.to_json`. The result is then passed to `flask.json.dumps` with `separators=(",", ":")`. `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` uses `untag`/`_untag_scan` to reverse it.

The logic is in `App.add_url_rule` in `src/flask/sansio/app.py`. First, if the `provide_automatic_options` argument is None, it falls back to `getattr(view_func, "provide_automatic_options", None)`. If it is still None, then when `"OPTIONS" not in methods` and `self.config["PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS"]` is true, it sets the flag to True and adds `"OPTIONS"` to `required_methods`; otherwise the flag becomes False. `methods |= required_methods`, and the rule built via `self.url_rule_class` gets `rule.provide_automatic_options` set. At request time, `Flask.dispatch_request` in `src/flask/app.py` checks `getattr(rule, "provide_automatic_options", False) and req.method == "OPTIONS"` and returns `make_default_options_response()`.

`copy_current_request_context` in `src/flask/ctx.py` gets the active request context from its context variable and raises `RuntimeError` if there is none. It then calls `ctx.copy()` while decorating. `RequestContext.copy` builds a new context of the same class with the same `app`, `environ`, `request` object and `session`. The returned `wrapper` does `with ctx:` and calls `ctx.app.ensure_sync(f)(*args, **kwargs)`. Pushing in the greenlet or thread sets fresh contextvar tokens there, so its context stack is isolated and is popped independently. Because `push` only opens a session when `self.session is None`, the shared session object is preserved rather than reloaded.

In `src/flask/debughelpers.py`, `UnexpectedUnicodeError(AssertionError, UnicodeError)` sits next to `DebugFilesKeyError(KeyError, AssertionError)` and `FormDataRoutingRedirect`. The mixin pattern means one exception is caught both by handlers for programmer-error assertions and by handlers for encoding failures. `AssertionError` marks it as a developer mistake surfaced only by debug-time checks. `UnicodeError` keeps compatibility with code expecting standard encoding errors. Debug-only diagnostics live in this separate module, away from core request handling in `app.py`, `wrappers.py` and `ctx.py`. Validation-style failures stay distinct from Werkzeug's HTTP exceptions, while existing except clauses keep working.

`PassDict.to_json` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` returns `{k: self.serializer.tag(v) for k, v in value.items()}`, with the comment that JSON objects may only have string keys, so keys are not tagged. Tagging a key could turn it into a dict like `{" t": [...]}`, which cannot be a JSON object key. Non-string keys would fail or be coerced by `json.dumps` anyway. Values can hold bytes, tuples, Markup, UUIDs or datetimes, so they recurse through `TaggedJSONSerializer.tag`. `PassDict` sets `tag = to_json` to skip wrapping. Ambiguous single-key dicts whose key matches a registered tag are handled earlier by `TagDict`, which appends `"__"` to the key.

`Flask.open_resource(resource, mode="rb", encoding=None)` in `src/flask/app.py`, mirrored by `Blueprint.open_resource` in `src/flask/blueprints.py`, raises `ValueError("Resources can only be opened for reading.")` if `mode` is not in `{"r", "rt", "rb"}`. It opens `os.path.join(self.root_path, resource)`. That path is the installed application or package source, which is often read-only, such as site-packages, zipped or system-managed directories. Writing there would mutate shipped code and data, and would not be safe across deployments or multiple processes. Writable, deployment-specific files belong in the instance folder, opened with `Flask.open_instance_resource`, which allows any mode relative to `instance_path`.

The decision happens in `FlaskGroup.get_command` in `src/flask/cli.py`. It first calls `self._load_plugin_commands()`, which adds `flask.commands` entry points to the group through `add_command`. It then calls `super().get_command(ctx, name)`, so directly registered and entry-point commands both come back from the same Click lookup and are returned if found. If that lookup returns nothing, it gets the `ScriptInfo` with `ctx.ensure_object(ScriptInfo)` and calls `info.load_app()`. On `NoAppException` it prints the error and returns `None`. Otherwise it pushes `app.app_context()` with `ctx.with_resource` if needed, and returns `app.cli.get_command(ctx, name)`.

This is the subdomain test in `tests/test_testing.py`. It depends on the `app` fixture from `tests/conftest.py`, which builds a `Flask("flask_test", root_path=...)`. It also uses the `client` fixture, which is `app.test_client()`. The test sets `app.config["SERVER_NAME"]` and registers a view with `@app.route("/", subdomain="<company_id>")`, adding a subdomain `Rule` to `app.url_map`. `app.test_request_context(subdomain=...)` uses `flask.testing.EnvironBuilder`, which builds `base_url` from SERVER_NAME, the subdomain, APPLICATION_ROOT and PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME. That creates a `RequestContext`, whose `create_url_adapter` lets `url_for` build the URL. `client.get` then dispatches it.

`TagUUID` in `src/flask/json/tag.py`, with key `" u"`, exists because JSON has no UUID type. `TaggedJSONSerializer`, used by `SecureCookieSessionInterface` for session cookies, must round-trip values without losing their type. `check` matches UUID instances, and `to_json` returns the compact `value.hex` string. `to_python` rebuilds the value with `UUID(value)`. The tag wrapper (`{" u": hex}`) separates real UUIDs from ordinary strings, so session data keeps its original Python types after decoding.
