In `tests/type_check/typing_route.py`, a view decorated with `@app.route(...)` returns a list of dicts and is annotated as a list type. `Scaffold.route` in `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py` is typed with `T_route`, which is bound to `ft.RouteCallable` (callables returning `ResponseReturnValue`). In `src/flask/typing.py`, `ResponseValue` includes `list[t.Any]`, so the annotation type-checks. `pyproject.toml` configures mypy (`files`) and pyright (`include`) to cover `tests/type_check`. At runtime, `Flask.make_response` in `src/flask/app.py` converts the list through `self.json.response`.

The test files are not in the provided source, so this is a best answer. A `TypedDict` (for example a status-JSON type in `tests/type_check/typing_route.py`) annotates the view's body only. In `src/flask/typing.py`, `ResponseValue` includes `t.Mapping[str, t.Any]`, with a comment noting this exists to allow TypedDict. The HTTP status is expressed separately through the `ResponseReturnValue` tuple forms `tuple[ResponseValue, int]` and `tuple[ResponseValue, int, HeadersValue]`. `Flask.make_response` in `src/flask/app.py` unpacks the tuple, serializes the dict via `json.response` (`DefaultJSONProvider`), and then applies `status_code`. The JSON shape and the status therefore stay independently typed.

The test files are not in the provided source, so this is a best answer. `TestStreaming` in `tests/test_helpers.py` exercises `stream_with_context` from `src/flask/helpers.py`. That function is a decorator and wrapper: it captures the current `RequestContext` from `_cv_request` and re-enters it with `with ctx` inside a wrapper generator. It primes the generator with `next()` so the context is pushed before the response begins, and closes the inner iterator in a `finally`. `RequestContext.push`/`pop` in `src/flask/ctx.py` use the `_cv_tokens` stack to run teardown only on the final pop. The tests use the test client, close-tracking wrapper iterators, and teardown hooks to confirm the separation.

In `src/flask/json/tag.py`, `PassList.to_json` maps every item through `self.serializer.tag(item)`, and `PassList.tag = to_json` so lists are not wrapped in a tag. `TaggedJSONSerializer.tag` dispatches by walking `self.order` (`TagDict`, `PassDict`, `TagTuple`, `PassList`, `TagBytes`, `TagMarkup`, `TagUUID`, `TagDateTime`) and calling the first matching tag's `tag`. Nested lists, dicts and tuples therefore recurse back through the dispatcher, while bytes, UUIDs and datetimes become `{" b": ...}`-style objects. On load, `_untag_scan` recursively walks lists and dicts and calls `untag` to restore the original types.

The test (likely `test_open_resource_with_encoding` in tests/test_helpers.py) calls `app.open_resource("test.txt", "rt", encoding=encoding)` on a `Flask` instance. In src/flask/app.py, `Flask.open_resource(self, resource, mode="rb", encoding=None)` first rejects any mode outside {"r", "rt", "rb"} with ValueError. It then builds `path = os.path.join(self.root_path, resource)`. In "rb" mode it calls `open(path, mode)` and ignores the encoding. Otherwise it passes the value through as `open(path, mode, encoding=encoding)`. The parallel `Flask.open_instance_resource` joins with `instance_path` instead. `Blueprint.open_resource` in src/flask/blueprints.py does the same but defaults encoding to "utf-8". `root_path` itself comes from `Scaffold.__init__` via `get_root_path`.

The async view class (e.g. in tests/test_async.py) subclasses `MethodView` from src/flask/views.py and only defines `async def get/post`. `MethodView.__init_subclass__` already collects the `methods` set from any defined handlers, whether sync or async. `MethodView.dispatch_request` looks up `getattr(self, request.method.lower())`, falls back from HEAD to GET, and returns `current_app.ensure_sync(meth)(**kwargs)`. `Flask.ensure_sync` in app.py detects coroutine functions with `iscoroutinefunction` and wraps them via `async_to_sync` (asgiref). `View.as_view` also routes through `ensure_sync`. Because the existing dispatch already handles coroutines, a separate async dispatcher would only duplicate this routing and method discovery.

`test_locate_app_raises` in tests/test_cli.py is parametrized over (iname, aname) pairs such as missing modules, modules with no app, bad attribute names, bad factory calls and unparsable expressions, and expects `NoAppException`. `locate_app` in src/flask/cli.py turns import failures into `NoAppException`, checking `tb_next` to tell "error while importing" from "not found". With no app name it calls `find_best_app`; otherwise it calls `find_app_by_string`. That function maps SyntaxError, ValueError, AttributeError and TypeError (using `_called_with_wrong_args`) to `NoAppException` via `raise ... from e/None`, and rejects non-Flask results. Since every failure path converges on one `click.UsageError` subclass, each parametrized combination fails the same way.

`Flask.__init__` in app.py calls `App.__init__` in src/flask/sansio/app.py. That calls `Scaffold.__init__` (sansio/scaffold.py), which sets `root_path` from `get_root_path(import_name)` if none was given. `App.__init__` then resolves `instance_path`, using `auto_find_instance_path()` (which relies on `find_package`) when it is None, and raises ValueError if the path is not absolute. Next it calls `self.config = self.make_config(instance_relative_config)`. `App.make_config` starts with `root_path = self.root_path`, but when `instance_relative` is true it replaces it with `self.instance_path`. It copies `default_config`, sets DEBUG from `get_debug_flag()`, and calls `self.config_class(root_path, defaults)`. `Config.__init__` in config.py stores that path as `self.root_path` for `from_pyfile`/`from_file`.

`App._find_error_handler` in sansio/app.py first normalizes the exception with `_get_exc_class_and_code`. It then loops over codes (code, None) and scopes (each blueprint name, then None for the app), and for each non-empty `error_handler_spec[name][c]` map it walks `exc_class.__mro__`, calling `handler_map.get(cls)`. The lookup is not cached per exception type, so every raised error repeats up to 2 × (blueprints+1) × MRO-depth dict probes. A deep inheritance chain lengthens each walk, and handlers registered in many scopes or codes make more maps non-empty, which multiplies the walks. The defaultdict access may also create empty entries. Each probe is O(1), so the cost grows linearly rather than badly, but it is paid on every error.

`TagBytes` in src/flask/json/tag.py uses key " b". Its `check` is `isinstance(value, bytes)`, `to_json` returns `b64encode(value).decode("ascii")`, and `to_python` returns `b64decode(value)`. `JSONTag.tag` wraps the result as {" b": "..."}. Base64 is lossless and ASCII-only, so arbitrary bytes survive JSON exactly. On load, `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` calls `_untag_scan` and `untag`, which recognize single-key dicts whose key is a registered tag and dispatch to `to_python`. Ambiguity with user data is prevented by `TagDict`, which escapes single-key dicts whose key matches a tag by appending "__". The ordered `default_tags` list ensures bytes are matched before generic handling. `SecureCookieSessionInterface` uses this serializer for sessions.

`Flask.test_cli_runner` in app.py instantiates `test_cli_runner_class`, which defaults to `FlaskCliRunner` in src/flask/testing.py, a subclass of `click.testing.CliRunner`. `FlaskCliRunner.__init__` stores the app. `invoke` defaults `cli` to `self.app.cli`, the `AppGroup` created in `Flask.__init__`. It also injects `obj=ScriptInfo(create_app=lambda: self.app)` unless an `obj` was supplied, then delegates to `CliRunner.invoke`, which isolates stdin/stdout and the environment. Inside commands, `with_appcontext` and `AppGroup.command` in src/flask/cli.py call `ctx.ensure_object(ScriptInfo).load_app()`. That returns the cached app produced by `create_app` and pushes `app.app_context()`, so commands run against the test app without import discovery.

`_AppCtxGlobals` in src/flask/ctx.py, the class behind `flask.g`, splits two protocols. The attribute protocol is strict: `__getattr__` and `__delattr__` catch KeyError from `self.__dict__` and raise `AttributeError(name) from None`. This keeps `hasattr` and `getattr(g, x, default)` working and hides the internal KeyError. The dict-like helpers are lenient: `get(name, default=None)` returns `__dict__.get`, and `setdefault` delegates to the dict. `pop(name, default=_sentinel)` uses the module-level `_sentinel` so that an explicit None default is honoured. Without a default it calls `__dict__.pop(name)` and raises KeyError, mirroring `dict.pop`. `__contains__` and `__iter__` also support membership checks without exceptions.

The `ensure_ascii` class attribute on `DefaultJSONProvider` in `src/flask/json/provider.py` defaults to `True`. `DefaultJSONProvider.dumps` passes it to `json.dumps` through `kwargs.setdefault("ensure_ascii", self.ensure_ascii)`. When it is `True`, every non-ASCII character is escaped as `\uXXXX`, with surrogate pairs for characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. The output is then pure ASCII, which is safer for older clients but larger. Setting it to `False` on a subclass, on the `app.json` instance, or per call emits the raw Unicode characters instead, giving smaller output. `DefaultJSONProvider.response`, and therefore `jsonify`, calls `dumps`, so HTTP JSON responses follow the same setting.

In `src/flask/sessions.py`, `_lazy_sha1` only calls `hashlib.sha1(string)` when it is invoked. `SecureCookieSessionInterface` stores it as `digest_method = staticmethod(_lazy_sha1)` instead of referencing `hashlib.sha1` directly. `get_signing_serializer` passes this function to itsdangerous's `URLSafeTimedSerializer` in `signer_kwargs`. As a result, SHA-1 is only touched when a session cookie is actually signed or verified in `open_session` or `save_session`. On FIPS builds that exclude SHA-1, importing Flask and defining the class therefore does not fail. Developers can set a different `digest_method` before any request reaches the code path that would raise.

`TagMarkup` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` has three relevant methods. `check` tests for a callable `__html__`. `to_json` calls the object's own `__html__()` (the markupsafe API) and converts the result with `str`. `to_python` calls `markupsafe.Markup`. On the serialization side, `TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps` calls `tag`, which walks `order` until `TagMarkup.check` matches. `JSONTag.tag` then wraps the result as `{" m": ...}`, and `flask.json.dumps` in `src/flask/json/__init__.py` encodes it via `current_app.json.dumps` or the standard-library `json`. On the loading side, `flask.json.loads`, then `_untag_scan`, then `untag` call `to_python`.

The logic is in `App.add_url_rule` in `src/flask/sansio/app.py`. If the `provide_automatic_options` argument is `None`, it falls back to the view function's `provide_automatic_options` attribute, which `View.as_view` sets. If that is still `None`, there are two branches. If "OPTIONS" is not already in `methods` and `config["PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS"]` is true, the flag becomes `True` and OPTIONS is added to `required_methods`. Otherwise the flag becomes `False`. The code then merges `methods |= required_methods` and sets the flag on `rule_obj`. At request time, `Flask.dispatch_request` in `app.py` checks the flag and calls `make_default_options_response`.

`copy_current_request_context` in `src/flask/ctx.py` reads `_cv_request` and raises if no request context is active. It calls `RequestContext.copy()`, which builds a new context that shares the same app, environ and `Request` object and passes `session=self.session`. The wrapper enters `with ctx:`, which sets the `contextvars` (`_cv_request`, and `_cv_app` if needed) inside the greenlet. The copy has its own `_cv_tokens`, so its push and pop are isolated from the original. Because `session` is not `None`, `push` skips `open_session`, so the copy keeps the original's current session data. The function runs through `app.ensure_sync`. The shared `Request` object is not thread-safe, so this suits greenlets, not threads.

`UnexpectedUnicodeError(AssertionError, UnicodeError)` in `src/flask/debughelpers.py` follows the same pattern as `DebugFilesKeyError(KeyError, AssertionError)` and `FormDataRoutingRedirect(AssertionError)`. The `AssertionError` base marks these as developer-facing, debug-only signals of programming mistakes rather than client-facing `HTTPException`s. The domain base (`UnicodeError`) keeps existing `except UnicodeError` handlers working, so validation intent and encoding semantics are captured together. The `debughelpers` module lives in the WSGI layer, outside `sansio`, and is imported lazily (for example by `Request._load_form_data` and `raise_routing_exception`). This keeps diagnostics separate from the core request path. Within the source shown, this class is not raised anywhere and appears to be a legacy hook.

`PassDict.to_json` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` builds `{k: self.serializer.tag(v)}` and aliases `tag = to_json`, so no wrapper key is added. JSON object keys must be strings, and tagging a key would produce a dict or list that cannot serve as a key. Session keys are already strings, so tagging them would add nothing. The only ambiguity is a one-item dict whose key collides with a registered tag. `TagDict` handles that case first by appending a `__` suffix to the key. `TaggedJSONSerializer._untag_scan` likewise recurses only into values.

`Flask.open_resource` in `src/flask/app.py`, and `Blueprint.open_resource` in `blueprints.py`, raise `ValueError` unless the mode is in {"r", "rt", "rb"}. `root_path` points at the application's package source. That source may be installed in site-packages, shipped in a read-only image or zip, or shared across deployments, so writing there would be unsafe and non-portable. Mutable, deployment-specific files belong in the instance folder. That is why `open_instance_resource` allows any mode relative to `instance_path`. The `encoding` argument only applies in text mode; `"rb"` opens the file without it.

The logic is in `FlaskGroup.get_command` in `src/flask/cli.py`. It first calls `self._load_plugin_commands()`, which loads `importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="flask.commands")` once and adds them through `add_command`. It then calls `super().get_command(ctx, name)` (`AppGroup`/click `Group`). If that returns something, the command came either from direct registration (run, shell, routes) or from an entry point. Otherwise it gets `ScriptInfo` via `ctx.ensure_object` and tries `info.load_app()`. On `NoAppException` it prints the error with `click.secho` and returns `None`. If loading succeeds, it pushes `app.app_context()` with `ctx.with_resource` when that app is not already current. Finally it returns `app.cli.get_command(ctx, name)`.

The test files were not included, so this describes the source-side chain such a test would exercise. Setting `app.config["SERVER_NAME"]` (and usually `subdomain_matching=True` on `Flask`) comes first. `@app.route(..., subdomain=...)` in `sansio/scaffold.py` goes to `App.add_url_rule` (`sansio/app.py`), which builds a `Rule` with that subdomain and adds it to `url_map`. Then `app.test_request_context` (`app.py`) builds a `testing.EnvironBuilder`. That builder uses `SERVER_NAME`, `APPLICATION_ROOT` and the subdomain argument to make the host `subdomain.server`. It calls `request_context`, creating `RequestContext` (`ctx.py`). That calls `Flask.create_url_adapter`, which does `url_map.bind_to_environ` with `server_name`, and `push` then calls `match_request`.

`TagUUID` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` subclasses `JSONTag` with key `" u"`. Its `check` tests `isinstance(value, UUID)`. `to_json` returns `value.hex`, and `to_python` rebuilds the value with `UUID(value)`. JSON has no UUID type, so plain `json.dumps` would fail or lose the type. The tag wraps the value as `{" u": hex}`. `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` then uses `_untag_scan`/`untag` to restore a real `UUID`. This gives lossless round-trips of session data in `SecureCookieSessionInterface`, which uses `session_json_serializer`. The 32-character hex form is compact (no dashes) and deterministic. `TagUUID` is listed in `TaggedJSONSerializer.default_tags`.

The session is opened in `RequestContext.push` (`src/flask/ctx.py`). When `self.session` is `None` it calls `app.session_interface.open_session(app, request)`, falling back to `make_null_session`. It is saved in `Flask.process_response` (`src/flask/app.py`), called from `finalize_request` within `full_dispatch_request`/`wsgi_app`. That runs `save_session` unless `is_null_session`. Flask does no locking or race handling. The `SessionInterface` docstring in `sessions.py` says requests with the same session may run concurrently in any order, and backends must synchronize themselves. The default `SecureCookieSessionInterface` stores everything in the cookie, so the last response written wins. Each request keeps its own session object on its `RequestContext`, isolated through `_cv_request`.

`ScriptInfo` (`src/flask/cli.py`) only stores `app_import_path`, `create_app`, `set_debug_flag` and `load_dotenv_defaults` in `__init__`, and sets `_loaded_app = None`. `load_app` imports or creates the app and caches it in `_loaded_app`. Laziness is needed because `FlaskGroup.make_context` creates `ScriptInfo` before the eager `--app`, `--env-file` and `--debug` callbacks run. `_set_app` sets the import path later, and dotenv variables such as `FLASK_APP` must be loaded first. Commands like `--version`, `--help` and plugin commands should still work without an app. `get_command`/`list_commands` can then catch `NoAppException` and report it. Caching ensures one app instance per CLI invocation.

`Blueprint.app_template_filter` calls `add_app_template_filter` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`). That defines `register_template(state)`, which sets `state.app.jinja_env.filters[name or f.__name__] = f`, and passes it to `record_once`. `record_once` wraps it to run only when `state.first_registration` is true, and `record` appends it to `deferred_functions`. When `App.register_blueprint` calls `Blueprint.register`, `make_setup_state` creates a `BlueprintSetupState` and each deferred function runs with it. The filter goes into the app-wide `jinja_env` (a cached property built by `Flask.create_jinja_environment`). `url_prefix` only affects `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule`, so the filter is available in every template whatever the prefix.

`_AppCtxGlobals` (`src/flask/ctx.py`) is a plain object whose `__getattr__`, `__setattr__`, `get`, `pop` and `setdefault` operate on `__dict__`; it has no locks. Isolation comes from context ownership. Each `AppContext.__init__` creates a fresh `self.g = app.app_ctx_globals_class()`. `AppContext.push` calls `_cv_app.set(self)` and stores the token, and `pop` resets it and checks for mismatches. In `src/flask/globals.py`, `g = LocalProxy(_cv_app, "g", ...)` resolves `_cv_app.get().g` on every access. Because a `ContextVar` holds separate values per thread and per asyncio task, concurrent requests each see their own `g`. Sharing one context across threads, for example via `copy_current_request_context`, is not synchronized.

Blueprint methods in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py` defer their work with `record_once`. These are `add_app_template_filter`, `add_app_template_test`, `add_app_template_global` and `app_context_processor`. On `Blueprint.register` they write into the app's shared `jinja_env.filters`, `tests` and `globals`, and into `app.template_context_processors[None]`. Blueprint-scoped `context_processor` entries are copied by `_merge_blueprint_funcs` under the prefixed blueprint name. At render time, `render_template` → `_render` (`src/flask/templating.py`) calls `Flask.update_template_context` (`app.py`). That runs processors for `None` and each name in `request.blueprints`, then sends `before_render_template`. Templates come from `app.jinja_env`, made by `create_jinja_environment` with `DispatchingJinjaLoader` searching app and blueprint loaders.

The test (likely `test_open_resource_with_encoding` in tests/test_helpers.py) writes a text file into a temp directory and creates `Flask(..., root_path=tmp_path)`. It then calls `app.open_resource(name, mode="r"/"rt", encoding=...)` and compares what it reads. In src/flask/app.py, `Flask.open_resource` first checks that `mode` is one of `{"r", "rt", "rb"}`, otherwise it raises `ValueError`. It then builds the path with `os.path.join(self.root_path, resource)`. In binary mode (`"rb"`) it calls `open(path, mode)` and ignores the encoding. In text mode it calls `open(path, mode, encoding=encoding)`, passing the encoding straight to Python's built-in `open`. The app-level default is `None`, while `Blueprint.open_resource` in blueprints.py defaults to `"utf-8"`.

The async view in the tests (`AsyncMethodView` in tests/test_async.py) subclasses `flask.views.MethodView`, because `MethodView` already handles async methods without extra code. `MethodView.__init_subclass__` collects the HTTP method names (get, post, …) into `methods` whether they are sync or async. `MethodView.dispatch_request` finds the handler with `getattr(self, request.method.lower())`, falls back from HEAD to GET, and calls `current_app.ensure_sync(meth)(**kwargs)`. `Flask.ensure_sync` detects coroutine functions and wraps them with `async_to_sync` (asgiref). `View.as_view` also routes through `ensure_sync`. Writing a separate async dispatcher would duplicate the method collection, the HEAD fallback and the routing metadata.

`test_locate_app_raises` in tests/test_cli.py is parametrized with `(iname, aname)` pairs: unimportable modules, missing attributes, unparsable expressions, non-literal arguments, factories called with wrong arguments, and attributes that are not apps. Every case asserts `pytest.raises(NoAppException)` around `locate_app`. In cli.py, `locate_app` turns a top-level `ImportError` into `NoAppException`, using `tb_next` to tell nested import errors apart. `find_best_app` and `find_app_by_string` raise `NoAppException` for `ast` parse failures, `ValueError` from `literal_eval`, `AttributeError`, and non-`Flask` results. They also catch `TypeError` and use `_called_with_wrong_args` to decide whether the call itself was wrong. So every failure path ends in one exception type, a `click.UsageError` subclass.

`Scaffold.__init__` in sansio/scaffold.py first sets `root_path`, using `get_root_path(import_name)` if none is given. In sansio/app.py, `App.__init__` then sets `self.instance_path`, either from `auto_find_instance_path()` (via `find_package`) or from a path validated as absolute. It then calls `self.make_config(instance_relative_config)`. `App.make_config` starts with `root_path = self.root_path` and replaces it with `self.instance_path` when `instance_relative` is true. It builds defaults from `default_config` with `DEBUG=get_debug_flag()` and returns `self.config_class(root_path, defaults)`. `Config.__init__` in config.py stores the value as `self.root_path`. `from_pyfile` and `from_file` later use it with `os.path.join` to resolve relative filenames.

`App._find_error_handler` in sansio/app.py first calls `_get_exc_class_and_code`. It then loops over the status code and `None`, then over each scope in `(*blueprints, None)`, reading `error_handler_spec[name][c]`. For every non-empty handler map it walks `exc_class.__mro__` one class at a time with `dict.get`. The worst case is about 2 × (nesting depth + 1) × MRO length lookups for each error, with no caching of the resolved handler. Each lookup on the nested `defaultdict` can also create empty entries. `handle_user_exception`, `handle_http_exception` and `handle_exception` (which looks again for `InternalServerError`) each repeat this search, so cost grows with hierarchy depth and the number of registered scopes. In practice the overhead is usually small.

`TagBytes` in src/flask/json/tag.py has the key `" b"` and its `check` is `isinstance(value, bytes)`. `to_json` returns `b64encode(value).decode("ascii")`, which is ASCII text that JSON can hold safely. `JSONTag.tag` wraps that as `{" b": ...}`. On load, `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` calls `_untag_scan`, which recurses through the structure. `untag` spots a one-key dict whose key is registered and calls `to_python`, which is `b64decode`, giving back the exact bytes. `TagDict` keeps this reversible: a real one-key dict whose key happens to equal a tag name gets a `"__"` suffix so it is not mistaken for tagged data. The fixed tag order and the single-key structure make the round trip lossless, for example in session cookies.

`Flask.test_cli_runner` (app.py) creates `test_cli_runner_class`, which defaults to `FlaskCliRunner` in testing.py, a subclass of `click.testing.CliRunner`. `FlaskCliRunner.__init__` stores the app. Its `invoke` defaults `cli` to `self.app.cli` (an `AppGroup`). It also defaults `obj` to `ScriptInfo(create_app=lambda: self.app)`, so `ScriptInfo.load_app` (cli.py) returns that same app, caches it and sets its debug flag. Commands registered with `AppGroup.command` are wrapped by `with_appcontext`. That wrapper calls `ctx.ensure_object(ScriptInfo).load_app()` and pushes `app.app_context()` through `ctx.with_resource`. `CliRunner.invoke` then runs the command with isolated streams and environment and returns a `Result`.

`_AppCtxGlobals` in src/flask/ctx.py backs the `g` object. Its attribute-protocol methods raise `AttributeError` for missing names. `__getattr__` and `__delattr__` read or delete from `self.__dict__` and turn a `KeyError` into `AttributeError(name) from None`, so `hasattr`, `getattr(g, x, default)` and `del` behave as normal attributes do. The dict-style helpers take defaults instead. `get(name, default=None)` uses `__dict__.get`, and `setdefault` uses `__dict__.setdefault`. `pop(name, default=_sentinel)` uses a module-level sentinel to tell "no default given" from `None`. Without a default it calls `__dict__.pop(name)` and raises `KeyError`, matching `dict.pop` rather than raising `AttributeError`. With a default it returns that value.

In src/flask/views.py, MethodView.__init_subclass__ does not pick a winner between parents. If the subclass defines its own "methods" in its class __dict__, that explicit value is kept and nothing is computed. Otherwise it builds a set. For each class in cls.__bases__ with a truthy methods attribute, it merges that collection in with methods.update(base.methods). It then adds the upper-cased name of every entry in http_method_funcs that hasattr(cls, key) finds, including inherited get or post methods. If the set is non-empty it becomes cls.methods. So multiple parents' methods are unioned and deduplicated, and nothing overrides anything else. View.as_view later copies cls.methods onto the view function for App.add_url_rule.

In src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py, Blueprint.add_url_rule is wrapped by @setupmethod and rejects dots in the endpoint or view_func.__name__. It then calls self.record() with a lambda that later calls s.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, view_func, provide_automatic_options=..., **options). record() only appends this callable to self.deferred_functions. The blueprint has no app when it is defined. Later, App.register_blueprint calls Blueprint.register, which builds a BlueprintSetupState via make_setup_state and runs each deferred function with it. BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule then applies url_prefix, subdomain, url_defaults and the name/name_prefix endpoint prefix, and calls app.add_url_rule. Deferring this way lets each registration use different options.

TagBytes.to_python in src/flask/json/tag.py calls b64decode. TaggedJSONSerializer.loads first parses the string with flask.json.loads, then calls _untag_scan. _untag_scan recurses into lists and dict values and rebuilds each dict. For each rebuilt dict it calls untag(). untag checks that the dict has exactly one key that is registered in self.tags, such as " b". If so, it dispatches to self.tags[key].to_python(value[key]), which for bytes is TagBytes.to_python returning the decoded bytes. Because the recursion runs depth-first, inner values are untagged before their enclosing dict. This path runs when SecureCookieSessionInterface.open_session loads the cookie through URLSafeTimedSerializer with session_json_serializer.

I read this as referring to after_this_request in src/flask/ctx.py, though I'm not certain. That decorator stores the function on the current RequestContext from _cv_request, in ctx._after_request_functions, and does not keep any state of its own. Flask.process_response in src/flask/app.py runs those functions, before blueprint and app after_request functions, and only through finalize_request. The list is never cleared and is tied to one context object. RequestContext.copy (used by copy_current_request_context) creates a new, empty list, so functions registered in a copy are lost. Functions registered after process_response, for example in teardown or in streamed generators, never run. Calling it outside a request raises RuntimeError.

In src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py, add_app_template_filter uses record_once to register a closure that writes state.app.jinja_env.filters[name]. Accessing app.jinja_env, a cached_property, forces Flask.create_jinja_environment to run eagerly at registration time. Every distinct blueprint also adds its own deferred function and record_once wrapper, which Blueprint.register runs. Each Blueprint construction also does root-path discovery through get_root_path and importlib, and creates a new click AppGroup. With many blueprints this per-object work grows linearly at startup. Filters with the same name silently overwrite each other, so the repeated work is also wasted.

App._find_error_handler in src/flask/sansio/app.py first calls _get_exc_class_and_code(type(e)). It then loops over codes in the order (code, None), or just (None,) for exceptions that are not HTTP errors. Inside that loop it iterates names = (*blueprints, None), so blueprint scopes come from innermost to outermost and the app (None) comes last. For each pair it reads error_handler_spec[name][c] and walks exc_class.__mro__, returning the first handler found. So the actual nesting is status code first, then blueprint scope, then MRO, not scope first as the question states. Flask.handle_http_exception, handle_user_exception and handle_exception call it with request.blueprints.

The test files were not included in what I was given, so this is a best guess. The helper is most likely a small path-like test class whose __fspath__ method returns the path string it wraps. os.fspath() calls this method to get a plain str. That lets Flask code such as the Scaffold.static_folder setter, Config.from_pyfile/from_file, send_file and the template_folder handling accept os.PathLike objects as well as strings.

This is about the existing-handler test in tests/test_logging.py, which was not included, so the exact test is inferred.
