A StreamHandler added to logging.root has level NOTSET, which is at or below the effective level, so the function returns True. Flask then adds no handler, and app.logger.handlers stays empty. The test confirms that Flask respects existing logging configuration and avoids printing every message twice.

The decision is made in `FlaskGroup.get_command` in `src/flask/cli.py`. It first calls `self._load_plugin_commands()`, which loads every `importlib.metadata` entry point in the "flask.commands" group and adds each one to the group with `add_command`. It then calls `super().get_command` (click's `Group`). That single lookup returns either a directly registered command (`run`, `shell`, `routes`) or a plugin command, since both now live in `self.commands`. If the result is not `None`, it is returned. Otherwise it calls `ScriptInfo.load_app()`. On `NoAppException` it prints the error and returns `None`. If the app loads, it pushes `app.app_context()` with `ctx.with_resource` when that app isn't already current, and returns `app.cli.get_command(ctx, name)` from the app's `AppGroup`.

The test itself is not in the provided sources; this is my best inference of the likely `test_subdomain`. The app is created as `Flask(__name__, subdomain_matching=True)` with `app.config["SERVER_NAME"]` set, which `App.__init__` stores and `url_map` uses. `@app.route("/", subdomain="<company_id>")` goes through `Scaffold.route` to `App.add_url_rule`, which builds a `Rule` with that subdomain. `app.test_request_context(...)` then uses `testing.EnvironBuilder`, which builds `base_url` from `SERVER_NAME`, `subdomain` and `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME`. That produces a `RequestContext`, whose `__init__` calls `Flask.create_url_adapter`. Because subdomain matching is on, `create_url_adapter` binds with `url_map.bind_to_environ(server_name=SERVER_NAME, subdomain=None)`. `ctx.push()` then runs `match_request`, and `url_for` and `Flask.url_for` build the URL with `url_adapter.build`.

`TagUUID` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` is a `JSONTag` subclass with key `" u"`. Its `check` matches `isinstance(value, UUID)`, `to_json` returns `value.hex`, and `to_python` rebuilds the object with `UUID(value)`. JSON has no UUID type, and `TaggedJSONSerializer` (used by `SecureCookieSessionInterface` for session cookies) must round-trip values without losing their type. The tag wraps the value as `{" u": hex}`. On load, `TaggedJSONSerializer._untag_scan` and `untag` find the key in `self.tags` and call `to_python`, so a UUID comes back as a `UUID` rather than a plain string. The hex form is chosen because it is compact (32 characters, no dashes) and unambiguous, which suits size-limited cookies.

Session opening happens in `RequestContext.push` in `src/flask/ctx.py`. On first push it calls `app.session_interface.open_session(app, request)`, falling back to `make_null_session`, before `match_request`. Saving happens in `Flask.process_response` in `src/flask/app.py`, reached through `full_dispatch_request` and then `finalize_request`. After the after-request functions run, it calls `session_interface.save_session` unless `is_null_session` is true. Flask itself adds no locking or race handling here. The `SessionInterface` docstring in `src/flask/sessions.py` says concurrent requests may share a session, gives no ordering guarantee, and leaves synchronization to custom implementations. The default `SecureCookieSessionInterface` is "last cookie written wins".

`ScriptInfo` in `src/flask/cli.py` stores `_loaded_app = None` in `__init__` and fills it in `load_app()`. The app can't be loaded at construction time. `FlaskGroup.make_context` creates the `ScriptInfo` before options are parsed. Eager callbacks then fill in what loading needs: `_env_file_callback` loads dotenv, `_set_app` sets `app_import_path`, and `_set_debug` sets `FLASK_DEBUG`. Lazy loading also lets built-in and plugin commands (and `--help` or `--version`) work without importing the app or when it fails to load. `get_command` and `list_commands` catch `NoAppException`. Caching means repeated calls from `get_command`, `list_commands`, `with_appcontext` and `run_command` reuse one instance instead of calling the factory again.

`Blueprint.add_app_template_filter` in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py` (also reached through `app_template_filter`) does not touch Jinja directly. It records a `register_template(state)` closure with `record_once`, which appends to `deferred_functions`. When `App.register_blueprint` calls `Blueprint.register`, a `BlueprintSetupState` is created and each deferred function is called with it. The closure sets `state.app.jinja_env.filters[name or f.__name__] = f`. The `url_prefix` only affects routes added through `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule`. Filters go into the app-wide `Environment` created by `Flask.create_jinja_environment`, so they work in every template regardless of prefix. `record_once` ensures this runs only on the first registration.

`_AppCtxGlobals` in `src/flask/ctx.py` is a plain object that stores attributes in `__dict__` and has no locks of its own. Isolation comes from structure. Each `AppContext.__init__` creates its own instance with `app.app_ctx_globals_class()`. `AppContext.push` sets `_cv_app` (a `ContextVar` in `src/flask/globals.py`) and keeps the token, and `pop` resets it. The `g` `LocalProxy(_cv_app, "g")` resolves to `_cv_app.get().g` for the current thread, greenlet or asyncio task. Separate requests therefore get separate `g` objects. It is not thread-safe if one context object is deliberately shared across threads, for example through `copy_current_request_context`.

Blueprint-scoped processors registered with `Scaffold.context_processor` (in `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py`) are stored under `template_context_processors[None]` on the blueprint. During `Blueprint.register`, `_merge_blueprint_funcs` copies them into `app.template_context_processors` keyed by the dotted blueprint name. At render time, `templating._render` and `_stream` call `Flask.update_template_context`, which runs the processors for `None` plus `reversed(request.blueprints)` and then re-applies the explicit context. App-wide hooks (`app_context_processor`, `add_app_template_filter`, `add_app_template_test`, `add_app_template_global`) use `record_once` deferred functions. Those write into `app.template_context_processors[None]` or `app.jinja_env`. `DispatchingJinjaLoader` searches blueprint template folders through `iter_blueprints`.

The `_HighlightFunc` protocol is defined in src/_pytest/assertion/util.py, with a `lexer` argument of "python" or "diff". `assertrepr_compare` and `_compare_eq_any` take `highlighter=config.get_terminal_writer()._highlight` and pass it down. `_diff_text` and `_compare_eq_iterable` call it with `lexer="diff"`. `_compare_eq_sequence`, `_compare_eq_set`/`_set_one_sided_diff`, `_compare_eq_dict` and `_compare_eq_cls` use the default python lexer. The concrete implementation is `TerminalWriter._highlight` in src/_pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py. It calls `_get_pygments_lexer`, which picks `DiffLexer` or `PythonLexer`. `dummy_highlighter` in util.py is the no-op fallback.

In testing/test_assertion.py, `TestImportHookInstallation` checks that `AssertionRewritingHook` (src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py) is placed on `sys.meta_path` early enough to rewrite conftests, `pytest_plugins` modules and entry-point plugins. Inline runs would reuse the parent process's `sys.modules`, meta_path hooks and cached `.pyc` files, so modules already imported would never be rewritten. `runpytest_subprocess` gives a fresh interpreter. The constraints are that verification works only through output matching (`fnmatch_lines`, exit codes), not by inspecting hook objects. Tests also have to be parametrized over `--assert` modes, and entry-point plugins need wrapper scripts such as mainwrapper.py.

In testing/test_argcomplete.py, the file defines a local `FilesCompleter` that mirrors argcomplete's version. The real `FastFilesCompleter` lives in src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py. Both expose the same callable `__call__(prefix, **kwargs)` interface. The module-level `equal_with_bash(prefix, ffc, fc, out)` helper compares both results, along with bash `compgen` output from `_wrapcall`. `TestArgComplete.test_compare_with_compgen` and `test_remove_dir_prefix` use this oracle/strategy comparison, so either implementation can change independently as long as the results still match.

I am not certain of the exact lines. I believe `DataclassWithOneItem` is defined near the top of testing/io/test_pprint.py, roughly lines 20–25, as `@dataclass class DataclassWithOneItem: foo: str`. It sits next to `EmptyDataclass` and `DataclassWithTwoItems`. These are fixture data for the parametrized `test_consistent_pretty_printer`. That test checks `PrettyPrinter` in src/_pytest/_io/pprint.py, which is used for verbose assertion diffs. It is test-only infrastructure under testing/io, mirroring the src/_pytest/_io package.

`SysCapture` (src/_pytest/capture.py, built on `SysCaptureBase`) replaces `sys.stdout`/`stderr` with a `CaptureIO` tmpfile and keeps the original in `self._old`. `snap()` reads `tmpfile.getvalue()`, then seeks to 0 and truncates, so each read returns only new output. `writeorg()` writes straight to `self._old` and flushes, bypassing the tmpfile. Because the two use separate channels, interleaving them never duplicates or loses output and never re-captures text written to the terminal. `_assert_state` makes sure both run only in valid states (started/suspended). `MultiCapture.readouterr` depends on this.

`TerminalReporter.pytest_internalerror` in src/_pytest/terminal.py does `for line in str(excrepr).split("\n"): self.write_line("INTERNALERROR> " + line)` and then returns True. Splitting ensures every traceback line gets the `INTERNALERROR>` prefix, which a single `write_line` call would not do. If the repr were guaranteed to be one line, the split and loop could be dropped for a single `self.write_line("INTERNALERROR> " + str(excrepr))`. `Config.notify_exception` in src/_pytest/config/__init__.py has a similar per-line stderr fallback.

`TestEvaluation` in testing/test_skipping.py builds items with `pytester.getitem` and calls `evaluate_skip_marks`/`evaluate_xfail_marks` from src/_pytest/skipping.py. For string conditions, `evaluate_condition` builds a globals dict containing `os`, `sys`, `platform` and `config`. It then adds any dicts from `item.ihook.pytest_markeval_namespace`, plus `item.obj.__globals__` (the test module's globals), before compiling and evaluating the string. So `os.sep` resolves through that injected `os`. The tests need the `pytester` fixture, a collected `Item` with a `config`, and an importable test module.

`PytestPluginManager` in src/_pytest/config/__init__.py subclasses pluggy's `PluginManager`. It already applies some policy in `register()`, `consider_pluginarg` (`-p no:` blocking via `set_blocked`/`is_blocked`), `_check_non_top_pytest_plugins` and `parse_hookimpl_opts`. A redesign would put all policies (blocked names, deprecated plugins, duplicate registration, conftest scope, hook validation via `check_pending`) into one validator layer called from `register`/`import_plugin`. That layer would raise `UsageError` or `PluginValidationError` deterministically. Tests in testing/test_pluginmanager.py would then check the raised errors instead of asserting internal state.

`Pytester.runpytest_subprocess()` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py` runs pytest in a separate Python process through `Pytester.run()`, which uses `popen`. It returns a `RunResult` holding `ret`, `outlines`, `errlines` and `duration`. `RunResult.__init__` tries to convert the raw process return code into the `ExitCode` enum from `src/_pytest/config/__init__.py`, keeping a plain int if that fails. The codes mean: OK=0 (all passed), TESTS_FAILED=1, INTERRUPTED=2, INTERNAL_ERROR=3, USAGE_ERROR=4 and NO_TESTS_COLLECTED=5. `.ret` is therefore the session's overall outcome as computed by `pytest_sessionfinish`/`wrap_session`, observed across a real process boundary.

In `src/_pytest/skipping.py`, `Skip` is a small frozen dataclass with one field, `reason` (default "unconditional skip"). `evaluate_skip_marks(item)` first walks `item.iter_markers("skipif")`. For each condition it calls `evaluate_condition()`, which evaluates string expressions against a namespace (os, sys, platform, config and `pytest_markeval_namespace` results) or applies `bool()`. On the first true condition it returns `Skip(reason)`. It then checks `skip` marks and returns `Skip(*args, **kwargs)`, otherwise `None`. The `pytest_runtest_setup` hook stores `skipped_by_mark_key` in `item.stash` and raises `skip.Exception(skipped.reason, _use_item_location=True)`. So `reason` is what finally appears in the report.

In `src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py`, `AssertionRewritingHook._is_marked_for_rewrite(name, state)` first looks up `self._marked_for_rewrite_cache[name]`. On a `KeyError` it checks each entry in `self._must_rewrite`, matching either the exact name or `name.startswith(marked + ".")`. It then records True or False in the cache, tracing via `state.trace`. Callers include `_early_rewrite_bailout`, `_should_rewrite` (used by `find_spec`) and the already-imported warning logic. Repeated imports or spec lookups of the same module name therefore reuse the cached decision. `mark_rewrite()` clears the cache whenever new names are registered through `pytest.register_assert_rewrite`, so stale negative answers are invalidated.

In `testing/test_tmpdir.py`, `test_tmp_path_fallback_uid_not_found` uses the `break_getuser` fixture. That fixture monkeypatches `os.getuid` to return -1 and deletes the LOGNAME, USER and USERNAME environment variables. The test writes a module that asserts `tmp_path.is_dir()` and calls `pytester.inline_run()`, which runs `pytest.main` in-process with a `HookRecorder`. During setup the `tmp_path` fixture in `src/_pytest/tmpdir.py` calls `_mk_tmp` and then `TempPathFactory.mktemp`/`getbasetemp`. There, `get_user()` catches `KeyError`/`ImportError` and returns `None`, so the directory falls back to "pytest-of-unknown". `get_user_id()` returns `None` for uid -1, which skips the ownership checks. Finally `reprec.assertoutcome(passed=1)` confirms the result.

`FastFilesCompleter.__call__` in `src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py` sets `prefix_dir` to the length of `dirname(prefix) + os.sep` when the prefix contains a separator. If the prefix has no "*" or "?", it adds `glob(prefix + ".*")` when the prefix is empty or ends in a separator, because a plain "*" skips dotfiles. It then appends "*" to the prefix. User-supplied wildcard prefixes are globbed unchanged. The results are sorted as full paths, directories get "/" appended, and `x[prefix_dir:]` strips the shared directory. Every match shares the same leading directory, so stripping after sorting keeps the order. The cost is dominated by an O(n log n) sort over full path strings.

In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, discovery happens in `FixtureManager.getfixtureinfo()` and `getfixtureclosure()`. They build `FuncFixtureInfo` (argnames, `names_closure`, `name2fixturedefs`) without failing when a name has no definition. Validation is deferred to execution time. `FixtureRequest._get_active_fixturedef()` and `getfixturedefs()` raise `FixtureLookupError` when nothing matches. `FixtureLookupError.formatrepr()` builds a `FixtureLookupErrorRepr` reading "fixture 'x' not found" and listing the available fixtures. `Node._repr_failure_py` in `nodes.py` special-cases this exception. Exceptions raised inside fixture functions instead propagate through `FixtureDef.execute()`/`call_fixture_func()` and are reported as ordinary errors with tracebacks.

`TestParser.test_parse_from_file` in `testing/test_parseopt.py` writes test paths, one per line, into a file under `tmp_path`. It then calls `parser.parse(["@" + str(path)])` and asserts that `file_or_dir` equals the original list. This verifies that `MyOptionParser` in `src/_pytest/config/argparsing.py` is built with argparse's `fromfile_prefix_chars="@"`, and that expanded arguments still reach the positional file_or_dir option. The feature, added in pytest 8.2, lets users pass very large lists of test IDs without hitting OS command-line length limits, especially on Windows. It also lets tooling generate reusable argument files.

`TestImportHookInstallation.test_rewrite_ast` in `testing/test_assertion.py` builds a package whose `__init__.py` calls `pytest.register_assert_rewrite('pkg.helper')`. `conftest.py` loads `pkg.plugin` via `pytest_plugins`, and the plugin imports the helper. Automatic rewriting only covers test modules, conftest files and modules registered directly as plugins, not arbitrary helper modules they import. `register_assert_rewrite` calls `AssertionRewritingHook.mark_rewrite()`, adding names to `_must_rewrite`, and it must run before the helper is imported. Putting it in `__init__.py` guarantees that ordering. This shows that rewriting is an opt-in, import-hook-based (PEP 302 `find_spec`/`exec_module`) design that cannot rewrite modules after they have been imported.

Indirect parametrization never hashes the parameter values; it identifies them by position. In `src/_pytest/python.py`, `Metafunc.parametrize` normalizes the values through `ParameterSet._for_parametrize`/`extract_from`. `_resolve_args_directness` marks each argname as "indirect" or "direct". `CallSpec2.setmulti` stores each value in `callspec.params`, plus an integer in `indices` and an id built by `IdMaker`, which falls back to argname+index for dicts. In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, `SubRequest` gets `param` and `param_index`. `FixtureDef.cache_key` returns `request.param`, and `FixtureDef.execute` compares cache keys with `is`, not `==`, so unhashable dicts are safe. `get_parametrized_fixture_keys` and `reorder_items` key on `param_index`, so the dict never needs to be hashable.

In `testing/python/fixtures.py`, `TestShowFixtures` has methods such as `test_show_fixtures_trimmed_doc`, `test_show_fixtures_indented_doc`, `test_show_fixtures_indented_doc_first_line_unindented` and `test_show_fixtures_indented_in_class`. Each one needs its own `pytester.makepyfile` source (module-level versus class-level fixture, different docstring indentation) and its own exact `fnmatch_lines` expectation. Parametrizing would mean pairing large dedented source blocks with large expected outputs, which hurts readability. Separate methods give clear, isolated failures and descriptive names, documenting each regression in `_showfixtures_main`/`write_docstring` in `src/_pytest/python.py`, which relies on `inspect.getdoc`/dedent handling. This follows pytest's general test style.

Each `pytester.getitem()` (in `src/_pytest/pytester.py`) writes a new module and builds a fresh `Config` via `parseconfigure`. It then collects through `getmodulecol`/`genitems`, which imports the module through `AssertionRewritingHook`. That means AST parsing, rewriting and compiling, plus pyc I/O. `evaluate_xfail_marks` in `src/_pytest/skipping.py` walks `item.iter_markers("xfail")`. For string conditions, `evaluate_condition` builds a globals namespace and calls `compile`/`eval` every time. Possible mitigations: per-item caching via `item.stash[xfailed_key]`, the rewrite pyc cache (`_read_pyc`/`_write_pyc`), building one item and reusing it, or memoizing compiled condition code by expression string (like the removed `cached_eval`).

`Metafunc.parametrize` in `src/_pytest/python.py` calls `_validate_if_using_arg_names(argnames, indirect)`. For each argname not in `self.fixturenames`, it calls `fail(..., pytrace=False)`. If the name is a parameter with a default (found by `get_default_arg_names`), the message is "already takes an argument ... with a default value". Otherwise it says "function uses no fixture 'x'" when the name is in the indirect list, or "uses no argument" when it is not. Separately, `_resolve_args_directness` fails with "indirect fixture ... doesn't exist" when an indirect name is not among argnames. `fixturenames` comes from `getfuncargnames` (required positional parameters only) plus usefixtures and autouse. `Failed` then surfaces as a collection error.

`LocalPath` is defined in `src/_pytest/_py/path.py`, pytest's vendored copy of `py.path.local`. The test `test_gt_with_strings` lives in `testing/_py/test_local.py`. `LocalPath.__lt__` and `__gt__` compare `os.fspath(self)` with `os.fspath(other)`. `os.fspath` returns a `str` unchanged and calls `__fspath__` on path-like objects. So both operands become plain strings, and mixed `LocalPath`/`str` comparisons reduce to ordinary string ordering. `__eq__` similarly uses `os.fspath`, with `normcase` on Windows, so equality checks also work with strings.

`PyCollector.isnosetest` in `src/_pytest/python.py` returns `safe_getattr(obj, "__test__", False) is True`. `istestfunction` and `istestclass` OR it with `funcnamefilter`/`classnamefilter`. A refactor could move the safe attribute lookup into a small predicate helper, such as a `_has_explicit_test_marker(obj)` validator. Detection could then be expressed as a list of composable predicates: Strategy, or Chain of Responsibility over name-pattern, `__test__` and other detectors, consulted by `istestfunction`/`istestclass`. To stay backward compatible, `isnosetest` should remain as a thin delegating (possibly deprecated) method. Subclasses such as `Module` and `Class` that call or override it would then behave as before.

In `src/_pytest/junitxml.py`, `_NodeReporter.write_captured_output` first returns early for passed reports when `log_passing_tests` is false, and when `logging == "no"`. With "log" or "all", it starts `content_all` with `_prepare_content(report.caplog, " Captured Log ")`. With "system-out", "out-err" or "all", it appends captured stdout and writes `<system-out>` via `_write_content`. With "system-err", "out-err" or "all", it writes stderr to `<system-err>`. Any leftover log-only content goes to system-out. So "all" aggregates log and stdout into one system-out element, plus stderr. A single "system-out" or "system-err" option emits only that one stream, and "out-err" emits both without logs.

In `src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py`, `AssertionRewritingHook.find_spec` checks `_early_rewrite_bailout(name, state)` before calling `self._find_spec` (`importlib.machinery.PathFinder.find_spec`), which does the filesystem work. On first use after `set_session`, when `_session_paths_checked` is false, `_early_rewrite_bailout` adds the basenames of `session._initialpaths` to `_basenames_to_check_rewrite`. That set is seeded with "conftest". It returns False (continue) if the module's last dotted component is in that set, if a `python_files` pattern has a directory part or matches via `fnmatch_ex`, or if `_is_marked_for_rewrite` is true. Otherwise it returns True, and `find_spec` returns None without any filesystem lookup.

`TestReport.from_item_and_call` in `src/_pytest/reports.py` takes `when` from the `CallInfo` and asserts it is not "collect". If `call.excinfo` is None, the outcome is "passed" and longrepr is None. If excinfo is not an `ExceptionInfo`, the outcome is "failed" and longrepr is the raw value. If the exception is a `skip.Exception`, the outcome is "skipped". In that case longrepr is a (path, lineno, message) tuple built from `excinfo._getreprcrash()`. When `_use_item_location` is set, it uses `item.reportinfo()` instead. Any other exception gives "failed". In the "call" phase, longrepr comes from `item.repr_failure(excinfo)`. In setup or teardown, it comes from `item._repr_failure_py(excinfo, style=tbstyle)`. Sections come from `item._report_sections` as "Captured {key} {when}".

In `src/_pytest/capture.py`, `CaptureManager` has hookwrappers `pytest_runtest_setup`, `pytest_runtest_call` and `pytest_runtest_teardown`. Each one enters `item_capture(when, item)`. That function resumes global capture and activates any capture fixture (capsys/capfd through `CaptureFixture`). It then yields, deactivates, and suspends capture. Next, `read_global_capture()` snapshots and resets the buffers. `item.add_report_section(when, "stdout"/"stderr", ...)` stores the output under that phase. Because buffers reset per phase, output stays separate. Higher-scoped fixtures are set up through `SetupState` in `runner.py` during the first requesting item's setup. They are finalized during the last item's teardown, so their output is attributed to those items' phases. `TestReport.from_item_and_call` then renders the sections.

In `testing/io/test_terminalwriter.py`, `test_attr_hasmarkup` creates `tw = terminalwriter.TerminalWriter(file)` with a StringIO file. It asserts `not tw.hasmarkup`, because `__init__` in `src/_pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py` sets `self.hasmarkup = should_do_markup(file)`, which is False for a non-tty. The test then binds the attribute by direct assignment, `tw.hasmarkup = True`, right before calling `tw.line("hello", bold=True)`. `TerminalWriter.markup()` checks `self.hasmarkup` to decide whether to wrap text in ANSI escapes. The test then asserts that "\x1b[1m" and "\x1b[0m" appear in the output.

The dependency runs one way. `evaluate_skip_marks(item)` in `src/_pytest/skipping.py` knows nothing about pytester. It only needs an `Item`, whose `iter_markers("skipif")` and `iter_markers("skip")` it evaluates through `evaluate_condition`, using `item.config` and the module globals. `Pytester.getitem(source, funcname)` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py` writes the source and collects it through `getitems`/`genitems`. It returns a real `Function` item whose markers were applied during collection (`MarkDecorator`/`store_mark`, pytestmark). Tests such as `TestEvaluation` in `testing/test_skipping.py` use `getitem` as the item producer, then pass that item to `evaluate_skip_marks` and assert on the returned `Skip`.

In `testing/python/fixtures.py`, package-scoped fixtures are cached per package by `FixtureDef.execute` using `cache_key`, so they are not re-created per test. The premise is partly wrong. Cost at scale comes from elsewhere. Every autouse fixture is added to every item's closure via `FixtureManager._getautousenames` and `getfixtureclosure`. That makes closure computation O(items × fixtures), plus `getfixturedefs` baseid matching. `SetupState` in `runner.py` stacks setup and finalizer registration, and each teardown runs finalizers in reverse with `values.pop()` bookkeeping. Each `pytester.inline_run` also builds a full in-process session with file creation. Cleanup cost grows linearly with the number of fixtures and packages, not with the number of tests.

The logic is in `LocalPath.__init__(self, path=None, expanduser=False)` in `src/_pytest/_py/path.py`. If `path` is None, it sets `self.strpath = error.checked_call(os.getcwd)`. Otherwise it converts the value with `os.fspath(path)`, raising ValueError for unsupported types. It optionally applies `os.path.expanduser` when `expanduser` is true. It then assigns `self.strpath = abspath(path)`, where `abspath` is `os.path.abspath` imported at the top of the module. This ensures every LocalPath stores an absolute string path.

In `src/_pytest/legacypath.py`, the `tmpdir` fixture depends on `tmp_path`. `tmp_path` in `src/_pytest/tmpdir.py` depends on the session-scoped `tmp_path_factory`. `tmpdir` simply returns `legacy_path(tmp_path)`, where `legacy_path` in `src/_pytest/compat.py` wraps the path in `LEGACY_PATH` (LocalPath). The conversion adds no new fixture dependency or directory; isolation comes entirely from `tmp_path`'s unique numbered directory and retention cleanup. `LegacyTmpdirPlugin` is registered in `pytest_configure` only if the tmpdir plugin exists. If the conversion failed silently and returned None or a cwd-relative path, tests could write into a shared location. That would contaminate other tests and escape `tmp_path` cleanup, because `LocalPath` resolves relative paths with `abspath`.

`ensure_deletable(path, consider_lock_dead_if_created_before)` in `src/_pytest/pathlib.py` returns False for symlinks. An OSError from `lock.is_file()` returns False, and any exception from `lock.stat()` also returns False. Unlinking a stale lock is wrapped in `contextlib.suppress(OSError)`, covering PermissionError or another process removing it first. It returns True only when the unlink succeeds. Every failure therefore becomes a conservative "not deletable" answer instead of an exception. `try_cleanup` simply skips that directory, and `cleanup_numbered_dir`/`cleanup_candidates` continue with the rest. Concurrent pytest processes cleaning the same basetemp cannot crash each other, and `maybe_delete_a_numbered_dir` adds further tolerance via garbage renaming and `rm_rf` error handlers.

The test is `TestRequestMarking.test_accessmarker_dynamic` in testing/python/fixtures.py. Its conftest defines a class-scoped autouse fixture `marking` that calls `request.applymarker(pytest.mark.XYZ("hello"))`, plus a function fixture `keywords` that returns `request.keywords`. `FixtureRequest.applymarker` in src/_pytest/fixtures.py calls `self.node.add_marker()`. For a class-scoped `SubRequest`, `node` resolves through `get_scope_node` to the `Class` collector, so `Node.add_marker` (src/_pytest/nodes.py) updates that node's `keywords` and `own_markers`. Each `Function` sees the marker because `NodeKeywords` looks up parent keywords. Autouse names come from `getfixtureclosure`/`_getautousenames`. `FixtureDef.execute` caches the class-scoped result, so the marker is applied before any test in the class reads it.

`TestRequestScopeAccess` in testing/python/fixtures.py declares `pytestmark = pytest.mark.parametrize(("scope","ok","error"), ...)`. Parametrization, via `Metafunc.parametrize` in src/_pytest/python.py, feeds each scope case into `test_setup` and `test_funcarg`. Both use the `Pytester` fixture from src/_pytest/pytester.py: `makepyfile` writes a module whose fixture has the given scope, and `inline_run` plus `assertoutcome` runs it. Inside that module, the scoped `SubRequest`/`FixtureRequest` properties in src/_pytest/fixtures.py (`function`, `cls`, `instance`, `module`, `path`) check `self.scope`. They return values only for allowed attributes and raise `AttributeError` otherwise. The generated tests assert `getattr` succeeds for the "ok" names and `pytest.raises(AttributeError)` for the "error" names.

Tests in testing/test_terminal.py get the reporter with `request.config.pluginmanager.getplugin("terminalreporter")` instead of calling `TerminalReporter(config)` directly. The reason is that `pytest_configure` in src/_pytest/terminal.py creates and registers the one real instance. That instance is already bound to the config, options, `TerminalWriter`, capture handling, and hook subscriptions. A second, hand-built instance would not receive hook calls and could diverge in state. This reflects pytest's pluggy-based architecture: components are named plugins registered in the `PytestPluginManager`. They are reached through the registry and hooks (inversion of control, a kind of dependency injection) rather than built directly, so they stay replaceable and loosely coupled.

`Pytester.runpytest_subprocess` in src/_pytest/pytester.py creates a numbered basetemp directory and prepends `-p` options for string plugins. It builds the command with `_getpytestargs()` (`sys.executable -mpytest`) and delegates to `Pytester.run`. `run` calls `Pytester.popen`, a `subprocess.Popen` wrapper with an adjusted PYTHONPATH environment. Output goes to files, and `run` waits with an optional timeout, raising `Pytester.TimeoutExpired` on expiry. It returns a `RunResult` (exit code, stdout/stderr lines, duration). Exceptions raised during collection never cross the process boundary. The child pytest turns them into collection-error reports and an `ExitCode` (for example INTERRUPTED or USAGE_ERROR), which the parent only checks through `RunResult.ret` and the output lines.

`TestAccesses` in testing/code/test_source.py builds one `Source(...)` object (two small functions) in `setup_class`. `test_getrange`, `test_getline`, `test_len`, `test_iter` and the others then share it. `setup_class` already caches it once per class per session. Each pytest run is a fresh process, though, so the object cannot be reused across runs without external persistence. `Source.__init__` (src/_pytest/_code/source.py) only dedents and splits a few lines, so the cost is trivial. Caching mainly changes isolation: a shared mutable instance could leak state between tests. Any performance gain is negligible compared with per-run interpreter and collection overhead.

`TestReadme` in testing/test_cacheprovider.py puts verification in a helper, `check_readme(pytester)`. The helper calls `pytester.parseconfigure()`, asserts `config.cache` exists, and checks that `config.cache._cachedir / "README.md"` is a file. Execution is separate: `test_readme_passed` and `test_readme_failed` write a passing or failing test with `pytester.makepyfile`, run `pytester.runpytest()`, then assert `check_readme(...) is True`. The behavior under test lives in src/_pytest/cacheprovider.py, where `Cache._ensure_supporting_files` writes README.md, .gitignore and CACHEDIR.TAG when the cache directory is created. The layering is therefore setup (`makepyfile`), then execution (`runpytest`), then a reusable assertion helper (`check_readme`).

`RunAndParse` in testing/test_junitxml.py stores `pytester` and the `schema` (an xmlschema object loaded from the xunit2 XSD by the `schema` fixture). Its `__call__(*args, family="xunit1")` handles orchestration: it adds `-o junit_family=...` and `--junitxml=<path>`, then calls `pytester.runpytest`. Validation is a separate step, run only when `family == "xunit2"` by calling `self.schema.validate`. Parsing is a third step: `minidom.parse` output wrapped in the `DomNode` helper. The method returns `(result, DomNode)`. The `run_and_parse` fixture builds the object, so tests only state arguments and assert on the outcome and the DOM.

In src/_pytest/_io/saferepr.py, `_format_repr_exception(exc, obj)` first describes the exception with `_try_repr_or_str(exc)`. That helper tries `repr()` and falls back to `type(obj).__name__` plus `str()`. If that also fails, the `BaseException` handler produces "unpresentable exception (...)" instead. `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` are always re-raised. The final string uses only `type(obj).__name__` and `id(obj)`, which cannot fail. `SafeRepr.repr`/`repr_instance` and `saferepr` catch errors from `repr()` and call this function. Each layer falls back to cheaper, safer information, so error reporting never cascades.

The functions are in src/_pytest/assertion/util.py. assertrepr_compare chooses the highlighter: config.get_terminal_writer()._highlight, or dummy_highlighter as a fallback. It then passes this _HighlightFunc down to _compare_eq_any, which dispatches to the helpers. _diff_text and _compare_eq_iterable call the highlighter with lexer="diff" on ndiff output. _compare_eq_sequence, _set_one_sided_diff (used by _compare_eq_set, _compare_gt_set and the related set helpers), _compare_eq_dict and _compare_eq_cls call it with the default "python" lexer on saferepr/pformat output. The real implementation is TerminalWriter._highlight in src/_pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py. Its _get_pygments_lexer picks pygments' DiffLexer or PythonLexer based on that Literal["diff", "python"] argument.

TestImportHookInstallation in testing/test_assertion.py checks that conftests, -p plugins, PYTEST_PLUGINS and setuptools entry-point plugins are rewritten by the AssertionRewritingHook. That hook is set up by install_importhook (src/_pytest/assertion/__init__.py) and Config._consider_importhook / _mark_plugins_for_rewrite. Inside the running pytest, sys.meta_path already holds a hook and the target modules may already be in sys.modules, so rewriting would be skipped or misleading. runpytest_subprocess gives a fresh interpreter with real early startup. The constraints: verification is only black-box, through stdout fnmatch_lines and exit codes, not by inspecting the hook. Fixtures must be real files on disk, environment changes go through monkeypatch.setenv, and the tests are slower.

There is no formal architectural decoupling here. testing/test_argcomplete.py defines a local FilesCompleter class, copied from argcomplete, as a reference implementation. TestArgComplete (test_compare_with_compgen, test_remove_dir_prefix) runs it alongside FastFilesCompleter from src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py. Both are plain callables with the same contract, __call__(prefix, **kwargs) -> list[str]. The equal_with_bash helper compares each one's sorted output against bash's compgen, run through _wrapcall. Bash acts as a shared oracle (differential testing), so either completer can change independently as long as it still matches compgen.

I'm not certain of the exact location. My best estimate is near the top of testing/io/test_pprint.py, roughly lines 15–25, as a module-level @dataclass with a single str field (foo). It is a test fixture class, not part of src/_pytest. It feeds the large parametrized test of PrettyPrinter.pformat in src/_pytest/_io/pprint.py, specifically the _pprint_dataclass path. It sits next to similar helpers such as EmptyDataclass and DataclassWithTwoItems in the same test module.

In src/_pytest/capture.py, SysCaptureBase.__init__ stores the original stream (self._old) and swaps sys.stdout/stderr for a tmpfile (CaptureIO, or TeeCaptureIO when tee is on). SysCapture.snap() reads tmpfile.getvalue(), then does seek(0) and truncate(), so each chunk is returned only once. writeorg() writes straight to self._old and flushes, bypassing the capture buffer so the output is not captured again. _assert_state enforces the started/suspended/done state machine. MultiCapture.pop_outerr_to_orig (snap, then writeorg) relies on this to replay captured output, for example around debugging, without duplicating or losing data.

TerminalReporter.pytest_internalerror in src/_pytest/terminal.py converts the ExceptionRepr to a string and splits it on newlines. It calls self.write_line("INTERNALERROR> " + line) for each line, then returns True. Splitting is needed so every line of a multi-line traceback gets the INTERNALERROR> prefix, which keeps the output greppable. If the representation were guaranteed to be single-line, the split and loop could go: one write_line("INTERNALERROR> " + str(excrepr)) call would do. That removes the list allocation and per-line overhead, though the gain is negligible.

TestEvaluation lives in testing/test_skipping.py and uses pytester.getitem to build a real Function item from source. The tests call evaluate_skip_marks / evaluate_xfail_marks, which go through evaluate_condition in src/_pytest/skipping.py. For string conditions, evaluate_condition builds a globals dict containing os, sys, platform and config. It merges in hook results from pytest_markeval_namespace and item.obj.__globals__ (the test module's globals). It then compiles and evals the condition. So os.sep resolves through that injected namespace; it needs a Config, a collected item with an obj, and markers reachable via item.iter_markers.

Policy should be enforced centrally in PytestPluginManager (src/_pytest/config/__init__.py) rather than asserted in tests. One approach is a declarative policy object (allowed or blocked names, essential plugins, deprecated aliases) checked in register() and import_plugin(). Another is validating hookimpls in parse_hookimpl_opts and calling pluggy's check_pending after configure. _check_non_top_pytest_plugins and Config._validate_plugins (required_plugins) should raise UsageError consistently. Rejections would surface through warnings or errors via the pytest_plugin_registered hook. Tests would then only check that violations are rejected, not re-implement the checks.

Indirect parametrization does not need hashable values. `Metafunc.parametrize` in src/_pytest/python.py turns each value into a `ParameterSet` via `ParameterSet._for_parametrize` and `extract_from`. `CallSpec2.setmulti` then stores the raw dict in `callspec.params` and an integer in `callspec.indices`. When the fixture runs, a `SubRequest` in fixtures.py carries both `param` and `param_index`. `FixtureDef.cache_key` returns `request.param`, and `FixtureDef.execute` checks for a cache hit by equality, falling back to identity if `==` raises. It never hashes. Item reordering (`get_param_argkeys`, `ParamArgKey`, `reorder_items`) groups by `param_index`, not by value. For IDs, `IdMaker._idval` cannot describe a dict, so it falls back to argname plus index, for example "arg0".

Each `TestShowFixtures` test in testing/python/fixtures.py needs its own source file built with `pytester.makepyfile` and its own expected output checked with `fnmatch_lines`. They cover different paths through `_showfixtures_main` and `write_docstring` in src/_pytest/fixtures.py: docstring trimming with `inspect.getdoc` and dedent, indentation handling, a first line that is not indented, and fixtures defined inside classes, which have different location and baseid handling. Writing them as separate tests keeps every input next to its expected text, so the tests read like documentation. A failure then points at one exact formatting rule. Parametrizing would mean passing multi-line source and expected-output blobs as parameters, which hurts readability and makes failures harder to diagnose, with little real saving.

The check is `Metafunc._validate_if_using_arg_names` in src/_pytest/python.py, called from `parametrize`. For each argname not in `self.fixturenames`, it first checks whether the name is a parameter with a default value (`get_default_arg_names` in compat.py). If so, it fails with "function already takes an argument 'x' with a default value". Otherwise it reports "fixture" or "argument" depending on whether the name was listed as indirect, and calls `fail(..., pytrace=False)`, which raises `Failed` and shows up as a collection error. Separately, `_resolve_args_directness` fails with "indirect fixture 'x' doesn't exist" if an indirect name is not among the argnames. `fixturenames` comes from `getfuncargnames`, which reads the signature and drops defaulted, `self` and mock-patch arguments, plus the usefixtures/autouse closure.

It is in src/_pytest/_py/path.py, class `LocalPath`, the vendored `py.path.local`; the test is in testing/_py/test_local.py. `__lt__` returns `os.fspath(self) < os.fspath(other)`, and `__gt__` does the same with `>`. `os.fspath` returns a str unchanged and calls `__fspath__` on a `LocalPath`, which returns `self.strpath`. So mixed comparisons become plain string comparisons. `__eq__` also uses `os.fspath`, wrapped in try/except `TypeError`, and applies normcase on Windows. `__hash__` hashes `strpath`, which keeps path objects consistent with their string form.

In src/_pytest/junitxml.py, `_NodeReporter.write_captured_output` behaves as follows:
- It returns early if `log_passing_tests` is false and the report passed, or if `xml.logging == "no"`.
- For "log" and "all", it starts with the caplog content passed through `_prepare_content` with a " Captured Log " header.
- For "system-out", "out-err" and "all", it appends stdout and writes everything through `_write_content` into `<system-out>`, then resets the buffer.
- For "system-err", "out-err" and "all", it writes stderr into `<system-err>`.
- Any content left over (the "log"-only case) is written to `<system-out>`.

So "all" means log plus stdout together in `<system-out>` and stderr in `<system-err>`. The out/err combination ("out-err") produces the same two elements but leaves out the logging records.

In src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py, `AssertionRewritingHook.__init__` seeds `_basenames_to_check_rewrite = {"conftest"}`, and `set_session` resets `_session_paths_checked`. The session is passed in by `pytest_collection` in assertion/__init__.py. The first time `_early_rewrite_bailout` runs with a session, it adds the base name of every path in `session._initialpaths` to that set. Then for a module name:
- If the last dotted component is in the set, it returns False, meaning no bailout.
- If any `python_files` pattern contains a directory part, or `fnmatch_ex` matches the module's guessed .py path, it returns False.
- If `_is_marked_for_rewrite` is true, it returns False.
- Otherwise it returns True.

When it returns True, `find_spec` returns None at once and skips the expensive `importlib.machinery.PathFinder.find_spec` filesystem lookup and the `_should_rewrite` checks.

`TestReport.from_item_and_call` (src/_pytest/reports.py) reads `call.when` (it asserts the phase is not "collect") and `call.excinfo`. With no excinfo, the outcome is "passed" and `longrepr` is None. If excinfo is not an `ExceptionInfo`, the outcome is "failed" and `longrepr` is the raw object. If `excinfo.value` is a `skip.Exception` (`Skipped`), the outcome is "skipped" and `longrepr` is a tuple built from `excinfo._getreprcrash()`. That tuple uses `item.reportinfo()` when `_use_item_location` is set, otherwise the crash path, line and message. Any other exception gives "failed". In the "call" phase it uses `item.repr_failure(excinfo)`; in setup or teardown it uses `item._repr_failure_py(excinfo, style=tbstyle)`. Finally, the `item._report_sections` entries become "Captured {key} {when}" sections.

In src/_pytest/capture.py, `CaptureManager` defines wrapper hooks `pytest_runtest_setup`, `pytest_runtest_call` and `pytest_runtest_teardown`. Each one runs `item_capture(when, item)`. That method resumes global capture, activates any `CaptureFixture`, yields, then deactivates and suspends. It calls `read_global_capture()`, whose `snap()` reads and truncates the buffer. The output is stored with `item.add_report_section(when, "stdout"/"stderr", ...)`. Because each phase drains the buffer, its output stays separate. `TestReport.from_item_and_call` turns these into "Captured stdout setup/call/teardown" sections. A higher-scope fixture's setup output lands in the setup section of the first item that triggers it. Its teardown output lands in the teardown section of the last item, through `SetupState.teardown_exact`.

In testing/io/test_terminalwriter.py, `test_attr_hasmarkup` creates `TerminalWriter(file)` on a StringIO. `TerminalWriter.__init__` (src/_pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py) initially sets `hasmarkup` from `should_do_markup(file)`, which is False here, and the test asserts that. The test then assigns `tw.hasmarkup = True` directly on the instance, before calling `tw.line("hello", bold=True)`. `TerminalWriter.write()` calls `markup()`, which only wraps the text in ANSI codes when `self.hasmarkup` is true. The test checks that "\x1b[1m" and "\x1b[0m" appear in the output.

The dependency is one-way and only exists at test time. `evaluate_skip_marks(item)` in src/_pytest/skipping.py knows nothing about pytester. It just needs an `Item` with `iter_markers("skipif")`/`iter_markers("skip")` and a `config`, which `evaluate_condition` uses for globals and the `pytest_markeval_namespace` hook. In testing/test_skipping.py, `Pytester.getitem(source)` (src/_pytest/pytester.py) provides that item. It writes the module via `getmodulecol` (`makepyfile`, `parseconfigure`, `getnode`), collects it, and returns the "test_func" `Function`. Decorator marks are stored by `store_mark` and later collected through `get_unpacked_marks` and node keywords. Marks are therefore attached at collection and evaluated lazily when the test calls `evaluate_skip_marks`.

`test_package_fixture_complex` (testing/python/fixtures.py) checks that package-scoped and autouse fixtures in a package conftest are set up once and torn down at the package boundary. Results are cached in `FixtureDef.cached_result`, and `get_scope_package`/`get_scope_node` choose the owning `Package` node. Scaling to hundreds of such fixtures adds cost in several places. Every item recomputes the autouse names (`FixtureManager._getautousenames`) and its closure (`getfixtureclosure`), and lookups go through `_matchfactories`. `reorder_items`/`reorder_items_atscope` grows with the number of argkeys times items. Each fixture registers finalizers in `SetupState`. If items from different packages interleave, package fixtures are finalized and re-executed repeatedly, with the generator teardown running each time.

The logic is in `LocalPath.__init__(self, path=None, expanduser=False)` in src/_pytest/_py/path.py. If `path` is None, it sets `self.strpath = error.checked_call(os.getcwd)`. Otherwise it converts with `os.fspath(path)`, raising `ValueError` on `TypeError`. It optionally applies `os.path.expanduser`, then assigns `self.strpath = abspath(path)` (`os.path.abspath`). Other constructors set `strpath` directly on objects made with `object.__new__`: `_fastjoin`, `new()` and `join()`.

`LegacyTmpdirPlugin.tmpdir(tmp_path)` in src/_pytest/legacypath.py returns `legacy_path(tmp_path)` (src/_pytest/compat.py), which wraps the path in a `LocalPath`. The chain is tmpdir → tmp_path → `_mk_tmp(request, tmp_path_factory)` → the session-scoped `tmp_path_factory`/`TempPathFactory`. The conversion creates no directory, so isolation comes entirely from `tmp_path`. If it failed silently, for example by passing None, `LocalPath(None)` would resolve to `os.getcwd()`. Tests would then write into the shared working directory and collide with each other. Cleanup by the tmpdir.py retention logic (`pytest_runtest_makereport`, `pytest_sessionfinish`) would not cover them. Fixtures depending on tmpdir would inherit the broken location.

`ensure_deletable(path, consider_lock_dead_if_created_before)` in src/_pytest/pathlib.py treats every uncertainty as a local, conservative decision instead of raising. Symlinks return False. An `OSError` from `lock.is_file()` returns False. If `lock.stat()` fails, it returns False. For a stale lock, `lock.unlink()` runs under `contextlib.suppress(OSError)`. Since nothing propagates, `try_cleanup` simply skips that directory. `cleanup_numbered_dir` then continues with the other candidates from `cleanup_candidates` and the "garbage-*" directories. `maybe_delete_a_numbered_dir` also renames to garbage before deleting, uses `rm_rf` with `on_rm_rf_error`, and swallows `OSError`. So when processes race on the same directories, one failure cannot abort the whole cleanup or the session.

`Pytester.runpytest_subprocess()` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py` runs `python -mpytest` in a separate process through `Pytester.run()`. It adds `--basetemp` and an optional timeout. It returns a `RunResult` holding `ret`, `outlines`/`errlines` (captured stdout/stderr, wrapped as `LineMatcher`) and `duration`. `RunResult.__init__` tries to turn `ret` into the `ExitCode` IntEnum from `src/_pytest/config/__init__.py`. The codes are: `OK`=0 (all passed), `TESTS_FAILED`=1, `INTERRUPTED`=2, `INTERNAL_ERROR`=3, `USAGE_ERROR`=4 and `NO_TESTS_COLLECTED`=5. Any other value stays a plain int. These match the process status set by `wrap_session` in `main.py`. Because the run is a real subprocess, `ret` reflects true process isolation, unlike `inline_run`.

In `src/_pytest/skipping.py`, `Skip` is a frozen dataclass with one field, `reason: str = "unconditional skip"`. `evaluate_skip_marks(item)` first goes through `item.iter_markers("skipif")`. For each condition it calls `evaluate_condition`, which handles bool or string conditions and evals strings with os, sys, platform, config and `pytest_markeval_namespace` results. The first true condition returns `Skip(reason)`; an unconditional skipif uses the kwarg reason. It then checks `skip` marks, taking the reason from args or kwargs. It returns None if nothing matches. `pytest_runtest_setup` stores the result in `item.stash[skipped_by_mark_key]` and raises `skip.Exception(skipped.reason, _use_item_location=True)`. That reason then appears in the reports and the terminal summary.

In `src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py`, `AssertionRewritingHook.__init__` creates `_marked_for_rewrite_cache: dict[str, bool]`. `_is_marked_for_rewrite(name, state)` first returns the cached value for the module name. On a miss, it checks `self._must_rewrite` for an exact match or a `marked + "."` package prefix, traces the decision and caches True or False. Two callers rely on it during import: `find_spec` → `_early_rewrite_bailout`, which skips the bailout for marked names, and `_should_rewrite`, whose last check is this one. `mark_rewrite()` (used by `register_assert_rewrite` and plugin and conftest registration) adds names and clears the cache, so stale decisions are dropped.

The test is `test_tmp_path_fallback_uid_not_found` in `testing/test_tmpdir.py`. Its `break_getuser` fixture makes `os.getuid` return -1 and removes `LOGNAME`, `USER`, `LNAME` and `USERNAME`. `pytester.inline_run()` calls `pytest.main` in-process with a `HookRecorder`. `tmpdir.pytest_configure` builds `TempPathFactory.from_config`. Running the inner test requests the `tmp_path` fixture, which goes through `_mk_tmp` → `factory.mktemp` → `getbasetemp()`. There, `get_user()` swallows getpass errors and returns None, so the name becomes "unknown". `compat.get_user_id()` maps -1 to None, which skips the ownership and permission check. The inner test asserts `tmp_path.is_dir()`, and `reprec.assertoutcome(passed=1)` checks the recorded reports.

In `src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py`, `FastFilesCompleter.__call__` sets `prefix_dir` to the length of the prefix's directory part plus the separator, or 0. If the prefix has no `*` or `?`, it is treated as literal. When the prefix is empty or ends with `os.sep`, it also adds `glob(prefix + ".*")`, because plain `*` skips dotfiles. It then appends `*`. In every case it extends with `glob(prefix)`, so the two result sets do not overlap. Results are sorted on full paths, directories get "/", and each entry has `x[prefix_dir:]` stripped. Every match shares the same directory prefix, so stripping after sorting keeps the order and gives bash-like relative completions.

Discovery happens at collection. In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, `FixtureManager.getfixtureinfo`/`getfixtureclosure` build `FuncFixtureInfo` from `getfixturedefs`/`_matchfactories`. Unknown names are left out of `name2fixturedefs` rather than raising. Validation happens later at setup. `TopRequest._fillfixtures` → `getfixturevalue` → `_get_active_fixturedef` raises `FixtureLookupError` when no definition exists. `FixtureLookupError.formatrepr` builds a `FixtureLookupErrorRepr` with "fixture 'x' not found" and the list of available fixtures. `Node._repr_failure_py` in `nodes.py` checks for `FixtureLookupError` and uses that compact repr. Real exceptions inside fixture functions are cached by `FixtureDef.execute` and re-raised, so they produce normal full tracebacks. That split is what separates missing fixtures from internal failures.

`test_parse_from_file` in `testing/test_parseopt.py` writes node IDs to a file. The IDs include `::` paths and parametrized `[param0]`. It then calls `parser.parse(["@path"])` and asserts that the `FILE_OR_DIR` positionals equal those lines. `Parser._getparser` builds `MyOptionParser` with `fromfile_prefix_chars="@"`. `MyOptionParser` overrides `parse_args` and `error`, so the test confirms that argparse's from-file expansion still works. Keeping test paths in a file avoids OS command-line length limits, especially on Windows. It also lets tools or CI generate reproducible selections, such as failure lists, and reuse them.

`test_rewrite_ast` in `TestImportHookInstallation` (`testing/test_assertion.py`) sets up `conftest.py` with `pytest_plugins = ['pkg.plugin']`. That plugin is rewritten automatically through `PytestPluginManager.import_plugin`/`consider_module` → `mark_rewrite`. `pkg.helper` is just a module the plugin imports, so it is not rewritten automatically. Calling `pytest.register_assert_rewrite('pkg.helper')` in `pkg/__init__.py` marks it before import. That call is in `assertion/__init__.py`; it finds the `AssertionRewritingHook` in `sys.meta_path` and adds to `_must_rewrite`. The unregistered `pkg.other` gives only a bare `AssertionError`. This shows rewriting is decided per module name at import time by a meta-path finder. Helper modules must opt in explicitly and early, otherwise `_warn_already_imported` fires.

In testing/python/fixtures.py, test_accessmarker_dynamic (TestRequestMarking) writes a conftest. It has an autouse, class-scoped `marking` fixture that calls request.applymarker(pytest.mark.XYZ("hello")), and a `keywords` fixture that returns request.keywords. In src/_pytest/fixtures.py, FixtureRequest.applymarker calls self.node.add_marker(). For a SubRequest, `node` is resolved through get_scope_node to the scope collector, so the marker lands on that shared Class or Module node's NodeKeywords and own_markers. Each item's NodeKeywords falls back to its parent's keywords, so every test under that node sees XYZ. FixtureManager._getautousenames puts `marking` in each closure, and TopRequest._fillfixtures runs it before the first test. FixtureDef.execute caches it per scope, so it runs once.

TestRequestScopeAccess in testing/python/fixtures.py uses a class-level pytestmark = pytest.mark.parametrize over (scope, ok, error) for the session, module, class and function scopes. That parametrization is expanded through Metafunc.parametrize in src/_pytest/python.py. Its test_setup and test_funcarg take the Pytester fixture (src/_pytest/pytester.py). They write a module whose fixture or test asserts that the `ok` request attributes are accessible and the `error` ones raise AttributeError. They then call pytester.inline_run and reprec.assertoutcome(passed=1). The validated logic is the scope-guarded properties of FixtureRequest in src/_pytest/fixtures.py: function, cls, instance, module and path. Each checks self.scope (via _scope and SubRequest's Scope) and raises AttributeError when the attribute is unavailable at that scope.

TerminalReporter is created and registered as the "terminalreporter" plugin by pytest_configure in src/_pytest/terminal.py. It is bound to the live Config, its TerminalWriter, verbosity options and accumulated stats, and it receives hook calls such as pytest_runtest_logreport and pytest_collectreport. Tests therefore obtain it via request.config.pluginmanager.getplugin("terminalreporter") or a fixture wrapping that call. This uses the configured singleton that actually participates in the run. A manually instantiated copy would lack the registration, the hook wiring and the shared state. The design reflects pytest's plugin architecture: components are loosely coupled, hook-driven plugins managed by PytestPluginManager. Dependency injection through fixtures and the plugin registry replaces direct construction.

Pytester.runpytest_subprocess in src/_pytest/pytester.py adds --basetemp and any -p plugins, prefixes _getpytestargs() (sys.executable -mpytest) and calls Pytester.run. Run uses Pytester.popen, which wraps subprocess.Popen with PYTHONPATH and the CLOSE_STDIN handling. Output goes to files, and the process is waited on with the timeout. handle_timeout kills the child and calls pytest.fail. The output is returned as RunResult(ret, outlines, errlines, duration), with ret converted to ExitCode. Exceptions never cross the process boundary. In the child, wrap_session in src/_pytest/main.py maps exceptions to exit codes: UsageError, Failed, KeyboardInterrupt/Exit (INTERRUPTED) and BaseException (INTERNAL_ERROR via notify_exception). Collection errors are captured by CallInfo.from_call in runner.pytest_make_collect_report into a CollectReport.

TestAccesses in testing/code/test_source.py builds one Source in setup_class from a small triple-quoted string. Source.__init__ in src/_pytest/_code/source.py splits and deindents it. pytest already runs setup_class once per class through Class._register_setup_class_fixture, a class-scoped xunit fixture in python.py. The tests test_getrange, test_getline, test_len and test_iter therefore share that instance. Extra caching would barely change performance, because construction is tiny and already amortized. Across separate runs, nothing persists in-process anyway, since each run re-imports modules. Any cross-run cache would mostly add the risk of shared mutable state, while Source slicing returns new objects.

TestReadme in testing/test_cacheprovider.py separates concerns with a helper method, check_readme(pytester). That helper only verifies the cache artifact: it calls pytester.parseconfigure(), takes config.cache._cachedir and checks that README.md is a file. The test methods, test_readme_passed and test_readme_failed, handle setup with pytester.makepyfile and execution with pytester.runpytest. Their assertion phase delegates to check_readme. The behaviour under test lives in src/_pytest/cacheprovider.py, where Cache.set and mkdir call _ensure_cache_dir_and_supporting_files. That method writes README.md, .gitignore and CACHEDIR.TAG. This keeps the arrange, act and assert steps distinct and reuses the verification logic across outcomes.

RunAndParse in testing/test_junitxml.py is a small callable class built by the run_and_parse fixture from pytester and the session-scoped schema fixture, an xmlschema.XMLSchema loaded from junit-10.xsd. Its __call__ handles execution by adding -o junit_family and --junitxml, then calling pytester.runpytest. It validates the produced file against the schema only for xunit2. It then parses the file with minidom and wraps it in DomDocument and DomNode helpers for querying. It returns (RunResult, DomDocument). Report generation itself stays in LogXML and _NodeReporter in src/_pytest/junitxml.py. Each concern is therefore a separate injectable piece: the runner (Pytester), the validator (schema) and the parser/query wrapper (DomDocument).

In src/_pytest/_io/saferepr.py, SafeRepr.repr and repr_instance catch failures of repr() and call _format_repr_exception(exc, obj). That function first tries _try_repr_or_str(exc), which attempts repr() and falls back to a type-name plus str() form. If that also fails, it catches the inner exception and produces "unpresentable exception (...)". Every layer re-raises KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit but swallows other BaseExceptions. The final string, "<[... raised in repr()] TypeName object at 0x...>", uses only type(obj).__name__ and id(obj), which essentially cannot fail. Error reporting through saferepr, FormattedExcinfo.repr_locals/repr_args and assertion rewrite's _saferepr therefore never cascades.

In src/_pytest/assertion/util.py, assertrepr_compare takes highlighter = config.get_terminal_writer()._highlight (the _HighlightFunc) and passes it to _compare_eq_any. That function dispatches to helpers that call highlighter with a lexer argument. _diff_text and _compare_eq_iterable call highlighter(..., lexer="diff"). _compare_eq_sequence, _set_one_sided_diff (used by _compare_eq_set, _compare_eq_gt_set, _compare_eq_lt_set and the gte/lte variants), _compare_eq_dict and _compare_eq_cls rely on the default "python" lexer. _notin_text calls _diff_text with dummy_highlighter instead. The actual lexer choice happens in TerminalWriter._highlight and _get_pygments_lexer in src/_pytest/_io/terminalwriter.py, which pick PythonLexer or DiffLexer.

TestImportHookInstallation is in testing/test_assertion.py, which was not in the material provided, so this is inferred. Config._consider_importhook calls install_importhook, which puts an AssertionRewritingHook into sys.meta_path at startup. _mark_plugins_for_rewrite and register_assert_rewrite act on modules that have not been imported yet. An inline run shares sys.modules, sys.meta_path and already-imported conftest or plugin modules with the outer pytest, so rewriting could be masked by modules already imported or rewritten in the parent process. Running in a subprocess guarantees a fresh interpreter. The cost is that checks can only use output, through RunResult.stdout.fnmatch_lines and exit codes. Monkeypatched objects do not cross the process boundary, so setup must go through files, PYTHONPATH or `-p` arguments.

testing/test_argcomplete.py was not provided, so this is my best guess. The test module appears to define a reference FilesCompleter that shells out to bash `compgen`, while the production class is FastFilesCompleter in src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py, which uses glob. Both share one callable interface, `__call__(prefix, **kwargs) -> list[str]`. A helper like equal_with_bash(prefix, ffc, fc) just compares their outputs. This is a strategy interface plus differential (oracle) testing. Tests such as test_compare_with_compgen and test_remove_dir_prefix only check that the outputs match, so either implementation can change internally as long as it still agrees with bash.

DataclassWithOneItem was not in the provided files, so I cannot give an exact location. My best guess is near the top of testing/io/test_pprint.py, roughly lines 15–25, as a `@dataclass` with one field. It would sit alongside EmptyDataclass and DataclassWithTwoItems as module-level fixtures for parametrized tests. Those tests would exercise PrettyPrinter._pprint_dataclass in src/_pytest/_io/pprint.py. The testing/io directory mirrors the src/_pytest/_io package.

SysCapture (src/_pytest/capture.py) swaps sys.stdout/stderr for a CaptureIO tmpfile and keeps the original stream as self._old. snap() reads the tmpfile, then seeks to 0 and truncates it, so each captured chunk is returned only once. writeorg() writes straight to self._old and flushes, bypassing the capture buffer. Both call _assert_state, so they only run in the "started" or "suspended" states. MultiCapture.pop_outerr_to_orig relies on this: it reads with readouterr() and re-emits with writeorg(). Interleaving the two therefore never duplicates or loses output, and replayed text never ends up back in the capture.

TerminalReporter.pytest_internalerror in src/_pytest/terminal.py loops over str(excrepr).split("\n") and calls write_line("INTERNALERROR> " + line) for each line, then returns True. Splitting is needed so every line of a multi-line traceback gets the prefix; passing the whole string would prefix only the first line. Config.notify_exception follows the same pattern when writing to sys.stderr. If the representation were guaranteed to be single-line, the split and loop could be dropped and replaced by one write_line call. That saves building a list and repeated ensure_newline and write calls.

TestEvaluation is in testing/test_skipping.py, which was not provided; this describes the code it would test. Conditions are evaluated by evaluate_condition in src/_pytest/skipping.py. It builds globals_ containing os, sys, platform and config (item.config), and adds dictionaries returned by the pytest_markeval_namespace hook. If the item has obj, it also adds item.obj.__globals__. The string is then compiled and evaluated. So os.sep resolves through skipping.py's own import of os. The test therefore needs a real Item with a config, for example from pytester.getitem, with registered marks (skipif/xfail via evaluate_skip_marks and evaluate_xfail_marks) and any conftest namespace hooks.

Enforcement currently happens piecemeal inside PytestPluginManager in src/_pytest/config/__init__.py. register() handles DEPRECATED_EXTERNAL_PLUGINS, consider_pluginarg rejects disabling essential_plugins, set_blocked and unblock control blocked names, _check_non_top_pytest_plugins rejects non-top-level `pytest_plugins`, and parse_hookimpl_opts filters hook implementations. A system-level design would add a declarative policy object consulted by register() before calling pluggy, covering allowed and blocked names, essential plugins, and conftest-only hooks. Violations would raise UsageError or issue PytestConfigWarning in one central place and be announced through pytest_plugin_registered. Tests would then check the policy's decisions rather than asserting on manager internals.

`Pytester.runpytest_subprocess()` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py` runs `sys.executable -mpytest` in a fresh child process through `Pytester.run()`/`popen()`. It adds a numbered `--basetemp` directory and turns string plugins into `-p` options. It returns a `RunResult` holding stdout/stderr `LineMatcher`s, the duration, and `.ret`. `RunResult.__init__` converts the process return code to `ExitCode` (from `config/__init__.py`) when possible, otherwise keeping the raw int. The codes are: OK=0 (all passed), TESTS_FAILED=1, INTERRUPTED=2 (for example Ctrl-C or session interruption), INTERNAL_ERROR=3, USAGE_ERROR=4 and NO_TESTS_COLLECTED=5. These are the values `wrap_session`/`_main` in `main.py` place in `session.exitstatus`. A timeout raises `Pytester.TimeoutExpired` instead.

`Skip` in `src/_pytest/skipping.py` is a frozen dataclass whose only field is `reason`, defaulting to "unconditional skip". `evaluate_skip_marks(item)` first walks `item.iter_markers("skipif")`. It takes conditions from `mark.args` or `kwargs["condition"]` and calls `evaluate_condition()`, which evals strings with the globals from `pytest_markeval_namespace` and returns a (result, reason) pair. The first true condition yields `Skip(reason)`; a skipif without conditions skips unconditionally. It then handles `skip` marks with `Skip(*mark.args, **mark.kwargs)`, re-raising a `TypeError` with a hint. The `pytest_runtest_setup` hook raises `skip.Exception(skipped.reason, _use_item_location=True)`.

In `src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py`, `AssertionRewritingHook.find_spec` calls `_should_rewrite`. That method rewrites conftest files, initial command-line paths and modules matching `python_files` patterns, and otherwise falls back to `_is_marked_for_rewrite(name, state)`. `_early_rewrite_bailout` also consults it. `_is_marked_for_rewrite` first returns `self._marked_for_rewrite_cache[name]`. On a `KeyError` it scans `self._must_rewrite` for an exact match or a `marked + "."` prefix, stores True or False in the cache, and returns. This memoizes the decision across repeated imports. `mark_rewrite()` (called by `register_assert_rewrite` and `PytestPluginManager.import_plugin`) adds names to `_must_rewrite` and clears the cache so stale negatives are recomputed.

This is the uid-fallback test in `testing/test_tmpdir.py`. It writes a test using `tmp_path` and calls `pytester.inline_run()`, which runs `pytest.main` in-process with a `HookRecorder` from `make_hook_recorder`. The flow is `Session` to `runtestprotocol`, then fixture setup in `fixtures.py`, then the `tmp_path` fixture in `src/_pytest/tmpdir.py`. That calls `_mk_tmp` and then `TempPathFactory.mktemp`, which calls `getbasetemp()`. `getbasetemp` reads `PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT` (set by `Pytester`) and calls `get_user()`. `get_user()` catches the `KeyError` that `getpass.getuser()` raises when the uid has no pwd entry and returns None, so `"pytest-of-unknown"` is used. `get_user_id()` checks ownership, and `make_numbered_dir_with_cleanup` creates the directory. `reprec.assertoutcome(passed=1)` then confirms success.

`FastFilesCompleter.__call__` in `src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py` first computes `prefix_dir`, the length of the directory part plus `os.sep`, when the prefix contains a separator. If the prefix has no `*` or `?` and is empty or ends with `os.sep`, it adds `glob(prefix + ".*")`, because plain `*` skips dotfiles. It then appends `*` to the prefix. Explicit wildcard patterns are globbed as given, with no hidden-file expansion. Both result lists are merged, sorted, given a trailing `/` for directories, and stripped with `x[prefix_dir:]`. All matches share the same directory prefix, so sorting before stripping gives the same order as sorting the bare names. Stripping is just a cheap per-element slice after one sort.

In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, discovery happens at collection. `FixtureManager.parsefactories` and `_register_fixture` fill `_arg2fixturedefs`, and `getfixtureinfo`/`getfixtureclosure` build a `FuncFixtureInfo`. Unknown names are tolerated silently at this stage. Validation is deferred to setup. `FixtureRequest._get_active_fixturedef` raises `FixtureLookupError` when no definition applies, and `_check_scope` reports scope mismatches through `fail(pytrace=False)`. `FixtureLookupError.formatrepr()` builds a `FixtureLookupErrorRepr` listing the available fixtures and suggesting `pytest --fixtures`. `Node._repr_failure_py` in `nodes.py` checks `isinstance(excinfo.value, FixtureLookupError)` to render that repr. `test_parse_from_file` in `testing/test_parseopt.py` checks that `MyOptionParser` in `src/_pytest/config/argparsing.py` really enables argparse's `fromfile_prefix_chars="@"`. The feature lets users or tools pass very long lists of test ids without hitting OS command-line length limits, notably on Windows. It also helps with generated selection lists from CI sharding. The test guards against regressions if the parser construction changes.

`test_rewrite_ast` in `testing/test_assertion.py` (`TestImportHookInstallation`) builds a package. Automatic rewriting only covers test modules matching `python_files`, conftests, and plugins passed to `PytestPluginManager.import_plugin`, which calls `rewrite_hook.mark_rewrite`. This shows that rewriting is an opt-in, name-based import hook decided by `_should_rewrite` at import time, so registration must happen before the module is imported.

Pytest does not transform non-hashable dict parameter values. In `Metafunc.parametrize` (src/_pytest/python.py), `ParameterSet._for_parametrize` builds the parameter sets. `_resolve_args_directness` marks argnames as indirect. `CallSpec2.setmulti` stores each raw value in `params[argname]` and its position in `indices`. `IdMaker._idval` cannot make an id from a dict, so `_idval_from_argname` produces `argname+index`. In fixtures.py, `FixtureRequest._get_active_fixturedef` reads `callspec.params[argname]` and builds a `SubRequest` with `param` and `param_index`. `FixtureDef.cache_key` returns `request.param`. `execute` compares cache keys with `==`, falling back to `is` on ValueError/RuntimeError, so no hashing is needed. `reorder_items` uses `ParamArgKey`, keyed by `param_index` rather than the value.

The TestShowFixtures tests live in testing/python/fixtures.py, which is not among the files provided, so this is inferred.
