Separate methods also give a clear name and an isolated failure for each formatting rule, and they let some cases differ in verbosity or extra flags.

Each `Pytester.getitem` call writes a file with `makepyfile` and creates a new Config via `parseconfigure`, which loads plugins and runs `_do_configure`. It then builds a Session in `getmodulecol` and runs `perform_collect`, which imports the module. That import goes through `AssertionRewritingHook.exec_module`, which reads the source, calls `ast.parse` and `compile`, and writes a pyc. `evaluate_xfail_marks` in skipping.py walks `iter_markers`, and `evaluate_condition` calls the `pytest_markeval_namespace` hook and recompiles string conditions every time. Existing mitigations are the `item.stash[xfailed_key]` result cache, `_read_pyc` (mtime/size validation), and the lru_cached `_get_assertion_exprs`. Further gains could come from reusing a single Config and item, or from caching compiled condition strings by text.

In `Metafunc.parametrize` (python.py), `_validate_if_using_arg_names(argnames, indirect)` checks each argname against `self.fixturenames`, which is the `names_closure` from `FixtureManager.getfixtureinfo`. That closure is built from `getfuncargnames` plus usefixtures, autouse and transitive fixtures. If a name is missing but is in `get_default_arg_names(function)`, the call fails with "function already takes an argument with a default value". Otherwise it fails with "function uses no fixture/argument 'x'", choosing "fixture" when the name is indirect. Separately, `_resolve_args_directness` fails with "indirect fixture 'x' doesn't exist" if an indirect list names something not in argnames. `fail(..., pytrace=False)` raises `Failed`, which surfaces as a collection error. Signature details matter because defaulted params, mock-patched params and bound `self` are excluded from the closure.

The class is `LocalPath` in src/_pytest/_py/path.py; test_gt_with_strings is in testing/_py/test_local.py. `__lt__` returns `os.fspath(self) < os.fspath(other)`, and `__gt__` returns `os.fspath(self) > os.fspath(other)`. `os.fspath` returns a `str` unchanged and calls `__fspath__` (which returns `strpath`) on path objects. So both sides become plain strings and are compared lexicographically, which makes LocalPath-vs-str comparisons work directly. `__eq__` works the same way: it uses `os.fspath(other)`, returns False on TypeError, and lowercases both sides on Windows. `__hash__` hashes `strpath`, lowercased on Windows.

`PyCollector.isnosetest` (python.py) is just `safe_getattr(obj, "__test__", False) is True`. It merges a safe attribute lookup with the test-detection decision, and it is called from `istestfunction` and `istestclass`, alongside `funcnamefilter`, `classnamefilter` and `_matches_prefix_or_glob_option`. A Strategy or Specification (composite predicate) pattern would separate these. A small attribute-reader helper would wrap `safe_getattr` and keep the identity check against True so mocks and `__getattr__` objects are not matched. The detection rules (name prefix/glob, `__test__` marker) would become composable predicates combined with OR. `isnosetest` would stay as a thin wrapper that delegates to the marker predicate, so subclasses and plugins that override it keep working.

In junitxml.py, `_NodeReporter.write_captured_output` returns early when `log_passing_tests` is false and the report passed, or when `logging == "no"`. The "log" and "all" modes prepend caplog, framed by `_prepare_content` with a " Captured Log " header. "system-out", "out-err" and "all" append capstdout with a " Captured Out " header, write the result to `<system-out>`, then reset the buffer. "system-err", "out-err" and "all" write capstderr with a " Captured Err " header to `<system-err>`. In "log" mode alone, the leftover buffer goes to `<system-out>`. The semantic difference is aggregation: "all" merges the log and stdout into one `<system-out>` element and also emits stderr. "system-out" or "system-err" each emit only one stream, and their combined form, "out-err", omits the log.

In src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py, `AssertionRewritingHook.find_spec` returns None if `_writing_pyc` is set or if `_early_rewrite_bailout(name, state)` returns True. Only otherwise does it call `_find_spec` (`PathFinder.find_spec`), `os.path.exists` and `_should_rewrite`. The first time `_early_rewrite_bailout` runs in a session (guarded by `_session_paths_checked`, which `set_session` resets), it adds each initial path's stem to `_basenames_to_check_rewrite`, which starts as {"conftest"}. A module whose last dotted component is in that set returns False, as does any `python_files` pattern containing a directory or matching via `fnmatch_ex`, or `_is_marked_for_rewrite`. Anything else is skipped early, before any filesystem access.

`TestReport.from_item_and_call` in src/_pytest/reports.py first asserts `call.when != "collect"` and collects duration, start, stop and keywords. If `call.excinfo` is empty, the outcome is "passed" and longrepr is None. If excinfo is not an `ExceptionInfo`, the outcome is "failed" and the raw object becomes longrepr. If the exception is a `skip.Exception` (`Skipped`), the outcome is "skipped" and longrepr is a (path, lineno, message) tuple built from `excinfo._getreprcrash()`. When `_use_item_location` is set, `item.reportinfo()` supplies that location instead. Any other exception gives "failed": in the "call" phase it uses `item.repr_failure(excinfo)`; in setup or teardown it uses `item._repr_failure_py(excinfo, style=tbstyle)`. Finally, `item._report_sections` become sections named "Captured {key} {when}".

In src/_pytest/capture.py, `CaptureManager` defines hookwrappers `pytest_runtest_setup`, `pytest_runtest_call` and `pytest_runtest_teardown`, each wrapping the phase in the `item_capture(when, item)` context manager. That manager resumes global capture and activates any capsys/capfd `CaptureFixture`, then yields. Afterwards it deactivates the fixture, suspends global capture and calls `read_global_capture()`. Because `MultiCapture.readouterr` snaps and truncates the buffers, each phase gets only its own output, stored via `item.add_report_section(when, "stdout"/"stderr", ...)`. Higher-scoped fixture setup or teardown runs inside some item's setup or teardown phase (via `SetupState`), so its output is attributed to that item's setup or teardown sections. `TestReport.from_item_and_call` turns these into "Captured stdout setup" and similar sections. `set_fixture` forbids two capture fixtures at once.

There is no direct code dependency between the two; the tests in testing/test_skipping.py, which are not among the provided files, presumably connect them. `Pytester.getitem(source, funcname)` in src/_pytest/pytester.py calls `getitems`, which uses `getmodulecol` (`makepyfile`, `parseconfigure`, `getnode`) and then `genitems`. The body of `test_package_fixture_complex` is in testing/python/fixtures.py, which is not among the provided files, so this answer reasons from the fixture machinery. The logic is in `LocalPath.__init__(self, path=None, expanduser=False)` in src/_pytest/_py/path.py. If `path` is None, it sets `self.strpath = error.checked_call(os.getcwd)`. `LegacyTmpdirPlugin.tmpdir(tmp_path)` in src/_pytest/legacypath.py returns `legacy_path(tmp_path)`. `legacy_path` in src/_pytest/compat.py wraps the path as `LEGACY_PATH` (`LocalPath`). The chain is tmpdir → `tmp_path` → session `tmp_path_factory` → `TempPathFactory.getbasetemp`/`mktemp` in src/_pytest/tmpdir.py. `tmpdir` adds no teardown of its own; cleanup and retention stay with `tmp_path`, `pytest_sessionfinish` and `make_numbered_dir_with_cleanup`. If the conversion failed silently, for example by passing None, `LocalPath` would fall back to `os.getcwd()`. Tests would then write into a shared working directory instead of unique per-test directories. Files would leak between tests and xdist workers, and `tmp_path` retention cleanup would never remove them, breaking isolation.

`ensure_deletable` in src/_pytest/pathlib.py is conservative at every step. It returns False for symlinks. If checking `lock.is_file()` raises `OSError`, it returns False. If `lock.stat()` raises any exception, it returns False, meaning the directory is treated as not deletable rather than crashing. Only when the lock is older than `consider_lock_dead_if_created_before` does it try `lock.unlink()`, inside `contextlib.suppress(OSError)`, and return True. `try_cleanup` and `cleanup_numbered_dir` call it once per candidate directory, and `maybe_delete_a_numbered_dir` also swallows `OSError` and uses `rm_rf` with `on_rm_rf_error`. A failure on one directory therefore only skips that directory, and concurrent processes never propagate exceptions out of the cleanup loop.

In testing/python/fixtures.py, test_accessmarker_dynamic writes a conftest with an autouse fixture `marking(request)` that calls `request.applymarker(pytest.mark.XYZ("hello"))`. TopRequest._fillfixtures then runs it through FixtureDef.execute and pytest_fixture_setup before the other fixtures. Because the fixture is function-scoped, the cache key differs per item. It therefore re-executes for each Function, so every test sees the marker on its own node.

TestRequestScopeAccess in testing/python/fixtures.py uses a class-level `pytestmark = pytest.mark.parametrize(("scope","ok","error"), ...)`. Each test uses the Pytester fixture (pytester.py) to makepyfile a fixture with that scope that touches request.path, cls, module, function and instance. The terminal tests obtain the reporter through a fixture that uses request.config, typically `config.pluginmanager.getplugin("terminalreporter")`, instead of constructing a fresh TerminalReporter. The real reporter is created and registered by `pytest_configure` in src/_pytest/terminal.py. That registered instance is already wired to the Config, the TerminalWriter, verbosity, reportchars and other hook implementations. Retrieving it through the request gives tests the same configured singleton that the hooks use. This reflects pytest's inversion-of-control design: components are plugins registered in PytestPluginManager (a pluggy manager) and found by name or hook. They are not hard-wired dependencies, and fixtures act as the dependency-injection layer.

In src/_pytest/pytester.py, Pytester.runpytest_subprocess builds a numbered basetemp with make_numbered_dir and adds `-p` plugin args. It then calls `_getpytestargs()` (sys.executable -mpytest) and delegates to Pytester.run. Pytester.run calls Pytester.popen, which wraps subprocess.Popen with PYTHONPATH set and stdout/stderr redirected to files. It waits with an optional timeout, raising Pytester.TimeoutExpired, and returns a RunResult with ExitCode and the captured lines. Exceptions are not propagated across the process boundary. In the child, main and wrap_session in config/__init__.py and main.py turn collection errors into failed CollectReports and Session.Interrupted, or into UsageError, INTERRUPTED or INTERNAL_ERROR exit codes. The parent therefore only sees the exit code and text output.

TestAccesses in testing/code/test_source.py builds `self.source = Source(...)` once in setup_class rather than per test. Source.__init__ in _code/source.py dedents and splits lines, so this avoids repeating that work for each test in the class. The saving is tiny, and the cache lives only on the class object for one process. Repeated pytest runs start new interpreters, so nothing carries over and each run pays the construction cost once. Rerun loops such as --lf or pytester in-process runs still re-execute setup_class per collection. The main effect is shared state between tests, which is safe only because the tests treat Source as read-only, not a meaningful performance difference.

TestReadme in testing/test_cacheprovider.py uses a helper `check_readme(pytester)` that only checks whether `.pytest_cache/README.md` exists under pytester.path. Its tests, such as test_readme_passed and test_readme_failed, handle setup and execution through pytester.makepyfile and pytester.runpytest. They then assert on check_readme. The README is produced in src/_pytest/cacheprovider.py by Cache._ensure_cache_dir_and_supporting_files, triggered from Cache.set or mkdir. This happens for example when LFPlugin or NFPlugin write lastfailed or nodeids in pytest_sessionfinish. That keeps verification of on-disk state separate from running the session and from the outcome assertions.

RunAndParse in testing/test_junitxml.py is built by the run_and_parse fixture with a pytester and the xmlschema `schema` fixture loaded from junit-10.xsd. Its __call__ runs `pytester.runpytest("--junitxml=...", "-o junit_family=...", *args)`; LogXML in src/_pytest/junitxml.py writes the report. Only when family is "xunit2" does it validate the file with self.schema.validate. It then parses the file with xml.dom.minidom and wraps it in DomNode, returning (result, DomNode). Execution, optional schema validation and parsing are thus sequential, independent steps. Test bodies only assert on the result and nodes.

In src/_pytest/_io/saferepr.py there are three layers. _try_repr_or_str tries repr(obj), re-raises KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, and falls back to `f'{type(obj).__name__}("{obj}")'`. _format_repr_exception calls _try_repr_or_str on the raised exception. If that also fails with any BaseException except KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit, it uses "unpresentable exception (...)" from _try_repr_or_str of the inner exception. It then returns a fixed string `<[info raised in repr()] TypeName object at 0x...>` built only from type name and id. SafeRepr.repr, repr_instance and safeformat call it from their exception handlers. A failing __repr__ therefore never raises during assertion or traceback reporting, while interrupts still propagate.

guess_filename in requests/utils.py reads obj.name and returns it only if it is a string that is not wrapped in angle brackets (such as "<stdin>" or "<fdopen>"). It then returns only os.path.basename(name). RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files in requests/models.py calls it when building multipart bodies. Because of this check, pseudo-names from in-memory or OS streams are never sent as filenames. Non-string names, such as integer file descriptors, are also rejected. Taking only the basename means the client's absolute local path (directory layout, usernames) is not leaked in the Content-Disposition header. It also keeps directory components like "../" out of what the server receives. In short, the check limits information disclosure and avoids handing servers path-traversal-shaped filenames.

In requests/models.py, Response.__enter__ returns self and __exit__ calls self.close(). Response.close() closes self.raw (the urllib3 HTTPResponse set by HTTPAdapter.build_response in adapters.py) only when _content_consumed is False. It then calls raw.release_conn() if that method exists, returning the connection to the urllib3 pool. Double-close is not prevented by an explicit flag. It is avoided because _content_consumed is set once iter_content's generator is exhausted, so fully read bodies skip raw.close(). urllib3's close() and release_conn() are idempotent, so calling close() repeatedly, for example from with plus an explicit call, is safe. Session.send also releases connections for non-streamed responses after reading content.

requests/cookies.py merge_cookies is called in Session.prepare_request in sessions.py. There it merges self.cookies into a fresh RequestsCookieJar and then adds the per-request cookies, so request cookies override session cookies. It is also used in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects as merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies). Without these calls the PreparedRequest would carry only one source of cookies, losing either session login cookies or request-specific ones. Redirect hops would also drop session cookies gathered along the way. Auth flows that depend on cookies would then break, for example HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 in auth.py, which rebuilds the request via prep.prepare_cookies(prep._cookies) after extract_cookies_to_jar. The result is unauthenticated retries and failed authentication.

CaseInsensitiveDict in requests/structures.py stores entries as _store[key.lower()] = (key, value). __getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__ and __contains__ each call key.lower() again. Every call allocates a new string and costs O(len(key)) before the O(1) OrderedDict hash lookup. The overhead therefore scales with lookup frequency and key length, not with dictionary size. With millions of lookups, the repeated allocation and hashing of the lowered copy dominates. Possible optimizations: cache normalized keys with a functools.lru_cache helper, or have callers pre-normalize and reuse lowered keys. Another option is a key wrapper object that computes lower() and its hash once. Interning common header names (sys.intern), so lowered strings are shared and hashed once, also helps.

In tests/test_requests.py, TestTimeout.test_none_timeout is decorated with pytest.mark.parametrize("timeout", (None, Urllib3Timeout(connect=None, read=None))). pytest supplies the timeout argument directly from the parametrize marker, generating two test items. The httpbin argument resolves to the httpbin fixture in tests/conftest.py. That fixture depends on pytest-httpbin's plugin httpbin fixture (a live local server) and returns prepare_url(httpbin), a URL-builder closure. At runtime the test calls requests.get(httpbin("get"), timeout=timeout) and asserts status 200. The timeout flows through Session.send to HTTPAdapter.send in adapters.py, which builds or uses a TimeoutSauce/urllib3 Timeout that never times out.

The Server class is in tests/testserver/server.py; it subclasses threading.Thread. TestTestServer lives in tests/test_testserver.py. Server.__enter__ calls start() and waits on ready_event, which run() sets after _create_socket_and_bind picks a port; it then returns (host, port). run() calls _handle_requests to accept requests_to_handle connections. It optionally waits on wait_to_close_event, and in a finally block calls _close_server_sock_ignore_errors and sets stop_event. Server.__exit__ waits on stop_event normally; on exceptions it sets wait_to_close_event and closes the socket. It always joins the thread. Tests such as test_server_closes, test_basic_waiting_server, test_server_finishes_on_error and test_requests_after_timeout_are_not_received check this lifecycle.

TestContentEncodingDetection.test_pragmas in tests/test_utils.py is parametrized with four inputs: an HTML5 meta charset, an http-equiv Content-Type meta (with and without a self-closing slash), and an XML declaration with encoding="UTF-8". It asserts get_encodings_from_content in requests/utils.py returns exactly one item equal to "UTF-8". Contrary to the question's premise, nothing is normalized: case is preserved exactly as declared. The test also assumes the declaration is found in the body markup, via the charset_re, pragma_re and xml_re regexes, not in HTTP headers. It assumes quoting variants and self-closing tags are handled, and that duplicate matches are not produced.

Response in requests/models.py starts with _content = False and _content_consumed = False. The content property reads the body once via b"".join(iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)), caches it in _content and sets _content_consumed. It raises RuntimeError if the stream was already consumed without caching. iter_content chooses reused_chunks (iter_slices over the cached _content) when content is already cached, otherwise a streaming generate() over raw.stream. It raises StreamConsumedError if the stream was read but nothing was cached. With stream=True, users iterate chunks without buffering, which avoids memory exhaustion. Session.send eagerly accesses r.content when stream is False. text, json, iter_lines and __getstate__ all build on content, keeping both access patterns compatible.

In requests/models.py, the Response.links property reads the "link" header and parses it with parse_header_links in requests/utils.py. It builds a dict keyed by link.get("rel") or, if that is missing, link.get("url"), and assigns resolved_links[key] = link. When several entries share the same rel, each later entry silently overwrites the earlier one, so the last one wins and the others are lost. There is no error and no list accumulation. Building the dict is O(n) and each lookup is O(1). The cost of that fast lookup is that the mapping is not injective, so duplicate-rel entries are lost.

The test itself never branches. TestIsValidCIDR.test_invalid in tests/test_utils.py is parametrized by pytest.mark.parametrize with inputs such as "8.8.8.8", "192.168.1.0/a", "192.168.1.0/128", "192.168.1.0/-1" and "192.168.1.999/24", and simply asserts that is_valid_cidr(value) is falsy. The branching happens inside requests/utils.py is_valid_cidr. If string_network.count("/") != 1, it returns False at once. Otherwise int(mask) can raise ValueError and return False. A mask outside 1–32 returns False. Finally socket.inet_aton(address) can raise OSError and return False. Each parametrized value is chosen to exercise one of these paths.

In requests/exceptions.py, InvalidSchema(RequestException, ValueError) means the URL scheme is invalid or unsupported. RequestException derives from IOError (OSError), so InvalidSchema belongs to the library's I/O-flavoured error tree. Callers using "except RequestException" catch it with other transport failures. ValueError expresses that the caller passed a bad argument value, which follows Python convention for invalid input. It is raised by Session.get_adapter in sessions.py ("No connection adapters were found") and by HTTPAdapter.proxy_manager_for in adapters.py when SOCKS support is missing. The dual base lets generic validation code catch it as ValueError while staying in the requests hierarchy, and it keeps backward compatibility.

In requests/models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare_body decides that data is a stream when it is iterable but not a string, list, tuple or Mapping. In that case, if files is also set, it raises NotImplementedError("Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive."). Multipart encoding goes through RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files, which calls urllib3's encode_multipart_formdata and needs concrete fields and file contents in memory. An arbitrary stream is opaque, possibly unbounded and of unknown length. Merging would mean buffering the whole stream, which defeats streaming. It would also clash with the Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding: chunked handling. Failing loudly is clearer than guessing.

In requests/cookies.py, MockRequest wraps a PreparedRequest for http.cookiejar. Its host property calls get_host(), and get_host returns urlparse(self._r.url).netloc. Each access therefore pays for a property descriptor call, a method call and a full URL parse. Repeated millions of times, that overhead adds up compared with reading a stored attribute. One optimization is to compute the parsed URL or netloc once in __init__. Another is to use functools.cached_property or a lazily stored self._host, since _r.url does not change for a MockRequest's short life. In practice the impact is small: extract_cookies_to_jar and get_cookie_header create a fresh MockRequest per request, so host is only read a few times.

In requests/cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie starts with expires = None. If morsel["max-age"] is truthy, it tries expires = int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"])). A ValueError there is re-raised as TypeError("max-age: ... must be integer"). Otherwise, an elif on morsel["expires"] parses the value with time.strptime using the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" and converts it with calendar.timegm. If neither field is set, expires stays None. The result goes to create_cookie. So the TypeError comes from the max-age path, not from expires. A malformed expires string raises ValueError from strptime instead.

Requests already does this, in requests/__init__.py. check_compatibility(urllib3_version, chardet_version, charset_normalizer_version) parses the version strings and asserts the supported ranges. The module wraps the call in try/except (AssertionError, ValueError) and calls warnings.warn with RequestsDependencyWarning. That class is defined in requests/exceptions.py as a subclass of RequestsWarning, which derives from Warning. _check_cryptography follows the same pattern for pyOpenSSL. Because mismatches produce warnings rather than exceptions, imports never fail and existing code keeps working. Users can still escalate the warnings with filters. Any new checks should keep this warning-based design and avoid raising new exception types.

In requests/utils.py, get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=None) returns {} when should_bypass_proxies(url, no_proxy=no_proxy) is true, and otherwise returns urllib's getproxies(). In should_bypass_proxies, an explicit no_proxy argument replaces the NO_PROXY/no_proxy environment value. It is also temporarily injected through set_environ around proxy_bypass(). This lets per-request settings, passed from Session.rebuild_proxies or resolve_proxies via proxies.get("no_proxy"), override the environment. A non-empty dictionary means the URL was not excluded, so the environment proxy mappings apply. That dictionary is the full scheme-to-proxy mapping and is not filtered to the URL's scheme.

In requests/models.py, RequestHooksMixin.register_hook appends a single Callable to self.hooks[event]. If it gets an iterable instead, it extends the list with only the callable items and silently drops the rest. The iterable itself is never stored. RequestHooksMixin.deregister_hook just calls self.hooks[event].remove(hook) and returns False on ValueError. So passing the same list or tuple to deregister_hook fails, because list.remove looks for the container, not its members. Removal is not symmetric with registration: callers must deregister each function separately, and each call removes only the first matching occurrence. A generator passed to register_hook is consumed, so it cannot be replayed for removal either.

In requests/adapters.py, BaseAdapter.__init__ calls super().__init__() even though it only inherits from object. This is the cooperative multiple-inheritance idiom: every class in the MRO calls super() so that mixins placed beside or below BaseAdapter still get their initializers run. HTTPAdapter.__init__ does the same before setting max_retries, config and the pool managers. BaseAdapter acts as an abstract base or template-method interface: send() and close() raise NotImplementedError. That keeps the framework open for extension through Session.mount() with custom adapters, without breaking the MRO chain.

Response.apparent_encoding in requests/models.py checks whether chardet is None. The chardet name comes from requests/compat.py, which tries to import chardet, then charset_normalizer, else sets None. If no library exists it returns "utf-8" without touching content. Otherwise it returns chardet.detect(self.content)["encoding"], and the self.content property reads and caches the body via iter_content into _content. If detection fails, the result is None. Response.text then calls str(self.content, None, errors="replace"), catches the LookupError or TypeError, and falls back to str(self.content, errors="replace"). If detection succeeds, that encoding is used for decoding.

In requests/cookies.py, MockResponse wraps the http.client.HTTPMessage passed in by extract_cookies_to_jar as response._original_response.msg. info() returns that message, and getheaders(name) calls self._headers.getheaders(name) but has no return statement, so it always yields None. The method is a leftover from Python 2, whose mimetools messages had getheaders. Python 3 HTTPMessage has no getheaders. http.cookiejar.CookieJar.extract_cookies and make_cookies only call response.info().get_all("Set-Cookie"/"Set-Cookie2"), so the broken path is never used.

PreparedRequest.prepare_body in requests/models.py delegates to RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files when files are given. That method normalizes each entry, which may be a bare file object or a 2-, 3- or 4-tuple of (filename, fileobj, content_type, custom_headers). The filename comes from the tuple or from utils.guess_filename(fileobj), falling back to the field key. str, bytes or bytearray data is used directly, objects with read() are read, and anything else is passed through. It builds urllib3 RequestField objects, calls make_multipart(content_type=...), and runs encode_multipart_formdata, which returns the body and boundary Content-Type. prepare_content_length then uses utils.super_len.

In requests/exceptions.py, RequestException subclasses IOError and carries request and response attributes. HTTPError, ConnectionError, Timeout and others subclass it, and ConnectTimeout subclasses both ConnectionError and Timeout. HTTPError is raised only by Response.raise_for_status after a real response arrives, with response=self attached. Connection-level failures are translated in HTTPAdapter.send in requests/adapters.py: urllib3 ProtocolError, OSError, MaxRetryError and ReadTimeoutError become ConnectionError, ConnectTimeout, ProxyError, SSLError, RetryError or ReadTimeout. Callers can catch RequestException for everything, or tell an HTTPError (inspect e.response.status_code) apart from a ConnectionError (no response, so retry or fail over). urllib3's own HTTPError is imported as _HTTPError to avoid name confusion.

MockRequest in requests/cookies.py calls urlparse(self._r.url) in __init__ to get the scheme, again in get_host for the netloc, and again in get_full_url when a Host header forces a URL rebuild. http.cookiejar's add_cookie_header and extract_cookies call get_host, get_full_url and get_origin_req_host many times per cookie (request_host, request_path, request_port, domain checks). That repeats parsing work across thousands of cookies. Python's urlsplit cache softens this somewhat. A fix is to parse once in __init__ and keep it in a private attribute such as self._parsed, or use functools.cached_property. Every accessor would derive scheme, netloc and the rebuilt URL from it. This stays safe because MockRequest never mutates the wrapped PreparedRequest and only adds headers to _new_headers.

In requests/sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects copies the request for each hop and rebuilds the URL and method. It pops the stale "Cookie" header, then calls cookies.extract_cookies_to_jar(prepared_request._cookies, req, resp.raw) to absorb the redirect response's Set-Cookie headers. Next, merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies) layers in session cookies, and prepared_request.prepare_cookies() regenerates the header through get_cookie_header and MockRequest. Popping first matters because prepare_cookies won't overwrite an existing Cookie header. After rebuild_auth and rebuild_proxies it sends the request, and extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, prepared_request, resp.raw) updates the session jar. Cookiejar domain and path policy re-scopes cookies for each new host.

In requests/models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare() calls prepare_url() and later prepare_auth(). prepare_url() uses urllib3's parse_url to split the URL and rebuilds the netloc with the auth part kept, so long credentials stay in self.url. prepare_auth() then calls get_auth_from_url() in requests/utils.py, which uses urlparse and unquote on the username and password. A non-empty pair becomes a tuple, which is wrapped in HTTPBasicAuth (requests/auth.py). That class sets the Authorization header through _basic_auth_str, and prepare_content_length() is then re-run. Before this, Session.prepare_request in sessions.py merges session and request auth and may fall back to get_netrc_auth. The test test_long_authinfo_in_url in tests/test_requests.py covers this case.

TLSServer in tests/testserver/server.py subclasses Server. Its __init__ builds the context with ssl.create_default_context(ssl.Purpose.CLIENT_AUTH) and calls load_cert_chain(cert_chain, keyfile). When mutual_tls is set, it sets verify_mode to ssl.CERT_OPTIONAL and calls load_verify_locations(cacert). _create_socket_and_bind then wraps the socket with server_side=True. A refactor could add an SSLContextBuilder with separate steps, for example with_server_cert(chain, key) and with_client_verification(cacert, mode), plus build(). TLSServer would receive the finished context. This lets tests choose verification modes (CERT_REQUIRED or CERT_OPTIONAL), reuse the builder for client contexts, and test it alone. The costs are another fixture-level abstraction and changes to the constructor signature that conftest.py fixtures rely on.

In requests/sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects loops while get_redirect_target(resp) returns a Location value. get_redirect_target checks resp.is_redirect and fixes latin1 decoding. On each hop, the loop records history, drains the old body and enforces max_redirects (raising TooManyRedirects). It resolves "//" and relative URLs with urljoin and calls rebuild_method. For non-307/308 codes it drops body headers. It also removes the Cookie header and rebuilds cookies with extract_cookies_to_jar and merge_cookies, and calls rebuild_proxies. rebuild_auth removes Authorization when should_strip_auth(old, new) reports a host change, or a scheme or port downgrade, but allows http-to-https on default ports. It then re-applies netrc credentials when trust_env is set. Finally the loop rewinds the body and sends with allow_redirects=False.

In requests/models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare_headers() creates a new CaseInsensitiveDict, defined in requests/structures.py. For each item, it first calls check_header_validity() from requests/utils.py, which rejects bad names and values (including leading whitespace and CR/LF) with InvalidHeader. It then stores the value under to_native_string(name), from requests/_internal_utils.py, so bytes and str names both become native str. CaseInsensitiveDict keys its _store by name.lower() and keeps the original casing alongside the value. As a result, lookups ignore case, the last duplicate wins, and the original names are kept for the wire. PreparedRequest.copy() duplicates the headers with headers.copy() so the copies stay separate.

The function is in requests/_internal_utils.py as to_native_string(string, encoding="ascii"). If the input is already builtin_str it is returned unchanged; otherwise it is decoded with string.decode(encoding). requests/utils.py imports it and re-exports it, which keeps the public requests.utils.to_native_string name working. test_to_native_string in tests/test_utils.py imports it through requests.utils, so it ends up running the _internal_utils implementation. requests/models.py, sessions.py and auth.py use the same helper.

PreparedRequest.prepare() in requests/models.py runs its steps in order: method, url, headers, cookies, body, auth, hooks. Each step changes shared state on the request. Authenticators such as OAuth signers and HTTPDigestAuth in requests/auth.py need the final URL, headers and body to compute signatures. They may also change headers or the body, which is why prepare_auth re-calls prepare_content_length. The code comments that auth must come last so it sees a fully prepared request. prepare_hooks comes after because authenticators can call register_hook; HTTPDigestAuth.__call__, for example, adds handle_401 and handle_redirect. Running hooks after auth ensures user hooks are added on top of those, not lost or put in the wrong order. Parallel or reordered steps would break these dependencies.

test_transfer_enc_removal_on_redirect in tests/test_requests.py builds a prepared POST with a generator body, which sets Transfer-Encoding: chunked, plus a Content-Type. It then runs it through Session.resolve_redirects with a mocked 303 response. In sessions.py, rebuild_method turns the request into GET. Because the status is not 307/308, resolve_redirects pops Content-Length, Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding and sets body to None. If those headers stayed, a body-less GET would announce a chunked body. Servers or proxies could then hang waiting for chunks or misframe the next message on a kept-alive connection, which risks request smuggling or desync. A leftover Content-Type would also mislabel the request and could leak details of the original payload.

The SSL tests in tests/test_requests.py depend on fixtures in tests/conftest.py. These include pytest-httpbin's httpbin_secure, which runs a local HTTPS server with its own self-signed certificate, and trustme- or tests/certs-based servers. Tests use verify=False, or point verify at pytest_httpbin.certs.where() or the files in tests/certs. Prerequisites include an ssl module with SNI support and the certifi CA bundle (DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH) for default verification. Tests should run without REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE or CURL_CA_BUNDLE overriding settings, since trust_env is read from them; tests patch these with monkeypatch. They also need free local ports and threads for tests/testserver, and correct system time so certificates are valid. Some tests also need outbound network access to real HTTPS hosts.

In models.py, Response.links reads the "link" header, parses it with utils.parse_header_links, and builds a dict keyed by each link's "rel" value, or by its "url" if there is no rel. When several entries share the same rel, each assignment overwrites the previous one. Only the last entry survives, and nothing warns or raises. Algorithmically this is a single O(n) pass with O(1) dict inserts, so lookups like r.links["next"] are fast. The cost is that the mapping is lossy: rel is not unique per RFC 8288, and keying on it collapses duplicates. Callers who need every entry must call parse_header_links(r.headers["link"]) directly, which returns the full list.

TestIsValidCIDR.test_invalid in tests/test_utils.py has no branching of its own. It passes each parametrized value (for example "8.8.8.8", "192.168.1.0/a", "192.168.1.0/128", "192.168.1.0/-1", "192.168.1.999/24") to utils.is_valid_cidr and asserts the result is False. All branching happens inside is_valid_cidr. It returns False in four cases: when the string does not contain exactly one "/"; when int() on the mask raises ValueError; when the mask is outside 1–32; and when socket.inet_aton on the address part raises OSError. Each parametrized value is chosen to reach a different one of these exits.

In exceptions.py, InvalidSchema is defined as InvalidSchema(RequestException, ValueError). RequestException derives from IOError and carries optional request and response attributes, so it belongs to requests' network-error family; "except RequestException" catches it alongside connection failures. ValueError carries the standard Python meaning that an argument had an unacceptable value. That fits Session.get_adapter, which raises InvalidSchema when no mounted adapter matches the URL prefix (for example "ftp://"). It also fits the SOCKS proxy path in adapters.py when its dependencies are missing. Callers can treat the failure either as a requests failure or as plain input validation. MissingSchema and InvalidURL follow the same pattern.

In models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare_body detects a stream (an iterable or file-like object that is not a string, list, tuple or Mapping). That body is sent as-is, using Content-Length from super_len or else chunked Transfer-Encoding. Multipart encoding goes through RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files, which needs form fields as key/value pairs and builds the whole body in memory with boundaries via urllib3's encode_multipart_formdata. An opaque stream cannot be mapped into named form fields. Merging the two would mean reading the stream fully, which defeats streaming, and its length is unknown. So the method raises NotImplementedError("Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive.") instead of guessing.

The premise is mostly wrong. In cookies.py, MockRequest.host is a property that returns self.get_host(). The indirection adds one Python call frame per access, which is a constant per-call cost that grows linearly with the number of calls, not cumulatively. The real cost is that get_host runs urlparse(self._r.url).netloc on every call. The fix is to compute the netloc once in __init__, as is already done for self.type, or to use functools.cached_property. Caching is safe because the wrapped request's URL does not change during a MockRequest's short life inside get_cookie_header or extract_cookies_to_jar. In practice http.cookiejar calls host only a few times per request, so this is rarely a bottleneck.

In cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie sets expires = None and then branches. If morsel["max-age"] is truthy, it computes int(time.time() + int(max-age)) inside a try block, turning a ValueError into TypeError("max-age: ... must be integer"). Otherwise, if morsel["expires"] is truthy, it parses the value with time.strptime using the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" and converts it with calendar.timegm. A malformed expires string raises ValueError from strptime unchanged, not TypeError. If neither field is set, expires stays None, which makes a session cookie. The result is passed to create_cookie.

The existing design in src/requests/__init__.py already avoids raising exceptions here. check_compatibility asserts acceptable urllib3 versions and chardet or charset_normalizer ranges, and _check_cryptography compares the cryptography version. Failures (AssertionError or ValueError) are caught at import time and turned into warnings.warn(..., RequestsDependencyWarning). That class is defined in exceptions.py as RequestsDependencyWarning(RequestsWarning), a Warning subclass outside the RequestException tree. Import never fails, and users can filter or escalate the warning. Any extension should follow the same pattern: add new checks inside the guarded block and emit RequestsDependencyWarning or a subclass of it. New hard errors should not be added under RequestException, because existing "except RequestException" handlers expect only request-time failures.

In utils.py, get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=None) calls should_bypass_proxies(url, no_proxy). If no_proxy is given (usually from a proxies dict's "no_proxy" key via Session.merge_environment_settings, resolve_proxies or rebuild_proxies), it replaces the NO_PROXY/no_proxy environment variables. It is used for the CIDR and hostname matching. It is also applied temporarily via set_environ around urllib's proxy_bypass. A match returns {}, meaning connect directly. A non-empty dict means the host was not excluded, so the proxies from getproxies() (environment or registry) apply to this URL. The override only changes the bypass decision; the proxy URLs still come from the environment.

guess_filename in src/requests/utils.py reads obj.name and returns it only if it is a string that does not start with "<" and end with ">". That filters out pseudo-names such as "<stdin>" or "<fdopen>" and non-string names such as integer file descriptors. It then returns os.path.basename(name), which drops the directory part. RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files in src/requests/models.py calls it to pick the multipart filename. As a result, local absolute paths are not leaked to the server, and no "../" path components or bogus names get into the Content-Disposition header. It only prevents information leakage and malformed names on the client side. It does not stop server-side path traversal.

In src/requests/models.py, Response.__enter__ returns self and Response.__exit__ calls close(). Response.close() calls self.raw.close() only when _content_consumed is False, meaning the body was never fully read. It then calls raw.release_conn (looked up with getattr) when that exists, which returns the connection to urllib3's pool. Once the content property or iter_content's generate() has drained the stream, _content_consumed is True and the raw close is skipped. Repeated close() calls are safe because urllib3's HTTPResponse.close and release_conn are idempotent. HTTPAdapter.build_response in adapters.py attaches raw, and Session.send in sessions.py reads content eagerly when stream=False.

merge_cookies in src/requests/cookies.py is called by Session.prepare_request in sessions.py. It merges an empty RequestsCookieJar with session.cookies and then with the per-request cookies, converting dicts through cookiejar_from_dict. Without it, PreparedRequest.prepare_cookies would build the Cookie header from only one source. Session login or auth cookies, or the request-specific ones, would be silently dropped. SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects also calls merge_cookies to carry session cookies onto redirected requests. HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 in auth.py copies the prepared request's _cookies before retrying. So the challenge-response retry would also lack the session cookies, and stateful auth flows could fail with repeated 401s.

In src/requests/structures.py, CaseInsensitiveDict stores _store[key.lower()] = (key, value). __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__ each call key.lower(), and __contains__ goes through __getitem__. Every call allocates a new string and costs O(len(key)), on top of rehashing that new string. For HTTP headers this is negligible, but with millions of lookups or long keys it adds up. Possible optimizations: cache normalized keys in a dict mapping each original key to its lowercase form, or functools.lru_cache a normalizer. Another option is to wrap keys in a str subclass that precomputes its lowercase form and hash. Callers can also pre-lowercase keys and use lower_items() or _store directly in hot loops.

test_none_timeout is in tests/test_requests.py inside the TestTimeout class. A single @pytest.mark.parametrize("timeout", (None, Urllib3Timeout(connect=None, read=None))) supplies the timeout argument directly. pytest resolves the httpbin argument from tests/conftest.py, whose httpbin fixture wraps pytest-httpbin's session-scoped httpbin server in prepare_url(). That gives a callable that builds URLs such as httpbin("get"). The test calls requests.get(...) in api.py, which goes through Session.request and Session.send to HTTPAdapter.send in adapters.py. There a TimeoutSauce instance is passed through unchanged, while None becomes TimeoutSauce(connect=None, read=None). Both cases mean no timeout.

The Server class is in tests/testserver/server.py and subclasses threading.Thread. Server.__enter__ calls start() and waits on ready_event, raising RuntimeError on timeout, then returns (host, port). run() binds the socket with _create_socket_and_bind, sets ready_event, and handles requests_to_handle connections through _accept_connection, which uses select. It optionally waits on wait_to_close_event, and in its finally block closes the socket and sets stop_event. Server.__exit__ waits on stop_event if no exception occurred. Otherwise it sets wait_to_close_event, then closes the socket and calls join(). Tests in tests/test_testserver.py such as test_server_closes, test_basic_waiting_server and test_server_finishes_on_error exercise these paths.

test_pragmas is in tests/test_utils.py under TestContentEncodingDetection. It is parametrized with an HTML5 meta charset tag, an HTML4 http-equiv pragma, an XHTML pragma and an XML declaration. Every input is a str, not bytes, and declares exactly "UTF-8". The test asserts that get_encodings_from_content in src/requests/utils.py returns exactly one encoding, equal to "UTF-8". This assumes the function scans the response body, not headers, using charset_re, pragma_re and xml_re. Those regexes match case-insensitively but do not normalize the result. The test also assumes each declaration matches only one regex, so there are no duplicate entries.

In src/requests/models.py, Response starts with _content=False and _content_consumed=False. The content property reads the whole body once via b"".join(iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)), caches it in _content, and sets _content_consumed. It raises RuntimeError if the stream was already consumed without being cached. iter_content picks iter_slices over the cached _content when it is already loaded. Otherwise it uses generate(), which streams raw.stream() chunk by chunk and maps urllib3 errors to ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError and ConnectionError. It raises StreamConsumedError when a stream is reused. With stream=True in Session.send, nothing is buffered. text, json() and iter_lines are all built on content or iter_content, so both access patterns keep working.

tests/test_requests.py imports exception types from requests/exceptions.py (ConnectionError, ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, InvalidSchema, InvalidURL, MissingSchema, TooManyRedirects, RetryError, InvalidHeader, and others). All of them derive from RequestException, which subclasses IOError. In sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects raises TooManyRedirects with response=resp once len(resp.history) reaches max_redirects; test_HTTP_302_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS checks e.value.response and its history. While draining a redirect response, the same method catches ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError and RuntimeError. It calls rewind_body in utils.py, which can raise UnrewindableBodyError. For authentication, rebuild_auth strips the Authorization header on cross-host redirects, and HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 in auth.py retries the request on a 401. Response.raise_for_status raises HTTPError.

In cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie checks morsel["max-age"] before morsel["expires"]. Max-Age takes precedence under RFC 6265, and http.cookiejar.Cookie only stores an absolute expires epoch value. For max-age, it computes int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"])), turning a relative number of seconds into an absolute Unix timestamp. A non-integer value is caught as ValueError and re-raised as TypeError. Otherwise, it parses expires with time.strptime using the "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" template and converts the result with calendar.timegm. The resulting expires value is passed to create_cookie together with the morsel's path, domain, secure, httponly (via rest) and comment fields.

Both exceptions live in requests/exceptions.py and subclass RequestException; StreamConsumedError also subclasses TypeError. UnrewindableBodyError concerns the outgoing request body. utils.rewind_body raises it when a body cannot be re-sent: there is no seek method, _body_position is not an int, or seek raises OSError. That position is recorded by PreparedRequest.prepare_body via body.tell(), with an object() sentinel if tell fails. rewind_body is called from Session.resolve_redirects when a redirect must re-send a streamed body. StreamConsumedError concerns the incoming response body. Response.iter_content in models.py raises it when _content_consumed is true and _content is still a bool, meaning a streamed response was already read but never cached.

The method is CaseInsensitiveDict.__iter__ in requests/structures.py. The class keeps self._store, an OrderedDict that maps key.lower() to a (original_key, value) tuple; __setitem__ fills it. __iter__ returns (casedkey for casedkey, mappedvalue in self._store.values()). Iteration therefore yields the original-cased key from the most recent assignment, and there is exactly one entry per case-insensitive key. In tests/test_structures.py, TestCaseInsensitiveDict's setup fixture assigns self.case_insensitive_dict["Accept"] = "application/json". test_list then asserts list(self.case_insensitive_dict) == ["Accept"]. Lowercasing is used only for lookup and storage keys, never for the keys that iteration returns.

In requests/models.py, Response separates lazy content from pickling state. Streaming is handled by iter_content: its generate() reads raw.stream(), it falls back to iter_slices when content is already cached, and it raises StreamConsumedError for an uncached consumed stream. The content property materializes lazily: when _content is False, it joins iter_content chunks and sets _content_consumed. Serialization is handled by the __attrs__ list together with __getstate__ and __setstate__. __getstate__ first forces self.content if the body is not yet consumed, then returns only the attributes named in __attrs__, so the unpicklable raw stream is excluded. __setstate__ restores those attributes and sets _content_consumed=True and raw=None. An unpickled Response is therefore fully materialized and non-streaming.

TestGuessJSONUTF in tests/test_utils.py exercises utils.guess_json_utf, which inspects data[:4]. BOM detection runs first: codecs.BOM_UTF32_LE/BE give "utf-32", BOM_UTF8 gives "utf-8-sig", and BOM_UTF16_LE/BE give "utf-16". UTF-32 is checked before UTF-16 because the UTF-32-LE BOM begins with the UTF-16-LE BOM. test_guess_by_bom encodes "\ufeff{}" and expects the generic "utf-16" or "utf-32" result. Without a BOM, the function falls back to counting null bytes, since JSON starts with two ASCII characters. Zero nulls means utf-8; two nulls matched against _null2 patterns give utf-16-be or utf-16-le; three nulls matched against _null3 give utf-32-be or utf-32-le. test_encoded covers this path, and test_bad_utf_like_encoding expects None.

In tests/test_utils.py, test__parse_content_type_header is decorated with @pytest.mark.parametrize("value, expected", (...)). Pytest splits the argnames string, binds each name to the matching parameter in the function signature def test__parse_content_type_header(value, expected), and generates one test item per tuple. The cases cover plain types, spacing and quoting variations, multiple parameters such as charset and boundary, and keys without values. Each item asserts _parse_content_type_header(value) == expected. The function under test, in requests/utils.py, splits the header on ";", strips the content type, and lowercases each parameter key. It strips the characters "\"' " from keys and values, and maps a valueless key to True.

requests/exceptions.py defines ProxyError as a subclass of ConnectionError, which subclasses RequestException, which subclasses IOError. In requests/adapters.py, HTTPAdapter.send catches urllib3's MaxRetryError. If e.reason is an instance of urllib3's ProxyError (imported as _ProxyError), it raises requests' ProxyError(e, request=request). A bare _ProxyError is converted the same way. A malformed proxy URL instead raises InvalidProxyURL from get_connection_with_tls_context or proxy_manager_for. The exception propagates out of HTTPAdapter.send through Session.send, Session.request and api.request without being retried. Callers can handle it as ProxyError, ConnectionError or RequestException. ConnectTimeout, RetryError and SSLError are checked before it.

In models.py, RequestHooksMixin.register_hook appends a single Callable to self.hooks[event]. If it gets an iterable instead, it extends the list with only the callable members and silently drops the rest. RequestHooksMixin.deregister_hook just calls self.hooks[event].remove(hook) and returns False on ValueError. The stored list holds the flattened callables, never the original iterable. So passing the same list or tuple to deregister_hook finds no match and returns False, removing nothing. The caller must deregister each callable one by one. Registration flattens, but removal does not mirror it. Also, list.remove deletes only the first equal entry, so duplicates need repeated calls.

In adapters.py, BaseAdapter.__init__ calls super().__init__() even though BaseAdapter inherits only from object. HTTPAdapter.__init__ likewise calls super().__init__() before setting max_retries, config and the pool manager. This is cooperative multiple inheritance: every __init__ forwards along the MRO. That lets future subclasses mix BaseAdapter or HTTPAdapter with other mixins without skipping any initializer. It goes with BaseAdapter acting as an abstract interface (send and close raise NotImplementedError), in a Template Method or strategy style. Session.mount and Session.get_adapter then treat any subclass as a pluggable transport. The extensibility comes from cooperative inheritance plus an abstract base.

Response.apparent_encoding in models.py is a property that checks the chardet name imported from compat.py. compat._resolve_char_detection binds it to chardet, to charset_normalizer, or to None. If it is None, the property returns "utf-8" without touching self.content. Otherwise it returns chardet.detect(self.content)["encoding"]. Accessing self.content (the Response.content property) reads the body through iter_content and caches it in _content. When detection fails, it returns None. Response.text then calls str(self.content, None, errors="replace"), which raises TypeError. Text catches that and falls back to str(self.content, errors="replace"), the default UTF-8. On success, the same cached bytes are decoded with the detected encoding.

In cookies.py, extract_cookies_to_jar wraps response._original_response.msg, an http.client.HTTPMessage, in MockResponse. MockResponse.info() returns that object, and http.cookiejar.CookieJar.extract_cookies calls info().get_all("Set-Cookie"). MockResponse.getheaders(name) delegates to self._headers.getheaders(name) but has no return statement, so it always yields None. It is a Python 2 leftover: Python 3's HTTPMessage has no getheaders, so calling it would raise AttributeError anyway. Since cookielib only uses info(), the incomplete method is never exercised. That is why the defect is hidden rather than causing failures.

The normalization lives in RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files in models.py, called from PreparedRequest.prepare_body. It turns the files dict or list into key/value pairs with utils.to_key_val_list. Each value may be a bare file, or a tuple of 2, 3 or 4 items: filename, fileobj, content type and custom headers. Missing names come from utils.guess_filename. The payload is taken from str or bytes directly, from read() on file objects, skipped when None, or used as-is otherwise. Data fields are encoded too. Each part becomes a urllib3 RequestField via make_multipart, and encode_multipart_formdata returns the body and boundary content type. prepare_body sets the Content-Type header, and prepare_content_length then sets the length.

In exceptions.py, RequestException subclasses IOError. Its __init__ stores the response and request, taking request from response.request when only a response is given. HTTPError and ConnectionError are sibling subclasses. Response.raise_for_status in models.py raises HTTPError(response=self) for 4xx and 5xx statuses, so a server reply exists. HTTPAdapter.send in adapters.py turns urllib3 failures into ConnectionError, ProxyError, SSLError, ConnectTimeout or ReadTimeout, where no valid response exists. Catching RequestException covers both kinds, while catching specific subclasses lets retry or recovery logic separate server-side status failures from network failures. ConnectTimeout also inherits Timeout, so a single handler for timeouts can cover both connect and read timeouts.

In cookies.py, MockRequest.__init__ calls urlparse(self._r.url) to set type. get_host parses the URL again for netloc, and get_full_url parses again when a Host header is present. http.cookiejar's DefaultCookiePolicy calls these methods, plus the host and origin_req_host properties, many times for each cookie. This happens in add_cookie_header (via get_cookie_header) and in extract_cookies (via extract_cookies_to_jar). Large jars therefore re-parse the same string repeatedly. A fix is to parse once in __init__ and cache the result, for example self._parsed, or a functools.cached_property keyed on self._r.url. The wrapped PreparedRequest stays unmodified, and new headers still go only to _new_headers. That keeps the read-only semantics.

In sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects copies the PreparedRequest for each hop and pops the stale Cookie header. It then calls extract_cookies_to_jar(prepared_request._cookies, req, resp.raw) to capture Set-Cookie from the redirect response. Next, merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies) folds in the session jar. Finally prepared_request.prepare_cookies rebuilds the header through get_cookie_header, which only sets it because the old one was removed. Each hop is sent through Session.send with allow_redirects=False. Session.send also runs extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, ...) for every history response and the final one. The session jar stays authoritative, and per-request jars carry hop-specific cookies with correct domain and path matching.

In src/requests/models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare() calls prepare_url() first, which keeps the userinfo in the netloc. It then calls prepare_auth(auth, url). When no explicit auth is given, prepare_auth uses get_auth_from_url (src/requests/utils.py), which applies urlparse and unquote to the username and password. A two-item tuple is wrapped in HTTPBasicAuth (auth.py), and calling it sets the Authorization header through _basic_auth_str. That function uses b64encode, so long credentials produce no line breaks, and it returns a native string via to_native_string. prepare_auth then merges the auth-modified state into self.__dict__ and recomputes prepare_content_length. Session.prepare_request may supply netrc auth instead, and SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_auth handles this again on redirects.

TLSServer is not in the source map; it lives in tests/testserver/server.py as a subclass of Server. Its __init__ builds an ssl.SSLContext for PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER and calls load_cert_chain(cert_chain, keyfile). When mutual_tls is set, it sets verify_mode to CERT_OPTIONAL and calls load_verify_locations(cacert). _create_socket_and_bind then wraps the socket. A refactor would add an SSLContextBuilder with separate with_server_cert(chain, key) and with_client_verification(mode, cafile) steps, returning an immutable context. TLSServer would only accept a ready context. This allows unit-testing context building, reusing it for client fixtures and varying verify modes such as CERT_REQUIRED. The cost is an extra layer and indirection for small test code.

In src/requests/sessions.py, get_redirect_target returns the Location header only when resp.is_redirect is true, re-decoding latin-1 bytes as UTF-8. resolve_redirects loops on that target, enforcing max_redirects (TooManyRedirects) and resolving relative and scheme-relative URLs. It preserves fragments and applies requote_uri and rebuild_method. For non-307/308 codes it drops body headers, and it removes the stale Cookie header before re-extracting cookies. It then calls rebuild_proxies, which resets Proxy-Authorization, and rebuild_auth, then rewind_body, and sends with allow_redirects=False. rebuild_auth deletes Authorization when should_strip_auth(old, new) is true, meaning the host, scheme or port changed. The exception is an http-to-https upgrade on default ports. When trust_env is set, rebuild_auth re-applies get_netrc_auth credentials for the new host.

PreparedRequest.prepare_headers in src/requests/models.py creates a fresh CaseInsensitiveDict (structures.py). For each item it first calls check_header_validity (utils.py), which uses _validate_header_part and the HEADER_VALIDATORS regexes from _internal_utils. Names or values that are not str or bytes, or that contain CR/LF or leading whitespace, raise InvalidHeader. The name is then converted with to_native_string, which decodes bytes as ASCII, and stored. CaseInsensitiveDict keys its _store by lowercased name, holding (original name, value) pairs, so lookups are case-insensitive. Duplicates differing only in case collapse, with the last one winning. Values are left unchanged. PreparedRequest.copy duplicates the dict with headers.copy() to avoid shared mutation.

The function is to_native_string(string, encoding="ascii") in src/requests/_internal_utils.py. src/requests/utils.py imports and re-exports it from _internal_utils, so the test, test_to_native_string in tests/test_utils.py, reaches it through requests.utils. The function returns the input unchanged if it is already a str and otherwise decodes it with the given encoding. It is also used by models.py (prepare_headers, prepare_method), auth.py (_basic_auth_str) and sessions.py (redirect handling).

PreparedRequest.prepare in src/requests/models.py runs prepare_method, prepare_url, prepare_headers, prepare_cookies, prepare_body, prepare_auth and prepare_hooks in that order. The source comment says prepare_auth must come last so that schemes like OAuth can sign a fully prepared request: final URL, headers and body. Auth callables (AuthBase.__call__) may also change the body or headers, so prepare_auth recomputes Content-Length afterwards. prepare_hooks runs after auth because handlers such as HTTPDigestAuth.__call__ register response hooks (handle_401, handle_redirect) through register_hook. User hooks are then appended after them. Every step mutates shared self state, so the steps cannot be parallelized.

The test is in tests/test_requests.py. It builds a POST with a streamed (chunked) body, so the request carries Transfer-Encoding and Content-Type. It then feeds a mocked redirect response into Session.resolve_redirects. rebuild_method turns POST into GET for 303, and for 302/301 POSTs, and the body becomes None. For codes other than 307/308, resolve_redirects purges Content-Length, Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding. If they persisted, a body-less GET would claim chunked framing. The server or proxy would wait for chunk data or misparse the next message, risking hangs, connection desynchronization or request smuggling. A stale Content-Type would also misdescribe a nonexistent body and could affect caches or routing.

SSL-related TestRequests tests in tests/test_requests.py depend on the pytest-httpbin fixtures httpbin_secure and httpbin_ca_bundle. These provide a local HTTPS server with a self-signed certificate and the matching CA file passed as verify. The tests also need Python's ssl module, urllib3 with SNI support, and certifi's bundle from src/requests/certs.py. They use the certificate files under tests/certs and the TLSServer in tests/testserver for mutual TLS and expired-certificate cases. Environment variables REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE and proxy settings must not interfere, because Session.merge_environment_settings reads them when trust_env is set. Free local ports are required, and a few tests need real network access or are skipped when modern SSL is unavailable.

TestRequests in tests/test_requests.py imports exceptions from src/requests/exceptions.py: ConnectionError, ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, InvalidSchema, InvalidURL, MissingSchema, TooManyRedirects, InvalidHeader, UnrewindableBodyError, InvalidProxyURL, SSLError and others. All of them derive from RequestException(IOError), whose __init__ stores request and response. For redirects, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in sessions.py raises TooManyRedirects once len(resp.history) reaches max_redirects, attaching the response. Tests check e.response and its history. resolve_redirects also calls utils.rewind_body, which can raise UnrewindableBodyError. For authentication, HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 and handle_redirect in auth.py re-send or reset state rather than raise. SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_auth uses should_strip_auth to drop Authorization headers across hosts. Response.raise_for_status raises HTTPError for 4xx/5xx statuses.

In cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie converts a Morsel into a cookielib Cookie through create_cookie. Cookie stores expires as an absolute epoch, so the relative Max-Age must be converted. Max-Age is checked first, because RFC 6265 gives it precedence over Expires. The function computes expires = int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"])) and raises TypeError if the value is not an integer. Otherwise, if morsel["expires"] is set, it parses it with time.strptime using the "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" template and calendar.timegm. The result goes to create_cookie along with domain, path, secure, comment, discard=False, the HttpOnly rest attribute and other fields.

Both exceptions subclass RequestException in exceptions.py, but they cover different sides. UnrewindableBodyError is about the outgoing request body. utils.rewind_body raises it during SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in two cases: seek() raises OSError, or the body has no seek method or _body_position is not an int. PreparedRequest.prepare_body records _body_position via tell(), or a sentinel object() if tell() fails. StreamConsumedError (also a TypeError) is about the incoming response. Response.iter_content in models.py raises it when _content_consumed is True and _content is still a bool. That means the raw stream was already read without being cached, so it cannot be iterated again.

The method is CaseInsensitiveDict.__iter__ in src/requests/structures.py. It returns (casedkey for casedkey, mappedvalue in self._store.values()). __setitem__ stores self._store[key.lower()] = (key, value) in an OrderedDict, so lookups are keyed by the lowercased name. Iteration, however, yields the original casing from the most recent assignment, such as "Accept". __len__ and lower_items work on the same _store. That is why list(case_insensitive_dict) in test_list (tests/test_structures.py) gives exactly ["Accept"] with one entry, not a lowercased key.

Response in models.py keeps a sentinel _content = False and a flag _content_consumed. The content property materializes the body lazily as b"".join(iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)), or None when raw is missing or status_code is 0. It raises RuntimeError if the stream was already consumed. iter_content picks iter_slices(self._content) when the content has been consumed and the generate() stream otherwise. For pickling, __getstate__ forces self.content if not yet consumed, then returns only the attributes in __attrs__ (_content, status_code, headers, url, history, encoding, reason, cookies, elapsed, request). __setstate__ restores those, sets _content_consumed=True and raw=None. The socket-bound raw object is therefore never serialized.

In tests/test_utils.py, TestGuessJSONUTF covers utils.guess_json_utf. test_guess_by_bom encodes "\ufeff{}" in the BE and LE variants and expects the generic "utf-16" or "utf-32". test_encoded encodes "{}" without a BOM and expects the exact variant, such as "utf-16-le" or "utf-32-be". test_bad_utf_like_encoding expects None for four null bytes. guess_json_utf first checks the first four bytes against codecs BOMs, testing UTF-32 before UTF-16 because the UTF-32-LE BOM starts with the UTF-16-LE BOM. It returns "utf-8-sig" for the UTF-8 BOM. Without a BOM it counts null bytes and their positions (_null, _null2, _null3), since JSON starts with ASCII characters, to infer endianness.

In tests/test_utils.py, @pytest.mark.parametrize("value, expected", ...) takes a comma-separated argnames string whose names must match the parameters of test__parse_content_type_header(value, expected). pytest generates one test item per tuple, binding the header string to value and the (content_type, params dict) pair to expected. Each item asserts utils._parse_content_type_header(value) == expected. The cases exercise the parser's behaviour: it splits on ";" and takes the stripped first token as the content type. Remaining tokens are split on "=", with quotes and spaces stripped from values and keys lowercased. Tokens without "=" become True flags, and empty tokens are skipped.

ProxyError subclasses ConnectionError, which subclasses RequestException(IOError), all in exceptions.py. HTTPAdapter.send in adapters.py catches urllib3's MaxRetryError and checks e.reason in order: ConnectTimeoutError becomes ConnectTimeout, ResponseError becomes RetryError, and urllib3 _ProxyError becomes ProxyError(e, request=request). SSL errors become SSLError, and anything else becomes ConnectionError. A direct _ProxyError is also caught and re-raised as ProxyError. Malformed proxies raise InvalidProxyURL earlier, in get_connection_with_tls_context. Session.send, Session.request, resolve_redirects and api.request do not catch it, so it propagates to the caller. Callers can handle it as ProxyError, as ConnectionError, or as RequestException.

In src/requests/models.py, the Response.links property reads the "link" header and parses it with utils.parse_header_links. It then loops over the parsed entries and stores each one in resolved_links under link.get("rel") or link.get("url"). Because this is a plain dict assignment, a later entry with the same rel silently overwrites an earlier one, so only the last such entry survives. The pass is O(n), with O(1) average-cost dict inserts. The cost of keying by rel is that the mapping is lossy: rel is not treated as unique-per-target as RFC 8288 allows. Callers who need every entry must call parse_header_links directly, which returns the full list.

The test module is not among the shown files. TestIsValidCIDR.test_invalid presumably asserts not is_valid_cidr(value) with no branching of its own; all branching happens in utils.is_valid_cidr. It first checks string_network.count("/") == 1 and returns False otherwise, for example for a bare IP. Next it parses int(mask) and returns False on ValueError, for example "/a". It then returns False if the mask is below 1 or above 32. Finally it runs socket.inet_aton on the address and returns False on OSError, for example "192.168.1.999/24". Each parametrized value therefore exits at a different return False.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, InvalidSchema(RequestException, ValueError) uses multiple inheritance so one error can be caught two ways. RequestException subclasses IOError and carries request and response attributes, so a generic "except RequestException" around HTTP calls catches it. ValueError expresses that the caller supplied a bad argument value, matching Python convention for invalid input. It is raised by Session.get_adapter in sessions.py when no adapter matches the URL prefix, and by the SOCKSProxyManager stub in adapters.py. MissingSchema, raised in PreparedRequest.prepare_url, follows the same pattern.

In PreparedRequest.prepare_body (models.py), a body counts as a stream if it is iterable and not a string, list, tuple or Mapping. Such a body is passed to urllib3 unchanged, with Content-Length from super_len or Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Multipart bodies are built by _encode_files using urllib3's encode_multipart_formdata, which must fully materialise every field into one bytes body with a boundary and Content-Type. A one-shot iterator of unknown length cannot be embedded in that in-memory encoding without consuming or buffering it. That would defeat streaming and break the rewind logic based on _body_position. Requests therefore raises NotImplementedError("Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive.") rather than guess.

In src/requests/cookies.py, MockRequest.host is a property that returns self.get_host(), which computes urlparse(self._r.url).netloc. origin_req_host adds a further hop through get_origin_req_host. The extra Python call frames cost only tens of nanoseconds each. The real repeated cost is re-running urlparse on every access, although newer Python versions cache urlsplit results internally. In practice MockRequest is short-lived and built per call in get_cookie_header and extract_cookies_to_jar, so this rarely matters. If profiling showed a hotspot, netloc could be parsed once in __init__, as self.type already is. Alternatively, host could use functools.cached_property, since the wrapped request URL does not change during the wrapper's lifetime.

In cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie starts with expires = None. The first branch is "if morsel['max-age']:", which computes int(time.time() + int(max-age)) and converts a ValueError into TypeError("max-age: ... must be integer"). The second branch is "elif morsel['expires']:", which parses the string with time.strptime using the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" and converts it with calendar.timegm. If both fields are empty, expires stays None. The result is passed to create_cookie. Only the max-age path raises TypeError; a malformed expires string raises ValueError from strptime.

The existing pattern is in src/requests/__init__.py and should be kept. check_compatibility asserts on urllib3, chardet and charset_normalizer versions, and _check_cryptography inspects cryptography. Failures from these, caught as AssertionError or ValueError, are converted to warnings.warn using RequestsDependencyWarning. That class is defined in exceptions.py as a subclass of RequestsWarning, which subclasses Warning. Using warnings rather than raised exceptions keeps imports working on unexpected versions while still surfacing the problem. New checks should follow the same approach. They should parse versions defensively, for example padding urllib3 versions, and emit RequestsDependencyWarning or a new subclass so existing filters still apply. help.py's info() complements this by reporting the installed versions.

In src/requests/utils.py, get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=None) calls should_bypass_proxies(url, no_proxy). An explicit no_proxy argument takes precedence over the NO_PROXY or no_proxy environment variables, which are read via get_proxy only when the argument is None. It is also temporarily injected through set_environ before proxy_bypass runs, so caller settings such as proxies["no_proxy"] from Session.merge_environment_settings or resolve_proxies win. If the URL should be bypassed, the function returns {}. Otherwise it returns getproxies(), the full scheme-to-proxy map from the environment. A non-empty result therefore means the host was not excluded and environment proxies exist; select_proxy then picks the proxy for the URL's scheme and host.

In src/requests/models.py, RequestHooksMixin.register_hook appends a single Callable to self.hooks[event]. If it gets an iterable instead, it flattens it with extend, keeping only the elements that are Callable and silently dropping the rest. deregister_hook just calls self.hooks[event].remove(hook) and catches ValueError to return False. If you pass the same list or tuple you registered, remove() looks for the container object itself. That object was never stored, because only its elements were, so it returns False and removes nothing. Registration and deregistration are therefore not symmetric. Callers must deregister each callable one by one. remove() also deletes only the first occurrence of a duplicate. Non-callables that were filtered out cannot be reported.

In src/requests/adapters.py, BaseAdapter.__init__ calls super().__init__(), and HTTPAdapter.__init__ chains to it the same way. Even though BaseAdapter's only explicit parent is object, this keeps the Python MRO intact. Subclasses that combine BaseAdapter with mixins or other base classes under multiple inheritance then get every __init__ called. This is cooperative multiple inheritance. It sits alongside a Template Method or abstract-interface design, where send() and close() raise NotImplementedError and HTTPAdapter or third-party adapters fill them in. Those adapters are attached through Session.mount. The pattern lets new transport adapters be composed and extended without changing the base class.

Response.apparent_encoding in src/requests/models.py is a property. If the chardet name from compat.py is not None, it returns chardet.detect(self.content)["encoding"]. compat._resolve_char_detection loads chardet or charset_normalizer, else None. Otherwise it returns "utf-8" without reading content. self.content reads the whole body via iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE). When detection succeeds, Response.text uses that encoding in str(self.content, encoding, errors="replace").
