When detection fails, the encoding is None. str(content, None) then raises TypeError, which is caught, and the body is decoded with str(self.content, errors="replace"), i.e. UTF-8. Response.json uses guess_json_utf first and falls back to text.

In src/requests/cookies.py, extract_cookies_to_jar wraps response._original_response.msg (an http.client HTTPMessage) in MockResponse. It then calls jar.extract_cookies(res, req), and http.cookiejar reads headers through MockResponse.info(), which returns self._headers, using get_all. MockResponse.getheaders(name) delegates to self._headers.getheaders(name), but it has no return statement, so it always returns None. Python 3's HTTPMessage also has no getheaders method, so the call would raise AttributeError. It looks like a leftover from the Python 2 urllib/httplib API. CookieJar never calls it, which is why the bug stays hidden.

PreparedRequest.prepare_body in src/requests/models.py calls RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files when files is given. It raises NotImplementedError for streamed bodies combined with files. _encode_files rejects empty files and string data, and normalizes data and files with to_key_val_list. For each file value it handles four shapes. A 2-tuple gives (filename, fileobj), a 3-tuple adds content_type, and a 4-tuple adds custom_headers. A bare object gets its name from utils.guess_filename. File data is then taken from str/bytes/bytearray as-is, from .read() output, skipped if None, or used raw otherwise. Each part becomes a urllib3 RequestField with make_multipart(content_type=ft). encode_multipart_formdata returns the body and the boundary Content-Type. prepare_content_length then sets the length.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, RequestException subclasses IOError and carries the request and response. HTTPError and ConnectionError are sibling subclasses of RequestException. ProxyError and SSLError extend ConnectionError, and ConnectTimeout extends both ConnectionError and Timeout. HTTPError is raised by Response.raise_for_status in models.py for 4xx/5xx statuses, with response=self, so a server reply exists. ConnectionError and its subclasses come from HTTPAdapter.send in adapters.py, which translates urllib3 errors (ProtocolError, OSError, MaxRetryError, ClosedPoolError) when there is no usable response. Callers can catch RequestException for everything, HTTPError for status failures, and ConnectionError or Timeout for transport retries. Response.ok uses the HTTPError catch internally.

In src/requests/cookies.py, MockRequest.__init__ parses self._r.url to get the scheme. get_host parses it again for netloc, and get_full_url parses it a third time when a Host header exists. http.cookiejar calls these methods (through request_host, eff_request_host, domain and path checks) many times per cookie in add_cookie_header and extract_cookies. Large jars or many requests therefore repeat the same parsing. Python's own urlsplit cache reduces the cost only partly. Because the wrapped request is treated as read-only and new headers go to _new_headers, it is safe to parse once in __init__. MockRequest could store the parsed tuple (or use a cached property) and reuse it for type, host and full-URL reconstruction.

In src/requests/sessions.py, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects copies the prepared request on each hop with req.copy(); _copy_cookie_jar gives it its own jar. It removes the stale Cookie header from prepared_request.headers. Next, extract_cookies_to_jar(prepared_request._cookies, req, resp.raw) adds cookies from the redirect response, and merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies) layers in the session jar. prepared_request.prepare_cookies then rebuilds the header with get_cookie_header and MockRequest, so domain and path match the new URL. After each send, extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, prepared_request, resp.raw) updates the session jar. Session.send also extracts cookies from the history and final responses, so the session and the per-request jars stay consistent.

guess_filename in src/requests/utils.py reads the object's `name` attribute with getattr. It returns a value only if that name is a basestring and is not wrapped in angle brackets (pseudo-names such as "<stdin>" or "<fdopen>"). Even then it returns only os.path.basename(name). This rejects integer file descriptors and other non-string names, and synthetic names that are not real files. Because only the basename is kept, absolute paths and directory components are dropped. The Content-Disposition header that RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files (src/requests/models.py) builds through RequestField.make_multipart therefore cannot leak local directory structure. It also cannot carry "../" path-traversal parts to the server. If no safe name is found, the field key is used as the filename instead.

In src/requests/models.py, Response.__enter__ returns self and __exit__ calls self.close(). close() calls self.raw.close() only if _content_consumed is False. Fully consumed bodies have already been drained, so urllib3 has returned the connection to the pool. close() then calls the raw object's release_conn via getattr, if it exists. The double-close guard therefore depends on the _content_consumed flag plus urllib3's idempotent close() and release_conn(). Response itself keeps no "closed" flag. The flag is set by the iter_content generator and the content property. HTTPAdapter.build_response (src/requests/adapters.py) attaches the raw urllib3 response. Session.send reads r.content when stream=False, and __setstate__ sets raw to None for pickled responses.

merge_cookies (src/requests/cookies.py) is called in Session.prepare_request (src/requests/sessions.py) to build a fresh RequestsCookieJar from self.cookies plus the per-request cookies. PreparedRequest.prepare_cookies then turns that jar into the Cookie header. Without these calls, only one cookie source would reach the header. Session cookies holding login or authentication state would be lost, or request-specific cookies would be ignored. Cookie-based authentication would then fail. Session.resolve_redirects also calls merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies) before rebuild_auth, so redirected requests would lose session cookies too. HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 (src/requests/auth.py) re-prepares cookies from r.request._cookies, so the digest retry would also lose the merged cookies.

CaseInsensitiveDict in src/requests/structures.py stores entries in an OrderedDict `_store` keyed by key.lower(), holding (original_key, value). Every __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__ call runs str.lower() again. Each call allocates a new string, costs time proportional to key length, and needs a fresh hash, since nothing is cached. lower_items() and __eq__, which builds another CaseInsensitiveDict, repeat the same work. Under very frequent lookups this allocation and hashing adds up. Possible optimizations: memoize lowering (functools.lru_cache, or a dict mapping original key to its lowered form), or have callers normalize keys once. Another option is a key wrapper object that caches its lowered form and hash, or interned lowercase keys. In practice, header dicts are small.

test_none_timeout is in tests/test_requests.py and is decorated with @pytest.mark.parametrize("timeout", (None, Urllib3Timeout(connect=None, read=None))). Pytest creates one test item per value and passes `timeout` directly as an argument. The `httpbin` argument is resolved as a fixture. tests/conftest.py defines an httpbin fixture that wraps pytest-httpbin's server fixture and returns prepare_url, which joins the server URL with a path. The test calls requests.get(httpbin("get"), timeout=timeout). The call goes through api.request, Session.request and Session.send to HTTPAdapter.send (src/requests/adapters.py). There, a None value is turned into TimeoutSauce(connect=None, read=None), and a urllib3 Timeout instance is passed through unchanged.

Server is in tests/testserver/server.py and subclasses threading.Thread. __enter__ calls start() and waits on ready_event, then returns (host, port). run() creates and binds the server socket, records the port, sets ready_event and calls _handle_requests. It optionally waits on wait_to_close_event. In a finally block it closes the socket via _close_server_sock_ignore_errors and sets stop_event. __exit__ waits on stop_event when there was no exception; on error it sets wait_to_close_event. It then closes the socket, calls join() and returns False. The basic_response_server and text_response_server helpers build Server instances. TestTestServer in tests/test_testserver.py uses these to check socket closing, handling a limited number of requests, and shutdown after errors.

test_pragmas, in tests/test_utils.py (TestContentEncodingDetection), is parametrized with HTML meta charset, http-equiv Content-Type and XML declaration strings. Each declares UTF-8 once. The test calls get_encodings_from_content from src/requests/utils.py and asserts exactly one result equal to "UTF-8". This assumes the content is a str, not bytes. It assumes the regexes (charset_re, pragma_re, xml_re, all compiled with re.I) match regardless of attribute case and strip quotes. It also assumes the declared value is returned verbatim, with case preserved and no normalization to lowercase or codec names. Finally, it assumes each declaration matches only one pattern, so no duplicates appear. Note that the function inspects body markup, not HTTP headers.

Response in src/requests/models.py starts with _content = False and _content_consumed = False. The content property reads the body once with b"".join(self.iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)), caches it in _content and sets _content_consumed. It raises RuntimeError if the stream was already consumed without caching. iter_content streams from raw.stream (urllib3) or raw.read in chunks, which avoids loading large bodies into memory, and marks the response as consumed. If _content is already cached, it replays it with iter_slices. If the stream was consumed but nothing was cached (_content still a bool), it raises StreamConsumedError. Session.send reads content eagerly only when stream=False. iter_lines, text and json build on these, and __getstate__ forces content to load for pickling.

PreparedRequest.prepare in src/requests/models.py calls prepare_url first. prepare_url parses the URL with urllib3's parse_url and rebuilds the netloc as "auth@host:port", so the credentials stay in self.url. prepare_auth(auth, url) runs later. When no explicit auth is given, it calls get_auth_from_url(self.url) in utils.py, which uses urlparse and unquote on the username and password. A 2-tuple becomes HTTPBasicAuth in auth.py, whose __call__ sets the Authorization header through _basic_auth_str. That function latin1-encodes the credentials and uses b64encode, which adds no line breaks, so long credentials stay on one header line. prepare_auth then merges r.__dict__ and recomputes prepare_content_length. Separately, Session.prepare_request may fall back to get_netrc_auth.

TLSServer is in tests/testserver/server.py, which is not among the files shown, so this answer is a best guess. TLSServer subclasses Server. In __init__ it builds an ssl.SSLContext(PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER) and calls load_cert_chain(cert_chain, keyfile). If mutual_tls is set, it sets verify_mode to CERT_OPTIONAL and calls load_verify_locations(cacert). _create_socket_and_bind then wraps the socket with server_side=True. A refactor could add an SSLContextBuilder with steps such as with_cert_chain, with_client_verification(mode, cafile) and build(). TLSServer would then only receive a context. This separates file I/O from policy, lets tests inject contexts (for example CERT_REQUIRED or bad CAs), and enables reuse. The cost is an extra test-only abstraction and a constructor signature change for existing fixtures.

In src/requests/sessions.py, Session.send calls resolve_redirects when allow_redirects is true. get_redirect_target returns the Location header only when resp.is_redirect, re-decoding it from latin1 to utf8. resolve_redirects then loops:
- It drains and closes the response and enforces max_redirects (raising TooManyRedirects).
- It resolves "//" and relative URLs and keeps the fragment.
- It calls rebuild_method, and for non-307/308 redirects it purges the body headers.
- It refreshes cookies, then calls rebuild_proxies and rebuild_auth, rewinds the body, and sends.

rebuild_auth deletes Authorization when should_strip_auth(old, new) is true: on a host change, or a scheme or port change other than the default-port http→https upgrade. It then re-applies get_netrc_auth if trust_env. rebuild_proxies strips and recomputes Proxy-Authorization.

PreparedRequest.prepare_headers in models.py creates a fresh CaseInsensitiveDict (structures.py). For each item, check_header_validity in utils.py validates the name and value. It uses the HEADER_VALIDATORS byte/str regexes from _internal_utils.py and raises InvalidHeader for leading whitespace, CR/LF, or non-str/bytes types. It then stores headers[to_native_string(name)] = value, so bytes names are ASCII-decoded to str. CaseInsensitiveDict keeps _store[key.lower()] = (original_key, value) in an OrderedDict. Lookups are case-insensitive, the last casing set wins, and equality compares lower_items(). Session-level merging uses merge_setting(..., dict_class=CaseInsensitiveDict), which drops None values. PreparedRequest.copy duplicates headers with headers.copy(), so copies stay independent.

to_native_string is implemented in src/requests/_internal_utils.py as to_native_string(string, encoding="ascii"). If the value is already builtin_str (from compat.py) it is returned unchanged; otherwise it is decoded with the given encoding. src/requests/utils.py re-imports it from ._internal_utils with a comment that it is kept for backwards compatibility. test_to_native_string in tests/test_utils.py most likely imports it via requests.utils, but the code that runs is the _internal_utils function.

The comments in PreparedRequest.prepare (models.py) give the reasons. prepare_auth "must be last" so schemes like OAuth can sign a fully prepared request: final URL, headers, cookies and body. HTTPDigestAuth.__call__ also records r.body.tell() for rewinding on a 401 retry. prepare_auth then recomputes Content-Length after the authenticator may have changed the body. prepare_hooks "MUST go after prepare_auth" because authenticators register hooks, such as Digest's handle_401 and handle_redirect. Ordering puts those hooks before user hooks in the list. Every step mutates shared self state and reads earlier results (method, url, headers, body), so the steps cannot be reordered or parallelized safely.

The test is in tests/test_requests.py. It checks SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in sessions.py. For any status other than 307/308, that method pops purged_headers (Content-Length, Content-Type, Transfer-Encoding) and sets prepared_request.body to None, after rebuild_method has turned the POST into a GET. If "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" survived on a bodiless GET, the server or proxy would wait for chunk framing. That can hang the connection, desynchronize keep-alive pooling, or open request-smuggling ambiguity. A leftover Content-Type or Content-Length would describe a body that does not exist, which is an HTTP/1.1 violation and could leak metadata about the original POST payload. 307/308 keep the body, so those headers are kept for them.

SSL tests in TestRequests (tests/test_requests.py) depend on several things:
- The pytest-httpbin fixtures httpbin_secure and httpbin_ca_bundle (pytest-httpbin==2.1.0), which run a local HTTPS server on free localhost ports.
- trustme-generated certificates and the tests/testserver TLSServer with cert files from tests/certs.
- A working ssl module with SNI.
- certifi's bundle via certs.where().
- Compatible urllib3 versions, plus optional pyOpenSSL or cryptography checks from __init__.py.

The environment also matters. Session.merge_environment_settings reads REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE, HTTP(S)_PROXY and NO_PROXY, plus .netrc, and these can silently change verify or proxies. Some tests also need real network or DNS access.

TestRequests (tests/test_requests.py) imports exceptions such as ConnectionError, InvalidSchema, MissingSchema, InvalidURL, TooManyRedirects, Timeout, ChunkedEncodingError, UnrewindableBodyError, InvalidHeader and InvalidJSONError from src/requests/exceptions.py. All of them derive from RequestException, which subclasses IOError. For redirects, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in sessions.py raises TooManyRedirects (carrying response=resp) once len(resp.history) >= max_redirects. While draining a redirect body it swallows ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError and RuntimeError. It calls utils.rewind_body, which raises UnrewindableBodyError. For authentication, rebuild_auth and should_strip_auth remove the Authorization header when the host changes. HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 in auth.py resends the request with a digest header. Response.raise_for_status raises HTTPError. Tests assert these with pytest.raises.

In cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie converts a Morsel into a cookielib Cookie through create_cookie, and that Cookie's expires field needs an absolute epoch timestamp. A Morsel may instead carry a relative max-age, which per the RFCs takes precedence over expires, so it is checked first. The function computes expires = int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"])) and raises TypeError if the value is not an integer. Otherwise, when morsel["expires"] is set, it parses the string with the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" using time.strptime and turns it into a UTC epoch with calendar.timegm. The result is passed as expires= to create_cookie.

Both exceptions are defined in exceptions.py. UnrewindableBodyError(RequestException) concerns the outgoing request body. It is raised by utils.rewind_body when resolve_redirects must resend a body (_body_position is set and Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding is present) but the body has no seek method, or _body_position is not an integer, or seek raises OSError. PreparedRequest.prepare_body sets _body_position = object() when tell() fails, which forces this error later. StreamConsumedError(RequestException, TypeError) concerns the response body. Response.iter_content in models.py raises it when _content_consumed is true and _content is still a bool, meaning a streamed raw body was already read and not cached.

The method is CaseInsensitiveDict.__iter__ in src/requests/structures.py. It returns (casedkey for casedkey, mappedvalue in self._store.values()). Here _store is an OrderedDict keyed by key.lower(), and __setitem__ stores the tuple (key, value) under that lowercased key. Iterating therefore yields the original-case key that was last set, and any differently-cased duplicates collapse into one entry. That is why list(cid) in test_list (tests/test_structures.py) gives exactly ['Accept']. Strictly, this is the preserved original casing rather than a lowercase-normalized key; lower_items is the method that exposes lowercased keys.

In models.py, Response uses _content = False as a "not yet read" sentinel and tracks _content_consumed. The content property materializes the body lazily by joining iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE). iter_content either streams through raw.stream or read, or replays cached bytes via iter_slices, and raises StreamConsumedError when the stream is gone. Serialization is handled by __getstate__: if the body is not yet consumed it reads self.content first, then returns only the attributes listed in __attrs__, which excludes raw. __setstate__ restores those attributes, sets _content_consumed = True and sets raw = None. A pickled Response therefore always holds full content, while a live one keeps stream=True semantics.

TestGuessJSONUTF in tests/test_utils.py exercises utils.guess_json_utf. The function takes the first four bytes and checks byte-order marks first. codecs.BOM_UTF32_LE or BE gives "utf-32", BOM_UTF8 gives "utf-8-sig", and BOM_UTF16_LE or BE gives "utf-16"; UTF-32 is tested before UTF-16 because the UTF-16 LE BOM is a prefix of the UTF-32 LE BOM. Without a BOM, it relies on JSON beginning with two ASCII characters and counts null bytes. Zero nulls means utf-8. Two nulls are resolved by position (sample[::2] or sample[1::2] equal to _null2) into utf-16-be or utf-16-le. Three nulls (_null3 position) give utf-32-be or utf-32-le. Anything else returns None. Response.json uses the result.

In tests/test_utils.py, @pytest.mark.parametrize("value, expected", [...]) decorates test__parse_content_type_header(value, expected). Pytest splits the argnames string, matches each name to a parameter of the test function, and generates one test item per tuple. Each item asserts that _parse_content_type_header(value) == expected. The function under test lives in src/requests/utils.py. It splits the header on ";" and takes the first token, stripped, as the content type. Each remaining param is split at the first "=", has its key and value stripped of quotes and spaces, and gets a lowercased key. A param without "=" maps to True. It returns a (content_type, params_dict) tuple.

ProxyError is defined in exceptions.py as a subclass of ConnectionError, which subclasses RequestException, which subclasses IOError. In HTTPAdapter.send (adapters.py), urllib3's MaxRetryError is inspected in order: ConnectTimeout comes first, then RetryError, then ProxyError when e.reason is urllib3's ProxyError. A direct urllib3 ProxyError (_ProxyError) is also converted to ProxyError. get_connection_with_tls_context raises the related InvalidProxyURL for malformed proxies. Nothing in Session.send, Session.request, resolve_redirects or api.request catches it, so it reaches the caller. There, handlers for ConnectionError, RequestException or IOError intercept it.

guess_filename in src/requests/utils.py reads obj.name and accepts it only if it is a str or bytes (basestring). It also rejects names that start with "<" or end with ">". These are pseudo-names such as "<stdin>" or "<fdopen>" that are not real paths. It then returns os.path.basename(name), so directory components and local absolute paths are dropped and never leak into the Content-Disposition filename. RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files in models.py calls it, falling back to the form field key, and passes the result to urllib3's RequestField. It is a hygiene and privacy safeguard more than a complete defence. It does not sanitise quotes or other special characters; urllib3's field formatting handles those.

In src/requests/models.py, Response.__enter__ returns self and __exit__ calls close(). close() calls raw.close() only if _content_consumed is False; a fully read body has already been released by urllib3. It then looks up raw.release_conn with getattr and calls it if present, returning the connection to the pool. There is no explicit "closed" flag. Double-close safety relies on urllib3's HTTPResponse.close and release_conn being idempotent. Unpickled responses are safe because __setstate__ sets raw=None and _content_consumed=True. A bare Response() with raw=None and unconsumed content would raise AttributeError. HTTPAdapter.build_response sets raw, and Session.send reads content when stream=False, so normal responses are already consumed.

merge_cookies (src/requests/cookies.py) is called in Session.prepare_request in sessions.py. There it builds a fresh RequestsCookieJar from self.cookies, then adds the per-request cookies; a jar is merged via update(), so request cookies override, while a dict is merged with overwrite=False. SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects also calls it to re-add session cookies after each redirect. Without it, PreparedRequest.prepare_cookies would receive only one source. Session-held login or auth cookies, or the request-specific ones, would vanish from the Cookie header. Redirects and HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 re-prepare cookies from prep._cookies, so cookie-based authentication would break across redirects and challenge retries.

CaseInsensitiveDict in src/requests/structures.py calls key.lower() on every __setitem__, __getitem__ and __delitem__. Each call allocates a new string and costs O(len(key)), before the OrderedDict hash and lookup. The inherited __contains__ and get add more calls, and __eq__ and copy rebuild whole dicts through lower_items. For HTTP headers this is negligible, but heavy lookups over large mappings add allocation and GC pressure. Possible optimisations: memoise lowercasing with a functools.lru_cache helper or an interned-key cache. Callers could pass pre-lowercased keys to a fast-path method. Storing a key wrapper with a precomputed lowercase hash would also help. Swapping OrderedDict for a plain dict reduces overhead further.

test_none_timeout is in tests/test_requests.py, in the timeout tests (likely class TestTimeout). It is decorated with @pytest.mark.parametrize("timeout", (None, Urllib3Timeout(connect=None, read=None))). pytest resolves "timeout" from the parametrize ids and "httpbin" from tests/conftest.py. That conftest fixture wraps pytest-httpbin's httpbin server fixture and returns prepare_url, a URL builder. The test calls requests.get(httpbin("get"), timeout=timeout). The value flows through api.request, Session.request and Session.send to HTTPAdapter.send. There a None value becomes TimeoutSauce(connect=None, read=None), and a urllib3 Timeout passes through unchanged. The test then asserts status 200.

Server lives in tests/testserver/server.py as a threading.Thread subclass, with classmethods text_response_server and basic_response_server. run() binds a socket, records the port, and sets ready_event. It then handles requests and optionally waits on wait_to_close_event. Finally it closes the server socket and sets stop_event. __enter__ starts the thread, waits on ready_event and returns (host, port). __exit__ waits on stop_event if no exception occurred; otherwise it sets wait_to_close_event and force-closes the socket. It then joins the thread and returns False. tests/test_testserver.py (TestTestServer) exercises this, e.g. test_server_closes, test_request_recovery and test_requests_after_timeout_are_not_received.

test_pragmas in tests/test_utils.py is parametrized with HTML5 meta charset, HTTP-equiv meta (with and without a self-closing slash) and XML-declaration inputs. It asserts that utils.get_encodings_from_content returns exactly one result, equal to "UTF-8". This assumes the content is a str, not bytes, since the regexes are str patterns. It assumes quotes and delimiters are stripped by charset_re, pragma_re and xml_re. It also assumes each declaration matches only one regex, so there are no duplicates. Despite the question's premise, there is no normalisation: case is preserved as written. The function also emits a DeprecationWarning.

In src/requests/models.py, Response uses _content=False as an "unread" sentinel plus a _content_consumed flag. The content property drains iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE) once, caches the bytes and marks the response consumed. iter_content then replays the cached bytes through iter_slices, or streams from raw.stream() when nothing is cached. If the stream was consumed without caching, it raises StreamConsumedError. Session.send in sessions.py touches r.content only when stream=False. With stream=True, iter_content and iter_lines avoid full buffering and are the only memory-safe path. Accessing content, text or json, or pickling via __getstate__, loads the whole body. This keeps backward compatibility with both access patterns.

In src/requests/models.py, Response.links calls parse_header_links (src/requests/utils.py), which returns a list of dicts. It then loops over them, using `link.get("rel") or link.get("url")` as the key in `resolved_links`. When several entries share the same rel, each assignment overwrites the previous one, so only the last entry is kept. The others are silently lost, with no warning or list aggregation. The algorithm is a single O(n) pass with O(1) dict inserts, and the result holds at most one entry per distinct rel. A multi-token rel such as "next last" is treated as one opaque string key, not split into separate relations.

TestIsValidCIDR.test_invalid in tests/test_utils.py has no branching of its own. It is a pytest.mark.parametrize test that passes each value to is_valid_cidr and asserts the result is False. All the branching is in is_valid_cidr in src/requests/utils.py. If `count("/") != 1`, the else branch returns False (for example "8.8.8.8"). If the mask fails int(), the ValueError path returns False (for example "192.168.1.0/a"). A mask below 1 or above 32 returns False (for example "/128" or "/-1"). If socket.inet_aton rejects the address part, the OSError path returns False (for example "192.168.1.999/24"). Which path runs depends only on the parametrized string.

InvalidSchema in src/requests/exceptions.py subclasses both RequestException and ValueError. RequestException derives from IOError and carries request/response attributes, so the error can be caught by generic `except requests.RequestException` handlers along with other Requests errors. ValueError says the caller supplied a bad argument value, which is an input mistake rather than an I/O failure. That lets standard `except ValueError` validation code catch it too. It is raised by Session.get_adapter in src/requests/sessions.py when no mounted adapter prefix matches the URL. It is also raised by the fallback SOCKSProxyManager stub in src/requests/adapters.py when PySocks is missing. MissingSchema and InvalidURL follow the same dual-inheritance pattern.

In PreparedRequest.prepare_body (src/requests/models.py), a body counts as a stream when it is iterable and not a str, bytes, list, tuple or Mapping. A stream is sent as-is, with Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Multipart uploads go through _encode_files, which calls urllib3's encode_multipart_formdata. That function builds the whole body in memory, reads file objects completely, and expects data as key/value fields. A generator or stream has no field name and cannot become a form part without being fully consumed, which defeats streaming. Merging the two would be ambiguous and memory-unsafe, so Requests rejects the combination explicitly. Users who need streamed multipart uploads can use an external encoder such as requests-toolbelt's MultipartEncoder.

In src/requests/cookies.py, MockRequest.host is a property that calls get_host(), which returns `urlparse(self._r.url).netloc`. The extra call frame costs tens of nanoseconds and grows linearly with the number of calls; it does not compound. The real cost is re-running urlparse on every access, although recent Python versions cache urlsplit results internally. To optimize, parse self._r.url once in __init__, which already parses it to get the scheme, and store netloc. Alternatively, use functools.cached_property for host. Caching is safe because http.cookiejar uses MockRequest only briefly inside extract_cookies_to_jar and get_cookie_header, while the URL does not change.

In morsel_to_cookie in src/requests/cookies.py, expires starts as None. The first branch, `if morsel["max-age"]`, tries `int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"]))` and converts a ValueError into a TypeError ("max-age ... must be integer"). The `elif morsel["expires"]` branch parses the string with time.strptime using "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" and converts it to an epoch with calendar.timegm. If neither field is set, expires stays None. The TypeError comes only from the max-age path; a malformed expires string raises an uncaught ValueError from strptime. The result is passed to create_cookie.

Requests already handles this outside the RequestException hierarchy. check_compatibility in src/requests/__init__.py asserts the urllib3, chardet and charset_normalizer version ranges. The module-level call catches AssertionError and ValueError and emits warnings.warn with RequestsDependencyWarning instead of raising. _check_cryptography does the same for cryptography. RequestsDependencyWarning in src/requests/exceptions.py derives from RequestsWarning and Warning, so a version mismatch never breaks import or existing except clauses. New checks should reuse or subclass RequestsDependencyWarning and use explicit comparisons rather than asserts, because asserts are stripped under `python -O`. RequestException should stay untouched. help.py's info() reports the detected versions for bug reports.

get_environ_proxies in src/requests/utils.py passes no_proxy to should_bypass_proxies. An explicit value, for example from `proxies.get("no_proxy")` in Session.merge_environment_settings or in resolve_proxies, replaces the no_proxy/NO_PROXY environment variables. set_environ also temporarily writes it into os.environ so that the stdlib proxy_bypass honors it. Without an argument, the environment's no_proxy is used. A non-empty return means the URL's host matched no override entry (CIDR, IP or hostname suffix) and proxy_bypass did not exclude it. getproxies() then returns the configured environment proxies, which apply to this request. An empty dict means the URL is bypassed or no proxies are configured.

In `models.py`, `RequestHooksMixin.register_hook` appends a single `Callable` directly. For an iterable, it calls `extend` with a filter that silently drops non-callables, so the collection is flattened into individual list entries. `deregister_hook` only calls `self.hooks[event].remove(hook)`. Passing the same list or tuple back therefore matches nothing and returns `False`. Callers must deregister each element one by one. A generator is consumed during registration and cannot be replayed for removal. `remove` deletes only the first equal entry, so duplicates partially survive. Silently dropped non-callables can never be found, which also gives `False` with no indication why. Registration is variadic, but removal is strictly per-callable.

`BaseAdapter` in `adapters.py` implicitly inherits from `object`, yet its `__init__` calls `super().__init__()`. `HTTPAdapter.__init__` does the same. This is cooperative multiple inheritance: every class in the MRO chains to the next. If a user combines `BaseAdapter` or `HTTPAdapter` with mixins (logging, retry, instrumentation), all initializers in the MRO run instead of being cut off at `BaseAdapter`. Together with `send` and `close` raising `NotImplementedError`, this reflects an abstract interface (Template/Strategy) designed for mixin-based extension. Custom transports mounted through `Session.mount` can compose behaviours safely.

In `models.py`, `Response.apparent_encoding` checks `chardet`, which is resolved by `compat._resolve_char_detection` (chardet first, then charset_normalizer). If it is `None`, the property returns `"utf-8"`. Otherwise it reads `self.content`, which joins `iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)` and caches the result in `_content`, then calls `chardet.detect(...)["encoding"]`. On success, `Response.text` decodes the bytes with `str(self.content, encoding, errors="replace")`. If detection fails, the encoding is `None` and that call raises `TypeError`. `text` catches it and falls back to `str(self.content, errors="replace")`, i.e. the default UTF-8 with replacement. `json()` only reaches this path when `guess_json_utf` cannot decide.

In `cookies.py`, `extract_cookies_to_jar` wraps `response._original_response.msg`, an `http.client.HTTPMessage`, in a `MockResponse`. `MockResponse.getheaders(name)` delegates to `self._headers.getheaders(name)` but has no `return` statement, so it always yields `None`. It is also a Python 2 `mimetools` API that the Python 3 `HTTPMessage` lacks, so calling it raises `AttributeError`. In practice the stdlib `CookieJar.extract_cookies`/`make_cookies` uses `info().get_all("Set-Cookie")` via `MockResponse.info()`. As a result, `getheaders` is dead legacy shim code that nothing in the real delegation chain exercises.

`PreparedRequest.prepare_body` calls `RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data)` in `models.py` when files are given. It normalizes both arguments with `utils.to_key_val_list`. Each file value may be a bare object or a 2-, 3- or 4-tuple (filename, fileobj, content_type, custom_headers). Bare objects get a name from `utils.guess_filename`, falling back to the field key. Data comes from str/bytes/bytearray directly or from `.read()`, and `None` entries are skipped. Each file becomes a urllib3 `RequestField` followed by `make_multipart(content_type=ft)`. `encode_multipart_formdata` then produces the body and boundary content type. `prepare_content_length` sets Content-Length, and the Content-Type header is added if absent. Streams combined with files raise `NotImplementedError`.

In `exceptions.py`, `RequestException(IOError)` is the root and stores `request` and `response`. `HTTPError` is raised only by `Response.raise_for_status` in `models.py` for 4xx/5xx statuses, always with `response=self`. `Response.ok` catches it. `ConnectionError` is a sibling subclass with children `ProxyError`, `SSLError` and `ConnectTimeout`, raised in `HTTPAdapter.send` (`adapters.py`) when wrapping urllib3 `ProtocolError`, `OSError`, `MaxRetryError` and `ClosedPoolError`. Because they are siblings, recovery code can tell "server answered with an error" (`HTTPError`, with a response to inspect) from "no usable response" (`ConnectionError`/`Timeout`, often retryable). Catching `RequestException` or `IOError` handles both. urllib3's own `HTTPError` is imported as `_HTTPError`/`BaseHTTPError` to avoid a name clash.

`MockRequest` in `cookies.py` calls `urlparse(self._r.url)` in `__init__` and again in every `get_host` call. The `host` and `origin_req_host` properties also go through `get_host`, and `get_full_url` parses again when a Host header exists. `http.cookiejar` calls these accessors repeatedly per cookie during policy checks in `add_cookie_header`/`extract_cookies`. Many cookies, redirects and requests therefore multiply the parses. MockRequest never mutates `_r`; it writes only `_new_headers`. The parsed result can thus be computed once in `__init__`, or via `functools.cached_property`, and reused for type, netloc and full-URL reconstruction without breaking the read-only semantics.

In `sessions.py`, each hop of `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` copies the request with `req.copy()`, which uses `_copy_cookie_jar` so the original jar is untouched. It then removes the stale `Cookie` header. Next, `extract_cookies_to_jar(prepared_request._cookies, req, resp.raw)` reads the redirect's Set-Cookie using the pre-mutation request. `merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies)` folds in session cookies. `prepare_cookies` regenerates the header through `get_cookie_header`/`MockRequest` for the new URL, so domain and path rules apply. After sending, cookies are extracted into `self.cookies`, and `req = prepared_request` carries the jar into the next hop. `Session.send` also persists cookies from the history.

In src/requests/models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare() first calls prepare_url(), which runs urllib3's parse_url. The `auth` component is kept in the netloc as "user:pass@host", and the whole URL is re-quoted with requote_uri(). Later prepare_auth() runs. It receives a url argument but reads self.url. If no explicit auth was given, it calls get_auth_from_url() in src/requests/utils.py, which uses urlparse and unquote on the username and password. A 2-tuple is wrapped in HTTPBasicAuth, and src/requests/auth.py's _basic_auth_str() encodes it as latin1 and base64. The result goes into the Authorization header and is merged back with self.__dict__.update(). There is no length limit, so long credentials pass through unchanged. prepare_content_length() then runs again.

TLSServer is in tests/testserver/server.py, which is not included here, so this is a best guess. It probably builds an ssl.SSLContext, calls load_cert_chain() for the server cert and key, and for mutual TLS sets verify_mode and calls load_verify_locations() with the CA. A dedicated SSLContextBuilder could split this into separate steps: load server credentials, configure client verification, then build. TLSServer would only bind and wrap sockets. Benefits: each step is testable alone, fixtures can reuse it, and it mirrors adapters.py, where cert_verify() and _urllib3_request_context() already separate cert_reqs from cert_file. Costs: more abstraction in test-only code, and the context must still be finished before the socket is wrapped.

In src/requests/sessions.py, get_redirect_target() checks Response.is_redirect and re-decodes the Location header from latin1 to UTF-8. resolve_redirects() then loops. Each pass copies the request, records history, consumes and closes the old response, and enforces max_redirects (raising TooManyRedirects). It resolves scheme-relative and relative URLs with urljoin and requote_uri, carries the fragment forward, and calls rebuild_method(). It purges body headers except on 307/308, then strips the Cookie header and re-merges cookies. rebuild_proxies() drops Proxy-Authorization and re-adds it only for non-HTTPS. rebuild_auth() deletes Authorization when should_strip_auth() sees a different host, scheme or non-default port; plain http→https on default ports is exempt. It then reapplies .netrc credentials if trust_env is set. Session.send() drives this generator.

In src/requests/models.py, PreparedRequest.prepare_headers() always builds a fresh CaseInsensitiveDict (src/requests/structures.py). For each (name, value) item it calls check_header_validity() in utils.py. That function uses _validate_header_part with the HEADER_VALIDATORS regexes from _internal_utils.py and raises InvalidHeader for non-str/bytes parts, leading whitespace, colons in names, or CR/LF. Names are converted with to_native_string(), decoding bytes as ASCII; values are stored as given. CaseInsensitiveDict stores lowercased key → (original key, value), so the last casing written wins and lookups ignore case. Session.prepare_request() merges headers through merge_setting(dict_class=CaseInsensitiveDict) and drops keys set to None. PreparedRequest.copy() uses headers.copy().

The function is defined in src/requests/_internal_utils.py as to_native_string(string, encoding="ascii"). If the input is already builtin_str (str, via compat.py) it is returned unchanged; otherwise it is decoded with the given encoding. src/requests/utils.py re-imports it with a noqa F401 comment for backward compatibility. The test (likely tests/test_utils.py, not shown) imports it through requests.utils, which leads to the _internal_utils implementation.

The ordering is in PreparedRequest.prepare() in src/requests/models.py. prepare_auth() runs last because auth callables may need the final URL, headers, cookies and body. Signing schemes like OAuth hash the body, and HTTPDigestAuth.__call__ records body.tell() for rewinding. prepare_auth() also copies the auth object's state back with self.__dict__.update() and recomputes Content-Length. prepare_hooks() comes after because authenticators register their own hooks; HTTPDigestAuth adds handle_401 and handle_redirect through register_hook(). If hooks were prepared earlier, the __dict__ copy could overwrite user hooks. Every step mutates shared state on the same object, so reordering or parallelising them would produce inconsistent requests.

The test lives in tests/test_requests.py (not shown). It most likely builds a request with a streamed generator body (so it is chunked), fakes a 302/303 response, and checks the redirected request. It targets SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects() in sessions.py, which removes Content-Length, Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding and sets body to None for non-307/308 redirects (issue #3490), after rebuild_method() switches POST to GET. If these headers stayed, a bodyless GET would announce chunked framing, which can make servers hang, desynchronise connections or enable request smuggling. A leftover Content-Type would misdescribe the request. Leaving Transfer-Encoding would also mark the request as rewindable, so an unseekable stream would raise UnrewindableBodyError.

TestRequests is in tests/test_requests.py (not shown), so this is a best guess. The SSL tests depend on pytest-httpbin fixtures such as httpbin_secure and httpbin_ca_bundle, on trustme-generated certificates, and on local TLS servers from tests/testserver that need free localhost ports. Those packages are pinned in requirements-dev.txt. They also need a working ssl module with SNI, certifi's bundle (DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH from certs.where()), and supported urllib3 and cryptography versions. Session.merge_environment_settings() reads REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE and proxy variables when trust_env is set, so a polluted environment can break tests. Some tests may also need outbound network access.

TestRequests in tests/test_requests.py imports many classes from src/requests/exceptions.py. These include ConnectionError, ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, Timeout, MissingSchema, InvalidSchema, InvalidURL, InvalidHeader, ProxyError, SSLError, RetryError, TooManyRedirects, UnrewindableBodyError, ChunkedEncodingError and InvalidJSONError. All of them derive from RequestException, which subclasses IOError. In redirects, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects in sessions.py catches ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError and RuntimeError while draining resp.content. It raises TooManyRedirects(response=resp) past max_redirects, and utils.rewind_body raises UnrewindableBodyError. For authentication, rebuild_auth and should_strip_auth drop the Authorization header across hosts. auth.HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 re-sends the request through r.connection.send, so HTTPAdapter.send's urllib3-to-requests exception translation still applies.

morsel_to_cookie in src/requests/cookies.py checks max-age first because, under RFC 6265, Max-Age takes precedence over Expires. It also does this because http.cookiejar.Cookie, built by create_cookie, needs an absolute epoch-seconds expires value. A relative max-age becomes absolute through int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"])). A non-integer value raises ValueError, which is converted into TypeError. Otherwise an "expires" string is parsed with time.strptime using the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT". calendar.timegm then converts it as UTC into a timestamp. If neither attribute is present, expires stays None.

UnrewindableBodyError concerns the outgoing request body. utils.rewind_body raises it during SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects when the body cannot be seeked back to PreparedRequest._body_position. That happens when the body has no seek method, when the position is not an integer (prepare_body stores object() if tell() raised OSError), or when seek raises OSError. StreamConsumedError, which subclasses RequestException and TypeError, concerns the incoming response body. Response.iter_content raises it when _content_consumed is True but _content is still a bool. That state means the stream was already read and never cached, so it cannot be iterated again.

CaseInsensitiveDict in src/requests/structures.py defines __iter__ to return a generator over casedkey for casedkey, mappedvalue in self._store.values(). __setitem__ stores entries as _store[key.lower()] = (key, value). Iteration therefore yields the original-cased key that was last assigned, not the lowercase lookup key. Because all variants share one lowercase slot, list(cid) in test_list (tests/test_structures.py) produces exactly ['Accept']. __len__, which also uses _store, keeps the count consistent.

In src/requests/models.py, Response.__init__ sets _content=False and _content_consumed=False. The content property materializes the body lazily by joining iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE), and it marks _content_consumed. Pickling is handled separately. __getstate__ forces self.content if the body has not been consumed, then returns only the attributes listed in __attrs__. That excludes raw, connection and _next. __setstate__ restores those attributes, sets _content_consumed=True and sets raw=None. Afterwards, iter_content serves cached data through utils.iter_slices instead of the stream. Streaming behaviour stays intact until pickling happens.

TestGuessJSONUTF in tests/test_utils.py exercises utils.guess_json_utf. That function checks byte-order marks first, on a 4-byte sample. A BOM_UTF32 match returns "utf-32", BOM_UTF8 returns "utf-8-sig", and BOM_UTF16 returns "utf-16". UTF-32 is checked before UTF-16 because the UTF-32-LE BOM begins with the UTF-16-LE BOM. Without a BOM, it relies on JSON starting with two ASCII characters and counts null bytes. Zero nulls means "utf-8". Two nulls at the even or odd positions give "utf-16-be" or "utf-16-le", and three nulls give "utf-32-be" or "utf-32-le". Anything else returns None, which makes Response.json fall back to the text property.

In tests/test_utils.py, @pytest.mark.parametrize takes the argument names (for example "value, expected") plus a list of tuples. Each tuple pairs a raw header string with an expected (content_type, params_dict) result. pytest binds those names to the parameters of test__parse_content_type_header and generates one test item per tuple. Each item asserts utils._parse_content_type_header(value) == expected. That function splits on ";" and strips the media type. It lowercases parameter keys, strips quotes and spaces from keys and values, and maps parameters without "=" to True.

ProxyError inherits from ConnectionError, which inherits from RequestException and then IOError, all in src/requests/exceptions.py. HTTPAdapter.send in adapters.py raises it in two places. One is when a MaxRetryError has reason _ProxyError, giving ProxyError(e, request=request) after the ConnectTimeout and RetryError checks. The other is when a bare urllib3 _ProxyError is caught, giving ProxyError(e) without a request. A malformed proxy URL instead raises InvalidProxyURL, an InvalidURL subclass, from get_connection_with_tls_context. Session.send and api.request do not catch ProxyError, so it reaches the caller. Any handler for ConnectionError, RequestException or IOError will intercept it.

In `src/flask/cli.py`, `CertParamType.convert` (a `click.ParamType` used for `--cert` on `run_command`) first checks that the `ssl` module can be imported, and raises `click.BadParameter` if it can't. It then tries `self.path_type`, which is `click.Path(exists=True, dir_okay=False, resolve_path=True)`, and returns the resolved path to an existing file. If that raises `BadParameter`, it converts the value with `click.STRING` and lowercases it. If the result is "adhoc", it checks that `cryptography` can be imported and returns the string. Otherwise it calls werkzeug's `import_string(value, silent=True)` and returns the object if it is an `ssl.SSLContext`. If nothing matches, the bare `raise` re-raises the original file-path `BadParameter`. Because of the lowercasing, mixed-case import paths won't resolve. `_validate_key` later pairs the cert with `--key`.

Inheritance is handled in `Config.from_object` in `src/flask/config.py`, at lines 250–254. If given a string, it first imports the object with `werkzeug.utils.import_string`. It then loops over `dir(obj)` and copies every uppercase name into the config with `self[key] = getattr(obj, key)`. Because `dir()` lists attributes inherited through the class's MRO, uppercase settings defined on parent classes are included. `getattr` follows normal attribute lookup, so a value set on the child class overrides the parent's. `tests/test_config.py::test_config_from_class` checks this: `Test(Base)` inherits `TEST_KEY` from `Base` and defines its own `SECRET_KEY`, and both are loaded. The docstring warns that `@property` attributes only work if you pass an instance, not the class.

In `src/flask/app.py`, `Flask.open_resource` (and the matching `Blueprint.open_resource` in `src/flask/blueprints.py`) raises `ValueError("Resources can only be opened for reading.")` for any mode other than "r", "rt" or "rb". The reason is that `root_path` points at the application package's own code. That code may be installed in site-packages, under version control, or shared by several deployments, so it should be treated as read-only data like `schema.sql`, templates or static files. Files that change at runtime belong in the instance folder (`instance_path`), as `docs/config.rst` explains. `Flask.open_instance_resource` is the counterpart for that folder, and its docstring says that, unlike `open_resource`, it allows opening files for writing.

At this commit, plugin registration rules are spread across several places in `PytestPluginManager` (`src/_pytest/config/__init__.py`). `register()` silently drops names listed in `DEPRECATED_EXTERNAL_PLUGINS`. `consider_pluginarg()` hard-codes the rule that `essential_plugins` cannot be disabled, the link between cacheprovider and stepwise, and the `pytest_` name prefix. `import_plugin()` checks `is_blocked()`, and pluggy's `PluginManager.register` quietly returns None for blocked names. Tests such as `test_plugin_prevent_register` in `testing/test_pluginmanager.py` can only confirm all this by checking `get_plugins()` afterwards. My recommended redesign: put these rules in one declarative `RegistrationPolicy` object (protected names, deprecated names, dependency graph, name normalisation). Route `register`, `set_blocked` and `unregister` through one gate that applies blocking to dependent plugins automatically and raises clear errors, so the rules hold for every caller, not only tested paths.

The test modules that TestEvaluation builds (test_marked_one_arg, test_marked_one_arg_with_reason, test_marked_one_arg_twice and others in testing/test_skipping.py) never import os. String conditions like "hasattr(os, 'sep')" still work because evaluate_condition in src/_pytest/skipping.py runs eval() with a globals dict it builds itself, holding the os, sys and platform modules plus item.config. It then merges in the dicts from item.ihook.pytest_markeval_namespace(config=item.config), which conftest.py can supply, and finally item.obj.__globals__ (the test module's own namespace). So each test needs a real collected Item from the Pytester fixture's getitem/getitems: it needs a config, an ihook for that hook, and an obj. evaluate_skip_marks drives this through item.iter_markers("skipif").

In src/requests/models.py, RequestHooksMixin.register_hook handles the two input types differently. A single callable is added with self.hooks[event].append(hook). An iterable is flattened: extend() adds each callable element on its own and silently drops anything that isn't callable. deregister_hook is not symmetric. It only calls self.hooks[event].remove(hook) once and catches ValueError to return False. If you pass the same list or tuple you registered, it looks for that collection itself in the flat list, never finds it, and returns False, so none of the hooks are removed. You must deregister each function separately. remove() also deletes only the first equal entry, so a hook registered twice stays registered once. If a generator was consumed during registration, you can't recreate it to undo the registration.

In `tests/test_cli.py`, `test_locate_app_raises` is parametrized over (iname, aname) pairs, and each pair is aimed at a different failure path in `src/flask/cli.py`. All of them must raise `NoAppException`. In `locate_app`, a direct `ImportError` (for "notanapp.py", "cliapp/app" or "cliapp.message.txt") becomes "Could not import". A nested `ImportError` (for `cliapp.importerrorapp`), detected through `tb_next`, is always re-raised as `NoAppException`. In `find_app_by_string`, a missing attribute ("notanapp"), a `SyntaxError` from `ast.parse` ("create_app("), a wrong-arity `TypeError` checked by `_called_with_wrong_args` (`create_app2("foo")`) and a non-Flask result (`no_app`) each become `NoAppException`. Because `raise_if_not_found` defaults to True, every case fails the same way.

In `src/_pytest/pathlib.py`, `ensure_deletable` turns every failure into "not deletable" (`False`) instead of raising an error. If `lock.is_file()` raises `OSError`, it returns `False`, assuming the whole directory is inaccessible (#7491). If `lock.stat()` fails (for example, another process just removed the lock), it returns `False`. The `lock.unlink()` call sits inside `contextlib.suppress(OSError)`, and `return True` is reached only if the unlink succeeds; a `PermissionError` or a `FileNotFoundError` from another pytest process falls through to `return False` (#5456). The first failure returns immediately, so errors cannot pile up. `try_cleanup` then skips `maybe_delete_a_numbered_dir`, and `cleanup_numbered_dir` carries on with the other candidates, the `garbage-*` directories and `cleanup_dead_symlinks`. `test_suppress_error_removing_lock` in `testing/test_pathlib.py` checks this.

The interception points are set up in `MockTiming.patch` in `src/_pytest/timing.py`. That method imports the `_pytest.timing` module itself and calls `monkeypatch.setattr` three times, rebinding the module-level names `sleep`, `time` and `perf_counter` (originally imported from `time`). `sleep` goes to `self.sleep`, and both `time` and `perf_counter` go to `self.time`. `MonkeyPatch.setattr` in `src/_pytest/monkeypatch.py` records each original value in `_setattr` before replacing it. The three calls are independent and run in order, so they share no state. `MonkeyPatch.undo` later restores the originals in reverse order. The real side effect is that `perf_counter` and `time` return the same `_current_time`, which only `sleep` moves forward. The `Instant` lambdas pick up the mock because they look up these names at call time. The `mock_timing` fixture in `testing/conftest.py` sets all this up.

In src/requests/exceptions.py, RequestException subclasses IOError, so existing `except IOError/OSError` code still catches it. Its `__init__` pops the optional `response` and `request` keyword arguments and stores them as attributes. If a response was given but no request (or a falsy one), and the response has a `request` attribute, it sets `self.request = response.request`. It then calls `super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)` with the leftover arguments, so IOError never receives the requests-specific keywords. Every subclass (HTTPError, ConnectionError, Timeout, InvalidJSONError and others) gets this behaviour. JSONDecodeError's own `__init__` first calls CompatJSONDecodeError.__init__, then InvalidJSONError.__init__ with `self.args`, so the same initialisation runs through the multiple-inheritance chain.

In src/requests/cookies.py, morsel_to_cookie turns a stdlib http.cookies.Morsel into an http.cookiejar.Cookie through create_cookie. A Cookie's expires field must be an absolute Unix timestamp, but max-age is a number of seconds counted from now. So the function checks morsel["max-age"] first, which gives it priority over expires, matching RFC 6265. If it is set, the code computes int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"])): the current epoch time plus the offset. A value that isn't an integer raises a ValueError, which is re-raised as a TypeError. If max-age is empty, the function parses morsel["expires"] with time.strptime using the "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT" format, then converts it to an epoch timestamp with calendar.timegm. Otherwise expires stays None, making it a session cookie.

The only place it's raised is `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` in `src/requests/sessions.py`, at lines 190–193. The class itself is defined at `src/requests/exceptions.py:95` as a subclass of `RequestException`. The chain runs `requests.get`/`api.request` → `Session.request` → `Session.send`. After `adapter.send`, `send` calls `self.resolve_redirects(r, request, **kwargs)` when `allow_redirects` is true and drains the generator into a list (line 723). Inside the `while url:` loop, which uses `get_redirect_target`, each response is added to `hist`, `resp.history` is set to `hist[1:]` and the body is consumed. When `len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects` (default `DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT`, 30, set in `Session.__init__`), it raises `TooManyRedirects(f"Exceeded {self.max_redirects} redirects.", response=resp)`. Otherwise it calls `self.send(..., allow_redirects=False)` and loops again.

In src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py, Blueprint.add_url_rule (wrapped by @setupmethod, which calls _check_setup_finished) first rejects any endpoint or view_func.__name__ that contains a dot. It then calls self.record(...) with a lambda s: s.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, view_func, provide_automatic_options=..., **options). That closure keeps the arguments, and record simply appends it to self.deferred_functions. No app exists yet, so nothing is registered at this point. Later, Flask.register_blueprint calls Blueprint.register(app, options). That method builds a BlueprintSetupState through make_setup_state and loops "for deferred in self.deferred_functions: deferred(state)". Only then does BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule run. It adds url_prefix, subdomain, merged url_defaults and the name_prefix.blueprint-name endpoint prefix, then calls app.add_url_rule. This lets one blueprint be registered on several apps or under different prefixes.

The class is `TestStreaming` in `tests/test_helpers.py`. It is a plain pytest test-grouping class: it has no setup or state of its own and gets the `app` and `client` fixtures from `tests/conftest.py`. Its tests (`test_streaming_with_context`, `test_streaming_with_context_as_decorator`, `test_streaming_with_context_and_custom_close`, `test_stream_keeps_session`) check that `flask.stream_with_context` in `src/flask/helpers.py` keeps the request context alive while a response streams. That function uses a decorator/wrapper pattern. It wraps the user's generator, or a function that returns one, in an inner generator that runs `with ctx:` on the context taken from `_cv_request`. It primes that generator with `next()` on a dummy `None` value, then uses `yield from` and calls `close()` in a `finally` block. The custom `Wrapper` iterator test confirms that `close()` is called.

`TestReport.from_item_and_call` in `src/_pytest/reports.py` first takes `call.when` and asserts it is not "collect". It then branches on `call.excinfo`. If there is no exception, the outcome is "passed" and longrepr is None. If excinfo is not an `ExceptionInfo`, the outcome is "failed" and longrepr is excinfo itself. If the exception is a `skip.Exception`, the outcome is "skipped" and longrepr is a (path, lineno, message) tuple built from `excinfo._getreprcrash()`. When `_use_item_location` is set, the path and line come from `item.reportinfo()` instead, with the line plus 1. Any other exception is "failed": in the "call" phase longrepr comes from `item.repr_failure(excinfo)`, and in setup or teardown from `item._repr_failure_py(excinfo, style=tbstyle)`. Captured sections from `item._report_sections` are then added, and the method builds the report.

It happens in src/flask/json/tag.py, in `PassList.to_json` (line 153). That method returns `[self.serializer.tag(item) for item in value]`, so each item goes back to the type dispatcher, `TaggedJSONSerializer.tag` (line 289). The dispatcher walks `self.order` in the `default_tags` order (TagDict, PassDict, TagTuple, PassList, TagBytes, TagMarkup, TagUUID, TagDateTime). It calls `tag.check(value)` on each and uses the first match's `tag()`. For `PassList`, `tag` is just `to_json`, so a list gets no wrapper. A nested list therefore goes back into `PassList.to_json`, and that repeats at every depth, while tuples, bytes, UUIDs and so on get their own tags. `TagTuple.to_json` works the same way. On load, `_untag_scan` rebuilds lists item by item.

In `src/flask/json/tag.py`, `TagUUID` is a `JSONTag` subclass. Its job is to make serialization lossless, because standard JSON has no UUID type. Its `check()` matches `UUID` instances. `to_json()` returns `value.hex`, a compact 32-character string that is valid JSON. `JSONTag.tag()` then wraps that string under the key `" u"`. On load, `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads()` uses `untag()` / `_untag_scan()` to find the `" u"` key and calls `TagUUID.to_python()`, which rebuilds the object with `UUID(value)`. A UUID stored in the session, through `SecureCookieSessionInterface`'s serializer, therefore comes back as a real `UUID` object rather than a plain string. Both directions are needed: the tag key records the original type, and the hex string can be turned back into an equal `UUID`.

`_NodeReporter.write_captured_output` in `src/_pytest/junitxml.py` does nothing if `log_passing_tests` (the `junit_log_passing_tests` ini option) is False and the report passed, or if `self.xml.logging` (`junit_logging`) is "no". Otherwise it fills a buffer, `content_all`. The modes "log" and "all" put `report.caplog` in it under a " Captured Log " header from `_prepare_content`. The modes "system-out", "out-err" and "all" add `capstdout`, write it with `_write_content` as `<system-out>`, then clear the buffer. The modes "system-err", "out-err" and "all" do the same with `capstderr` as `<system-err>`. Any leftover buffer, which only happens in "log" mode, goes to `<system-out>`. `junit_logging` takes one value, so "out-err" is the system-out-plus-system-err combination: it writes stdout and stderr to separate tags. "all" also puts the captured log first inside `<system-out>`, ahead of stdout.

In `src/requests/models.py`, `Response.__init__` sets two flags: `_content = False`, meaning nothing is cached yet, and `_content_consumed = False`. `iter_content()` has an inner `generate()` that streams from `raw.stream()` (urllib3) or `raw.read()` and sets `_content_consumed = True` once the stream is exhausted, so a large body is never held in memory. If the content is already cached, it instead re-serves it in chunks through `utils.iter_slices`. If the stream was consumed but nothing was cached, it raises `StreamConsumedError`. The `content` property joins `iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE)` once and caches the bytes. It raises `RuntimeError` if the stream was already read. `Session.send` in `sessions.py` reads `r.content` when `stream=False`. `__getstate__`, `__setstate__`, `close()` and `iter_lines` depend on the same flags.

In `src/_pytest/capture.py`, `SysCapture` (a subclass of `SysCaptureBase`) stays consistent because each operation touches a different object. `__init__` saves the real stream in `self._old` and sets up a separate `CaptureIO` `tmpfile`, which `start()` and `resume()` install as `sys.stdout` or `sys.stderr`. `snap()` reads the buffer with `getvalue()`, then calls `seek(0)` and `truncate()`, so each output is handed over once and never twice. `writeorg()` writes straight to `self._old` and flushes it, without going through `sys.*`, so replayed output cannot land back in the capture buffer. Both methods call `_assert_state` to require the "started" or "suspended" state. That lets `MultiCapture.pop_outerr_to_orig()` (snap, then writeorg) send output to the real terminal once, in order, with nothing lost or duplicated.

`Pytester.runpytest_subprocess` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py` builds the arguments (`--basetemp` set to a numbered `runpytest-` directory, `-p` for each plugin named as a string, then `_getpytestargs()`, which gives `sys.executable -mpytest`) and calls `Pytester.run`. `run` uses `Pytester.popen` (`subprocess.Popen` with the current directory added to `PYTHONPATH`), sends stdout and stderr to files, waits with an optional timeout (raising `TimeoutExpired`), and returns a `RunResult` holding an `ExitCode`. No exception crosses the process boundary, so only exit codes and output come back. In the child, `pytest_make_collect_report` in `src/_pytest/runner.py` calls `CallInfo.from_call(..., reraise=(KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit))`, so these escape collection. `wrap_session` in `src/_pytest/main.py` turns `KeyboardInterrupt` into `INTERRUPTED`, and `SystemExit` into `INTERNAL_ERROR` with "mainloop: caught unexpected SystemExit!".

In `src/requests/sessions.py`, `Session.prepare_request` (lines 474–476) calls `merge_cookies` twice. It first copies `self.cookies` into a fresh `RequestsCookieJar`, then adds the per-request cookies, which have already been turned into a jar by `cookiejar_from_dict`, so they win on name clashes. Without those calls, `PreparedRequest.prepare_cookies` (`models.py`) would build the `Cookie` header from only one source. Session cookies such as login or session IDs, or the request's own cookies, would be lost, so authentication that relies on cookies would fail. The digest retry in `HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401` (`auth.py:270`) reuses `prep._cookies`, so it would also lack them. On redirects, removing `resolve_redirects`' `merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies)` (line 241) would drop session cookies before `rebuild_auth` resends the request.

`CaseInsensitiveDict.__iter__` is in `src/requests/structures.py` at line 57. It returns `(casedkey for casedkey, mappedvalue in self._store.values())`. One correction to the question: the key 'Accept' isn't normalized. It is the original-case key. `__setitem__` (line 46) saves each entry in the `OrderedDict` `self._store` as `self._store[key.lower()] = (key, value)`. The lowercase "accept" is only used internally for lookups by `__getitem__` and `__delitem__`, and `lower_items()` exposes it. Iteration reads the stored `(key, value)` tuples, so it yields the key exactly as the last caller set it. In `tests/test_structures.py`, the `setup` fixture of `TestCaseInsensitiveDict` sets `["Accept"]`, so `test_list` gets `["Accept"]`. Because the dict has only one entry per lowercase key, there are no duplicates.

In `src/requests/models.py`, `PreparedRequest.prepare_body()` treats `data` as a stream when it is iterable but not a string, list, tuple or `Mapping`. A stream is sent to urllib3 unchanged as the raw body: it gets `Content-Length` from `super_len()` or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, and its `tell()` position is saved so the body can be rewound on redirect. Multipart encoding works differently. `_encode_files()` needs `data` as key/value form fields (via `to_key_val_list`), reads every file fully with `.read()`, and builds a bytes body in memory with urllib3's `encode_multipart_formdata`. An opaque generator or file object has no field name, may have no known length, and can only be read once. Merging would mean buffering it all, which defeats streaming, so requests rejects the combination with "Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive" instead of guessing.

In src/flask/ctx.py, copy_current_request_context reads the active RequestContext from the _cv_request ContextVar (defined in src/flask/globals.py) at decoration time. If there isn't one, it raises RuntimeError. Otherwise it calls RequestContext.copy(), which builds a new RequestContext with the same app, environ and request object and the current live session (self.session), rather than reloading the session from cookies. The wrapper then runs `with ctx:`, so RequestContext.push sets _cv_request (pushing an AppContext if needed) inside the greenlet's own contextvars context, and calls the function through app.ensure_sync. Because session is already set, push skips open_session, which keeps session changes. pop resets the tokens. The request object itself is shared and not thread-safe.

The lookup is in `App._find_error_handler` in `src/flask/sansio/app.py` (lines 823–846). The nesting order is not quite what the question says. First, `Scaffold._get_exc_class_and_code` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py`) gets the exception class and HTTP code. The outer loop goes over the status code: the specific code first, then `None` (line 834). The middle loop goes over the blueprint names in `request.blueprints`, then `None` for the app itself (lines 832–835), reading `self.error_handler_spec[name][c]`. The inner loop walks `exc_class.__mro__` (line 841) and returns the first handler it finds. So the status code is checked before blueprint scope, and the class hierarchy is checked last. It is called from `Flask.handle_http_exception`, `handle_user_exception` and `handle_exception` in `src/flask/app.py`.

The test `test_dotted_name_not_allowed` in `tests/test_blueprints.py` uses `pytest.raises(ValueError)` around `flask.Blueprint("app.ui", __name__)`. It does this because Flask uses the dot as its separator for blueprint names and endpoints. `Blueprint.__init__` in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py` explicitly raises `ValueError("'name' may not contain a dot '.' character.")`. Endpoints are built as `"{name_prefix}.{name}.{endpoint}"` in `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule`, nested blueprints get dotted names in `Blueprint.register`, and `url_for` and `request.blueprint` split on dots. A dotted name like "app.ui" would therefore be confused with a blueprint "ui" nested inside "app", which breaks endpoint lookup. The test checks that this guard fails early. Related tests also cover the endpoint and view-name checks in `Blueprint.add_url_rule`.

The best match is `test_blueprint_with_subdomain` in `tests/test_testing.py` (`test_subdomain` in the same file follows a similar chain). The chain starts with `Flask(__name__, subdomain_matching=True)` and the `SERVER_NAME` and `APPLICATION_ROOT` config values. Next, a `Blueprint` with `subdomain="xxx"` gets a route through `bp.route` and `app.register_blueprint`. Then `app.test_request_context("/", subdomain="xxx")` creates a `flask.testing.EnvironBuilder`, which builds the host `xxx.example.com:1234` and the base URL `/foo` from that config. That gives a `RequestContext`. When the context is pushed, `Flask.create_url_adapter` calls `url_map.bind_to_environ` with `SERVER_NAME`, and because `subdomain_matching` is on, the request matches the blueprint route. So `request.url` and `request.blueprint` are correct, and `FlaskClient.get(..., subdomain=...)` confirms the result.

The cache lives in `AssertionRewritingHook` in `src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py`. `__init__` sets `_marked_for_rewrite_cache` to an empty dict mapping module names to bools (line 81). `_is_marked_for_rewrite` (lines 248–259) returns the cached value for a name if it has one. Otherwise it checks `_must_rewrite` for an exact or parent-package prefix match, stores True or False, and returns it. Two callers use it: `_early_rewrite_bailout`, which `find_spec` runs before the expensive `PathFinder.find_spec`, and `_should_rewrite`, which `find_spec` runs after resolving the spec. So repeated imports skip the prefix scan. `mark_rewrite` adds names to `_must_rewrite` and then calls `_marked_for_rewrite_cache.clear()` (line 277), so cached answers never go stale.

`TestRequestScopeAccess` (`testing/python/fixtures.py`) sets a class-level `pytestmark = pytest.mark.parametrize(("scope","ok","error"), ...)`, which `Metafunc.parametrize` in `src/_pytest/python.py` expands into four variants each of `test_setup` and `test_funcarg`, one per scope. Each variant asks for the `pytester` fixture (`Pytester` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py`). It uses `makepyfile` to write a module with a scoped fixture that takes `request`, runs it with `inline_run("-l")`, and checks the result with `HookRecorder.assertoutcome`. In the inner run, `FixtureRequest._get_active_fixturedef` creates a `SubRequest` that carries the fixture's `Scope`. The `function`, `cls`, `module` and `path` properties on `FixtureRequest` (`src/_pytest/fixtures.py`) compare `self.scope` with the allowed scopes and raise `AttributeError` when the scope is too broad.

In `testing/code/test_source.py`, `TestAccesses.setup_class` builds one `Source` from a short string. pytest wraps it in a class-scoped autouse fixture (`_register_setup_class_fixture` in `src/_pytest/python.py`), so it runs once per class, not once per test. All five tests (`test_getrange`, `test_getline`, `test_len`, etc.) share one class attribute. `Source.__init__` splits the string and calls `deindent` (which uses `textwrap.dedent`), so the work is done once instead of five times. Sharing is safe because `Source` is immutable and `__getitem__` returns new objects. Across separate runs nothing is kept, because each run is a new interpreter and `setup_class` runs again. So the saving is tiny and the same for every run, and repeated runs do not get faster.

No hashing happens, so a dict never needs to be hashable. In `src/_pytest/python.py`, `Metafunc.parametrize` turns each value into a `ParameterSet`, and `_resolve_args_directness` marks the argument as "indirect". `CallSpec2.setmulti` then stores the original dict, uncopied, in `params[argname]` and records only its integer position in `indices[argname]`. The test ID comes from `IdMaker._idval`: a dict matches no case in `_idval_from_value`, so it becomes something like `arg0`. In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, `FixtureRequest._get_active_fixturedef` builds a `SubRequest` with `param` and `param_index`. `reorder_items` groups tests by `ParamArgKey`, which uses the index, not the value. `FixtureDef.cache_key` returns `request.param`, and `FixtureDef.execute` checks a cached result with `==`, falling back to `is` if that comparison raises. Tests: `testing/python/collect.py::test_parametrize_with_non_hashable_values_indirect`.

In `tests/test_utils.py` (lines 566–627), `@pytest.mark.parametrize("value, expected", (...))` gives the comma-separated argument names "value" and "expected". These match the parameters of `test__parse_content_type_header(value, expected)` exactly. When pytest collects the test, it unpacks each of the nine 2-tuples into those two arguments and creates a separate test item for each one (IDs like `value0-expected0`). Each item calls `_parse_content_type_header` from `src/requests/utils.py` and checks that the result equals the expected `(content_type, params_dict)` tuple. The cases cover a bare type, spaces around `;`, mixed-case `Charset`, `boundary` values wrapped in single or double quotes, a flag with no `=` (which becomes `True`), and empty segments (`"application/json ; ; "`).

TestRequests in `tests/test_requests.py` depends on the hierarchy only through its imports from `requests.exceptions`: ConnectionError, InvalidHeader, InvalidProxyURL, InvalidSchema, InvalidURL, MissingSchema, ProxyError, RetryError, SSLError, Timeout, TooManyRedirects and UnrewindableBodyError. All of these come from RequestException(IOError) in `src/requests/exceptions.py`. Its `__init__` stores `response` and `request`, which is how `test_HTTP_302_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` can check `e.request.url` and `e.response.history`. During redirects, `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` in `sessions.py` raises TooManyRedirects once `max_redirects` is reached. It also catches ChunkedEncodingError and ContentDecodingError while draining each response, and calls `utils.rewind_body`, which raises UnrewindableBodyError. For authentication, `rebuild_auth` drops credentials when the host changes. HTTPDigestAuth's `handle_redirect` and `handle_401` in `auth.py` use the `num_401_calls` counter to limit retries; they never raise errors.

In `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, `Blueprint.app_template_filter` is a decorator that calls `Blueprint.add_app_template_filter`. That method does not touch any app directly. It defines a closure, `register_template(state)`, which runs `state.app.jinja_env.filters[name or f.__name__] = f`, and stores it with `record_once`. `record_once` wraps the closure so it only runs when `state.first_registration` is true, then `record` appends it to `deferred_functions`.
