When `Flask.register_blueprint` calls `Blueprint.register(app, options)`, `make_setup_state` builds a `BlueprintSetupState` that holds the app, the options and the `url_prefix`. Each deferred function is then called with that state. The filter closure only uses `state.app`, not the prefix, so the filter lands in the app's shared Jinja environment and works in every template, whatever the URL prefix is.

The real implementation is `to_native_string(string, encoding="ascii")` in `src/requests/_internal_utils.py` (lines 25–35). `test_to_native_string` in `tests/test_utils.py` (line 712) imports the function from `requests.utils`. That module doesn't define it; it re-imports it from `._internal_utils` only for backwards compatibility, as the comment at `src/requests/utils.py:27` says. The function checks whether the input is already a `builtin_str` (imported from `requests.compat`). If it is, it returns the string unchanged. If not, it treats the input as bytes and decodes it with the given encoding, which defaults to ASCII. `models.py`, `auth.py`, `cookies.py` and `sessions.py` also import it directly from `_internal_utils`.

In src/requests/cookies.py, MockRequest.__init__ parses self._r.url with urlparse just to get the scheme. get_host parses it again on every call, and so does get_full_url whenever a Host header is set. http.cookiejar.CookieJar.add_cookie_header and extract_cookies reach these methods many times per request, often once per cookie, through the host and origin_req_host properties, request_host, eff_request_host, domain_return_ok and set_ok_domain. These run from get_cookie_header and extract_cookies_to_jar on every send and redirect. With large jars, that means the same URL is split over and over, plus repeated header lookups and urlunparse calls. Python's urlsplit cache only partly hides this cost. Because the wrapped request is treated as read-only, the fix is to parse once in __init__, store the result, and compute host and the reconstructed full URL lazily (for example with functools.cached_property). The original request stays untouched.

The decision is made in `App.add_url_rule` in `src/flask/sansio/app.py` (lines 630–651). It first collects `required_methods` from the view function. If the `provide_automatic_options` argument is None, it falls back to the view function's `provide_automatic_options` attribute, which `View.as_view` in `src/flask/views.py` sets. If it is still None, OPTIONS is added to `required_methods` and the flag is set to True only when "OPTIONS" isn't already in `methods` and `self.config["PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS"]` is on (it defaults to True in `src/flask/app.py`). Otherwise the flag is set to False. The methods are then merged, and the flag is stored on the `Rule` object. At request time, `Flask.dispatch_request` in `src/flask/app.py` checks `rule.provide_automatic_options` together with `req.method == "OPTIONS"` and returns `make_default_options_response()`.

Blueprint registration works by deferring the work and then writing into the app's single Jinja environment. In `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, `Blueprint.add_app_template_filter`, `add_app_template_test` and `add_app_template_global` (and the decorators `app_template_filter`, `app_template_test`, `app_template_global` that call them) each wrap a `register_template` closure and pass it to `record_once`. `record_once` adds it to `deferred_functions` and runs it only when `BlueprintSetupState.first_registration` is true. When `Flask.register_blueprint` calls `Blueprint.register`, each deferred function receives the setup state and writes into `state.app.jinja_env.filters`, `.tests` or `.globals`. `jinja_env` is a `cached_property` in `sansio/app.py`, created once by `Flask.create_jinja_environment` in `app.py`. Because `render_template` in `templating.py` renders through that same `app.jinja_env`, blueprint filters, tests and globals are available in every template.

The premise is mostly wrong: setting the flag on every read does not cause any extra cookie serialization or signing. In `src/flask/sessions.py`, `SecureCookieSession.__getitem__`, `get` and `setdefault` set `self.accessed = True` on each call. That is a plain instance-attribute write, so its cost per read is negligible. The expensive step is `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session`, which calls `get_signing_serializer(app).dumps(dict(session))` (an itsdangerous `URLSafeTimedSerializer` with `TaggedJSONSerializer`, then HMAC signing). That step is gated by `should_set_cookie`, which checks only `modified`, or `permanent` together with `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST`. It never checks `accessed`. The only effect of `accessed` is `response.vary.add("Cookie")`. That header can lower hit rates in downstream HTTP caches, but it does not slow down the conversion to a signed cookie string.

In `src/_pytest/python.py`, `PyCollector.isnosetest` mixes two jobs: reading `__test__` safely through `safe_getattr` from `_pytest/compat.py`, and deciding that only a value that `is True` opts an object in. The same attribute is read separately in `PyCollector.collect`, `Class.collect`, `pytest_pycollect_makeitem`, and `UnitTestCase.collect` in `src/_pytest/unittest.py`, where a falsy value opts out. I'd move the reading into one module-level helper that returns True, False or None (not set), plus small checks such as "explicitly enabled" and "not disabled" (a Strategy approach). Keep `isnosetest` as a thin wrapper (Template Method) that calls the "explicitly enabled" check. Then `istestfunction`, `istestclass`, `Module`/`Class` subclasses and plugin overrides keep working, and the "is True" protection against custom `__getattr__` stays.

The wrapping logic is in `ReprFuncArgs.toterminal(self, tw: TerminalWriter)` in `src/_pytest/_code/code.py` (lines 1458–1474). `ReprFuncArgs` is a `TerminalRepr` dataclass whose `args` field holds (name, value) tuples. For each argument, `toterminal` builds the string `f"{name} = {value}"` and adds it to a running `linesofar` buffer. The check is `if len(ns) + len(linesofar) + 2 > tw.fullwidth` (the 2 covers the ", " separator). If the next argument would go past the terminal width, it prints the buffer with `tw.line(linesofar)` and starts a new buffer with that argument. Otherwise it appends ", " plus the argument. At the end it prints whatever is left in the buffer, then a blank line.

In `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`, `FixtureFunctionMarker.__call__` runs three checks in order. First, it rejects classes with a ValueError. Second, if the function is already a `FixtureFunctionDefinition` (meaning `@pytest.fixture` was applied twice), it raises ValueError "@pytest.fixture is being applied more than once to the same function". Third, if the function has a `pytestmark` attribute, it only issues a `MARKED_FIXTURE` warning, a `PytestRemovedIn9Warning` from `deprecated.py`, and continues. The difference: an existing `FixtureFunctionDefinition` is a hard error because the function is already a fixture. `pytestmark` means `@pytest.mark.*` was applied below the fixture decorator; those marks have no effect but are tolerated as deprecated. `store_mark` in `mark/structures.py` warns about the reverse order.

TLSServer is a test helper in tests/testserver/server.py, not part of the requests library. Its `__init__` currently does everything at once: it creates `ssl.SSLContext(PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)`, calls `load_cert_chain(cert_chain, keyfile)`, and, when `mutual_tls` is set, sets `verify_mode = CERT_OPTIONAL` and calls `load_verify_locations(cacert)`. A cleaner split would use two helpers, `_load_server_identity()` and `_configure_client_verification()`, or a small SSLContextBuilder that `__init__` receives or calls. `_create_socket_and_bind` would just use the finished context. This makes contexts easier to reuse and test, allows a strict CERT_REQUIRED mode, and lets the tests in tests/test_requests.py pass prebuilt contexts. The cost is extra indirection for about ten lines, and it doesn't affect requests' runtime code.

`_body_position` needs three states, and a boolean only has two. It also has to hold the actual offset to seek back to. In `PreparedRequest.prepare_body` (`src/requests/models.py`), it stays `None` when no rewind is needed: the body isn't a stream, or the stream has no `tell()`. It becomes an integer when `body.tell()` works, which records the starting offset, so even a partly read file goes back to the right place. It becomes a unique `object()` when `tell()` raises `OSError`. In `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` (`src/requests/sessions.py`), the check `_body_position is not None` makes this failed case count as "rewindable". `rewind_body` in `src/requests/utils.py` then checks for `integer_types`, rejects the sentinel and raises `UnrewindableBodyError` instead of hanging the connection.

In `src/_pytest/main.py`, `_bestrelpath_cache` subclasses `dict[Path, str]` and is a `@dataclass` with `__slots__ = ("path",)`, where `path` is the root path. It overrides `__missing__`, so a normal `cache[path]` lookup that misses calls `bestrelpath(self.path, path)` from `src/_pytest/pathlib.py`, stores the result, and returns it. Later lookups are plain C-level dict hits with no Python call. `Session.__init__` creates it as `self._bestrelpathcache` using `config.rootpath`. `Session._node_location_to_relpath` (commented "bestrelpath is a quite slow function") just indexes into it. `Item.location` in `src/_pytest/nodes.py` calls that for every test item, and many items share the same file. So each path is computed only once, lazily, with very little overhead and no separate memoize wrapper.

It all lives in `src/requests/models.py`, in the `RequestEncodingMixin` and `PreparedRequest` classes. `requests.post` goes through `Session.request` and `PreparedRequest.prepare` to `PreparedRequest.prepare_body`. That method first checks `is_stream`; if the data is a stream and files are also given, it raises `NotImplementedError`. Otherwise, when files are present, it calls `RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data)`. That function raises `ValueError` if there are no files or if `data` is a string ("Data must not be a string."), which is what `test_conflicting_post_params` hits. If both checks pass, `utils.to_key_val_list` turns data and files into key/value pairs, each file becomes a urllib3 `RequestField`, and urllib3's `encode_multipart_formdata` builds the body and Content-Type. Bad file input, such as `files=["bad file data"]`, raises `ValueError` while it is being unpacked into pairs. Dict data avoids all of these errors.

The test in `tests/test_requests.py` builds a POST whose body is a generator. `PreparedRequest.prepare_body` in `models.py` sends that body with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. The test then fakes a 302 and calls `Session.resolve_redirects` in `sessions.py`, which uses `rebuild_method` to turn the POST into a GET. For any status other than 307 or 308, the code then removes `Content-Length`, `Content-Type` and `Transfer-Encoding` and sets `body = None` (issue #3490). If those headers stayed, the GET would claim a chunked body that is never sent. The server could wait for chunks and hang, misread the next request on a reused connection (a request-smuggling or desync risk), or get a wrong `Content-Type`. A leftover `Transfer-Encoding` would also wrongly make the `rewindable` check try to rewind a body that no longer exists.

The namespace object, `_AppCtxGlobals` in `src/flask/ctx.py`, has no locks or thread-safety code of its own. Its attribute methods and the helpers `get`, `pop` and `setdefault` just read and write its `__dict__`. Isolation comes from giving each context its own copy: `AppContext.__init__` builds a new instance with `app.app_ctx_globals_class()` and stores it as `self.g`. `AppContext.push` binds that context with `_cv_app.set(self)`, where `_cv_app` is a `ContextVar` in `src/flask/globals.py`, and saves the returned token in `_cv_tokens`; `pop` undoes this with `_cv_app.reset(token)`. The `g` object is a werkzeug `LocalProxy(_cv_app, "g")`, so every access looks up the context belonging to the current thread or async task. Two concurrent contexts never share a `g`, though code that passes one context to several threads could still race on it.

The flag is `Blueprint._got_registered_once`, a class attribute in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py` that defaults to False. `Blueprint.register()` sets it to True when the blueprint is added to an app or parent blueprint. Every method decorated with `@setupmethod` (defined in `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py`, such as `route`, `record`, `before_request` and `register_blueprint`) first calls `self._check_setup_finished(f_name)`. The Blueprint version of that check raises an AssertionError when the flag is True. This matters because registration applies the blueprint's recorded `deferred_functions` and merges its handlers into the app at that moment, so anything added later would not be applied consistently. The error therefore makes developers finish all imports, decorators and routes before registering the blueprint, instead of having later changes go missing without any warning.

In tests/test_helpers.py, test_open_resource_with_encoding is parametrized with encoding values "utf-8" and "utf-16-le". It builds a flask.Flask app with root_path=tmp_path and writes a file named "test" using that encoding. It then calls app.open_resource("test", mode="rt", encoding=encoding). This calls Flask.open_resource in src/flask/app.py (lines 330–361), where encoding is a keyword parameter that defaults to None. The method first rejects any mode other than "r", "rt" or "rb" with a ValueError. It then builds the path with os.path.join(self.root_path, resource). In "rb" mode it calls open(path, mode) and ignores encoding. In the test's "rt" mode it passes the value straight to Python's built-in open(path, mode, encoding=encoding), so the file is decoded with the same encoding it was written in.

The dependency goes one way: `evaluate_skip_marks` uses what `getitem` produces, and neither module imports the other. `Pytester.getitem` in `src/_pytest/pytester.py` creates the test item. It calls `getitems`, which calls `getmodulecol`. That writes the source with `makepyfile`, builds a configured `Config` with `parseconfigure`, gets the `Module` node with `getnode`, and then `genitems` collects the `Function` items, so `@pytest.mark` decorators are already attached. `evaluate_skip_marks(item)` in `src/_pytest/skipping.py` only needs a finished `Item`. It reads markers with `item.iter_markers("skipif"/"skip")` and calls `evaluate_condition`, which uses `item.config`, `item.ihook.pytest_markeval_namespace` and `item.obj.__globals__`. `TestEvaluation` in `testing/test_skipping.py` links the two: it builds items with `pytester.getitem` and passes them straight to `evaluate_skip_marks`, skipping the normal `pytest_runtest_setup` path.

In `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, `Blueprint.add_app_template_filter` (used by `app_template_filter`, which `tests/test_blueprints.py` tests such as `test_template_filter` call) does not register anything right away. It wraps a `register_template` closure with `record_once`, which adds it to that blueprint's `deferred_functions`. `record_once` only avoids repeats for the same blueprint object, using `state.first_registration`. Distinct blueprints share no deduplication, so `Blueprint.register` runs every closure for every blueprint. Each run writes into `state.app.jinja_env.filters`, and the first access forces `Flask.create_jinja_environment` to build the cached environment during startup. `register` also scans all of `app.blueprints` for each registration, so the total work grows roughly quadratically. Duplicate filter names are silently overwritten, so the repeated work is wasted.

The test_1 in testing/example_scripts/customdirectory/tests/test_first.py (also doc/en/example/customdirectory) is just `def test_1(): pass`. To make it data-driven, add `@pytest.mark.parametrize("value, expected", [...])` and accept those arguments, using `pytest.param(..., id=..., marks=...)`, which is backed by ParameterSet in src/_pytest/mark/structures.py. Don't give those arguments default values: Metafunc.parametrize in src/_pytest/python.py rejects names that already have a default. pytest_generate_tests calls Metafunc.parametrize to build CallSpec2 entries. PyCollector._genfunctions then creates one Function per case, named test_1[id], with originalname="test_1". So `-k test_1` and the manifest.json listing that customdirectory/conftest.py uses still work, though exact node IDs gain the [id] suffix. To keep an unchanged case, include it as one of the parameter sets.

`LocalPath` is defined in `src/_pytest/_py/path.py` (line 265). That file is pytest's vendored copy of `py.path.local`. The test `test_gt_with_strings` is in `testing/_py/test_local.py`, in class `TestLocalPath`. `LocalPath.__lt__` and `__gt__` (lines 579–583) turn both sides into strings with `os.fspath()` and compare those. `os.fspath()` returns a `str` unchanged, and for a `LocalPath` it calls `__fspath__`, which returns `self.strpath`. So a path can be compared with a string. When the string is on the left, as in `"ttt" > path2`, `str`'s comparison returns NotImplemented and Python tries the path's reflected method (`__lt__`). The same mechanism makes `sorted()` work on a list mixing paths and strings. `__eq__` also uses `os.fspath`, lowercases both sides on Windows, and returns False on TypeError. `__ne__` is its negation, and `__hash__` hashes `strpath`.

The double-close protection is only partial. In `src/requests/models.py`, `Response.__enter__` returns `self` and `Response.__exit__` just calls `Response.close()`. `close()` calls `self.raw.close()` only if `self._content_consumed` is False. That flag is set by `iter_content`'s inner `generate()` once the stream is used up, and by the `content` property. Fully read bodies are left alone, because urllib3 has already returned their connection to the pool. `close()` then always calls `raw.release_conn()` if it exists (found with `getattr`), and does not set `_content_consumed`. So a second `close()` on an unread stream calls `raw.close()` again; urllib3's `close()` and `release_conn()` are safe to repeat. Unpickled responses work because `__setstate__` sets `_content_consumed=True` and `raw=None`.

In `testing/test_assertion.py`, `TestImportHookInstallation.test_rewrite_ast` calls `register_assert_rewrite('pkg.helper')` because the automatic mechanism would never rewrite `pkg.helper`. In `src/_pytest/assertion/rewrite.py`, `AssertionRewritingHook._should_rewrite` only rewrites `conftest.py` files, files given on the command line, files matching `python_files`, and names in `_must_rewrite`. `PytestPluginManager.import_plugin` (`src/_pytest/config/__init__.py`) adds only `pkg.plugin` from `pytest_plugins` through `mark_rewrite`. `_is_marked_for_rewrite` matches only that name and its submodules, not siblings. The call sits in `pkg/__init__.py`, which runs before the helper is imported, so `mark_rewrite` doesn't warn "already imported". `pkg.other`, never registered, shows a plain AssertionError for contrast. This shows an opt-in design: rewriting happens at import time through a `sys.meta_path` hook, and only for modules on an explicit list.

In `src/requests/utils.py`, `get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=None)` passes its `no_proxy` argument to `should_bypass_proxies`. If that argument is given, it replaces the `no_proxy`/`NO_PROXY` environment variables instead of being added to them: the host/CIDR matching uses only the argument, and `set_environ("no_proxy", no_proxy_arg)` temporarily overrides the environment while `proxy_bypass` runs. So the caller's list (e.g. the `proxies["no_proxy"]` value passed in by `resolve_proxies`) wins. A non-empty dict means the URL was not bypassed, so `getproxies()` returns the environment proxies, which will be used. `test_not_bypass_no_proxy_keyword` in `tests/test_utils.py` checks this: hosts listed in the environment's `no_proxy` still go through the proxy once the keyword replaces that list.

Server is in tests/testserver/server.py, and test_testserver.py imports it. It subclasses threading.Thread. Server.__enter__ calls start(), so run() opens and binds the socket (port 0 picks a free port), then sets ready_event. __enter__ waits for that event (WAIT_EVENT_TIMEOUT) and returns (host, port). In run(), _handle_requests accepts up to requests_to_handle connections, using select so each wait is bounded. Each connection goes to the handler, its result is added to handler_results, and the socket is closed. A finally block always closes the server socket and sets stop_event. __exit__ waits for stop_event on a clean exit. On an exception it sets wait_to_close_event instead. Then it closes the socket and calls join(). This is why test_server_closes, test_multiple_requests and test_server_finishes_on_error/when_no_connections end cleanly instead of hanging.

In `src/flask/views.py`, `MethodView.__init_subclass__` doesn't pick one parent's `methods` over another's; it combines them. It first calls `super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)`. If the new class sets `methods` itself (`"methods" in cls.__dict__`), that value is kept and nothing is computed. Otherwise it builds a set: for each direct parent in `cls.__bases__` with a non-empty `methods`, it adds those values with `methods.update(base.methods)`. It then checks every name in the module-level `http_method_funcs` frozenset ("get", "post", "head", "options", "delete", "put", "trace", "patch"). Any name found with `hasattr(cls, key)`, including inherited handlers, is added in uppercase. If the set isn't empty, it becomes `cls.methods`. `View.as_view` later uses this to register the allowed methods.

The steps in `PreparedRequest.prepare()` in `src/requests/models.py` all change the same object one after another, and each step depends on what the earlier ones produced, so they can't be reordered or run in parallel. `prepare_auth()` calls `auth(self)` and then copies the result into the request with `self.__dict__.update(r.__dict__)`. Schemes like OAuth sign the final method, URL, headers and body, so the body must already be built; afterwards `prepare_content_length()` is recomputed. The code comments say auth must come last for this reason. `prepare_hooks()` must come after auth because authenticators can add hooks (for example, `HTTPDigestAuth.__call__` in `auth.py` registers `handle_401` and `handle_redirect`). My reading, not stated in the code: running user hooks last keeps them from being overwritten by the `__dict__` copy and adds them after the auth hooks.

In `tests/test_helpers.py`, the test helper class `FakePath` stands in for a `pathlib.Path` object, following the PEP 519 PathLike protocol. Its `__fspath__` method is what lets `os.fspath()` work on it, and it simply returns `self.path`. That is the plain path value given to `FakePath.__init__`, returned unchanged. In this repository, the only place it is used is `TestSendfile.test_static_file`, which calls `app.send_static_file(FakePath("index.html"))`. There, `__fspath__` returns the string `"index.html"`. The test then checks that the response's `cache_control.max_age` equals 3600, which shows that Flask's static-file sending works with path-like objects, not just plain strings.

The class is `TestUrlFor`, defined in `tests/test_helpers.py` at line 102. Each test uses the `app` and `req_ctx` fixtures and calls `flask.url_for`. `test_url_for_with_anchor` checks that `_anchor` gets percent-encoded ("/#x%20y"). Four tests cover schemes: `test_url_for_with_scheme`, `test_url_for_with_scheme_not_external` (passing `_scheme` alone makes the URL external, while `_external=False` raises ValueError) and `test_url_for_with_alternating_schemes`. `test_url_with_method` registers a `flask.views.MethodView` subclass, `MyView`, on several rules and uses `_method="GET"`/`"POST"` to pick which URL is built. `test_url_for_with_self` checks that a URL argument can be named `self`.

In tests/test_async.py, AsyncMethodView subclasses flask.views.MethodView and only defines `async def get` and `async def post`. It doesn't need its own async dispatch because MethodView already handles both kinds of handler. MethodView.__init_subclass__ builds `methods` from whichever HTTP-verb methods the class defines, whether they are sync or async. MethodView.dispatch_request in src/flask/views.py looks up the handler for request.method (falling back from HEAD to get) and calls it through current_app.ensure_sync(meth). Flask.ensure_sync in src/flask/app.py checks iscoroutinefunction and wraps coroutine functions with async_to_sync (asgiref), so they run inside the synchronous WSGI flow. View.as_view also wraps dispatch_request in ensure_sync. Async support therefore lives in one place in the app, and the test checks that the normal class-based view path supports async handlers without a separate async class.

`RunAndParse` in `testing/test_junitxml.py` mostly delegates rather than doing the work itself. It receives a `Pytester` and an already-built `xmlschema.XMLSchema` through its constructor. The session-scoped `schema` fixture builds that schema once from `example_scripts/junit-10.xsd`, so the class never loads or compiles it. `__call__` adds `-o junit_family=...` to the arguments and runs `pytester.runpytest(--junitxml=junit.xml)`. Only for "xunit2" does it pass the file to `self.schema.validate`. It parses with `minidom.parse` and returns a `(RunResult, DomDocument)` pair, leaving queries and assertions to the `DomDocument`/`DomNode` wrappers and `assert_attr`. The `run_and_parse` fixture provides the callable, so tests never handle running, validation or parsing directly.

There isn't really a named architectural pattern here. In `testing/test_argcomplete.py`, the separation comes from duck typing plus a module-level helper used for differential testing. Both completers are plain callables that take a prefix and return a list of completions. `FastFilesCompleter` lives in `src/_pytest/_argcomplete.py` and uses `glob`, `os.path.isdir` and prefix stripping. The test file's own `FilesCompleter` was copied from argcomplete to avoid the fd-9 import side effect, and it calls bash `compgen` through `_wrapcall` (`subprocess.check_output`). The function `equal_with_bash(prefix, ffc, fc, out)` holds the comparison logic: it calls both, compares the results as sets and prints the differences. `TestArgComplete.test_compare_with_compgen` asserts that they agree, and `test_remove_dir_prefix` asserts that they differ, so either side can change on its own.

`Response.links` (a property in `src/requests/models.py`, around lines 983–997) reads the "link" header and passes it to `parse_header_links` in `src/requests/utils.py`. That function splits the header on `, *<` and returns a list of dicts, one per link, keeping the original order. `links` then loops over that list and stores each dict in `resolved_links` under `link.get("rel") or link.get("url")`. If several entries share the same rel, there is no merge, list or warning: each later entry silently overwrites the earlier one, so only the last one survives. The lookup is a single O(1) dict access, but the result loses data, and its size equals the number of distinct keys, not the number of links. A rel like "next last" is not split, so it becomes one key.

The tests in `testing/test_assertion.py::TestImportHookInstallation` check whether modules get rewritten when they are first imported. That makes them depend on interpreter-wide state. `install_importhook` in `src/_pytest/assertion/__init__.py` puts an `AssertionRewritingHook` at the front of `sys.meta_path`, driven by `Config._consider_importhook` and `_mark_plugins_for_rewrite` in `src/_pytest/config/__init__.py`. Running inline would reuse the parent's `sys.modules` (for example, `pytester` and `conftest` modules that are already imported), its hook, and its `--assert` mode, so the result would be wrong. A fresh process gives clean `plain` versus `rewrite` behaviour. `test_installed_plugin_rewrite` goes further and uses `pytester.run(sys.executable, "mainwrapper.py")` to patch `importlib.metadata.distributions` before `pytest.main()` runs. The cost is that results can only be checked from outside: `fnmatch_lines` on stdout (for example `*assert 10 == 30*` versus `E AssertionError`), `assert_outcomes`, or `result.ret`. Checks on internals such as `rewrite_hook._must_rewrite` or `find_spec` must be written as assertions inside the generated test files.

The flow is `request.applymarker` → `node.add_marker` → `NodeKeywords` → `request.keywords`. In the conftest, the class-scoped autouse fixture `marking` gets a `SubRequest` (src/_pytest/fixtures.py) and calls `FixtureRequest.applymarker`. That method calls `self.node.add_marker`. `Node.add_marker` (src/_pytest/nodes.py) writes `keywords["XYZ"]` and appends to `own_markers`. Because `test_fun1` and `test_fun2` are module-level functions, `get_scope_node` finds no `Class`, so `SubRequest.node` falls back to `_pyfuncitem`, the test item itself. Autouse names are added first to each item's fixture closure, so `marking` is set up before the `keywords` fixture. That fixture returns `request.keywords`, which is the item's `NodeKeywords` (src/_pytest/mark/structures.py). `FixtureDef.execute` registers `finish` with `request.node.addfinalizer`, so `SetupState` tears `marking` down after each test and reruns it for the next. That rerun is how every test gets the marker.

The test method in tests/test_utils.py (TestIsValidCIDR.test_invalid, lines 288–299) has no branches of its own. It just asserts `not is_valid_cidr(value)`. All the branching happens in is_valid_cidr in src/requests/utils.py (lines 709–730). "8.8.8.8" fails the `string_network.count("/") == 1` check and goes to the else branch, which returns False. "192.168.1.0/a" makes `int()` raise ValueError, which is caught and returns False. "192.168.1.0/128" and "192.168.1.0/-1" fail the `mask < 1 or mask > 32` range check. "192.168.1.999/24" makes `socket.inet_aton` raise OSError, which is caught and returns False. Each value therefore reaches a different early `return False`.

In `src/requests/exceptions.py`, `HTTPError` directly subclasses `RequestException`, which subclasses `IOError`. Its sibling `ConnectionError` (with `ProxyError`, `SSLError` and `ConnectTimeout` below it) also subclasses `RequestException`. `RequestException.__init__` stores `request` and `response`. The two branches are raised in different places. `HTTPAdapter.send` in `adapters.py` turns urllib3 failures (`ProtocolError`/`OSError`, `MaxRetryError`, `ClosedPoolError`, `_SSLError`, `ReadTimeoutError`) into `ConnectionError`, `ConnectTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `SSLError`, `ProxyError` or `RetryError`, and none of these carries a response. `HTTPError` comes only from `Response.raise_for_status` in `models.py`, for 4xx/5xx statuses, with `response=self` attached. `Response.ok` catches it. Callers can catch `RequestException` for every failure, or catch `HTTPError` (which has a response to inspect) separately from `ConnectionError`/`Timeout` (no response) to choose retries or fallbacks.

In `src/requests/adapters.py`, `BaseAdapter` is a plain class that implicitly inherits from `object`. It only defines `send()` and `close()`, which raise `NotImplementedError`. Its `__init__` calls `super().__init__()` even though its only parent is `object`, because this keeps the class safe for cooperative multiple inheritance. `super()` follows the method resolution order (MRO) of the actual subclass, not `BaseAdapter`'s own parents. So when a user's adapter mixes `BaseAdapter` or `HTTPAdapter` with other classes, such as mixins or other base classes, every class's `__init__` in the chain still runs. `HTTPAdapter.__init__` does the same by calling `super().__init__()`. This is the cooperative `super()` pattern, combined with a template-method interface that leaves the framework open for extension.
